en: In the subsequent section, the sages said: "The creation of Svāyambhuva has been correctly described by you."
The extent of this cosmic egg and the determination of the Manvantaras [are here explained].

In that regard, you have described the Lord of Lords as one who is to be constantly worshipped by those wearing the marks of religious students (varṇin), who are devoted to dharma and intent upon the yoga of knowledge.
In the same way, may we behold that supreme knowledge which has Brahman as its sole object—the unsurpassed destroyer of all the miseries of saṃsāra. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.1.3)
For you, O Lord, have directly obtained all-encompassing wisdom from Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself; therefore, we question you once again regarding that reality.
Having heard those words of the sages and remembering the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Sūta, the reciter of the Purāṇas, began to speak.
Then, O best of sages, Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself arrived at that place where they were performing the sacrificial session.
Seeing that Vyāsa, the knower of the Vedas, who possessed the luster of a dark cloud and lotus-petal eyes, those foremost of the twice-born bowed down to him.
Seeing him, Romaharṣaṇa fell prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then, having circumambulated his teacher, he stood by his side with palms joined in reverence.
Having been asked about his well-being by the great sage, those brahmins, headed by Śaunaka,
comforted him and prepared for him a seat suitable for that occasion.
Then the Lord, the son of Parāśara, spoke these words to them:
"I hope there has been no loss of your austerity, nor of your private Vedic study, nor of your sacred learning?"
Then that charioteer, having bowed to his own guru, the great sage, said:
"O Sage, you ought to speak that knowledge concerning Brahman which belongs to the sages."
"For these sages are peaceful ascetics devoted to dharma;
a desire to serve them has arisen in me. You ought to speak to them according to the truth."
This divine knowledge that bestows liberation, which was spoken by you to me in person,
was previously proclaimed by the sages and by Viṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise.
Having heard the words of the Sūta, the sage who is the son of Satyavatī bowed his head to Rudra and spoke these comforting words.
Vyāsa said:
I shall declare that which the god Mahādeva himself spoke in the past when questioned by the lords of yogins,
headed by Sanatkumāra.
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and likewise Sanandana;
Aṅgiras together with Rudra, and Bhṛgu, the knower of the supreme dharma.
Kaṇāda, the yogi Kapila, the great sage Vāmadeva,
Śukra, and the venerable Vasiṣṭha— all of them possessed restrained minds.
Deliberating with one another, their minds possessed by doubt,
they performed severe penance at the sacred hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
Then they beheld that great yogin, the pure son of Dharma,
Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end, together with Nara.
Having praised him with various hymns originating from the Vedas, all those yogis, filled with devotion, bowed down to the foremost knower of yoga.
Having understood their desire, the Blessed One, the omniscient one, spoke with profound words: "For what purpose do you perform this ascetic penance?"
With joyful minds, they spoke to the eternal Soul of the Universe,
the god Nārāyaṇa himself, who had arrived as a sign of their spiritual perfection.
We have all fallen into doubt, O expounders of Brahman;
we have sought refuge in you alone, the Supreme Person.
For you alone know that supreme [truth], O Blessed One,
the omniscient Ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa himself, the ancient, unmanifest Puruṣa.
"O Supreme Lord, there exists no other knower than you;
we desire to hear [your teaching], for you ought to sever all our doubts. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.1.25)
What is the cause of this entire world? Who is it that perpetually transmigrates?
Is there a self, and what is liberation? What is the cause of saṃsāra?
Who is the Lord who causes transmigration, or who perceives everything?
What is that supreme Brahman? You ought to tell us all of this.
When this had been said, the sages beheld the Supreme Person, who,
having abandoned his ascetic form, stood there by his own splendor.
The god was resplendent, stainless, adorned with a circle of light,
bearing the Śrīvatsa on his chest, and possessing the luster of refined gold.
A man who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, with the Śārṅga bow in his grasp and surrounded by Śrī,
is not seen even at that very moment due to the splendor of that very [deity].
In that interval, Mahādeva, the Great Lord Rudra, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, appeared, facing [the gods] with favor.
Having beheld the Lord of the World, the three-eyed one adorned with the moon, they praised that Supreme Lord with joyful minds and devotion. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.1.32)
Victory to you, O Īśvara, Great God! Victory to you, O Śiva, Lord of Beings!
Victory to you, Sovereign of all sages, who are fully honored by ascetic penance!
O thousand-formed one, universal self, driver of the machine of the world;
victory to you, O Ananta, the cause of the creation, protection, and destruction of the universe!
O Lord of the thousand-footed, O Śambhu, worshipped by the lords of yogins!
Victory to you, O Lord of Ambikā! O God, salutations to you, O Supreme Lord! (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.1.35)
The Lord Īśvara Tryambaka, who is compassionate toward his devotees and has been praised,
embraced Hṛṣīkeśa and spoke with a profound voice.
"For what purpose, O lotus-eyed one, have these lords of sages, exponents of the Veda, gathered in this region? Or what task is there for me to perform, O Acyuta? (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.1.37)
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, Janārdana, the God of gods,
spoke to Mahādeva, who stood before him with a face turned toward grace.
For these sages, O God, are ascetics whose impurities have been exhausted;
desiring right vision, they have come to me for refuge.
If the Blessed One is pleased, you ought to speak here that divine knowledge in the presence of me and of the sages whose selves are purified.
For you alone know your own self, O Śiva, for no other exists;
therefore, by means of yourself, reveal the Self to these lords of sages.
Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, beholding the bull-bannered god, spoke to the foremost of sages while demonstrating his yogic power.
"By the very sight of Maheśa, Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident,
you ought to know yourselves to have truly achieved your purpose."
"You ought to question the Lord of All, who stands here visibly before you;
in my very presence, he is capable of speaking exactly as it is."
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu and having bowed to the bull-bannered Lord,
those headed by Sanatkumāra questioned Maheśvara.
Then, in that interval, a certain divine, stainless, and auspicious seat,
inconceivable and worthy of the Lord, appeared from the sky.
There the creator of the universe, whose essence is yoga, arrived together with Viṣṇu;
filling the entire world with his splendor, the god Maheśvara shone forth.
The exponents of the Veda beheld him, Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, shining brilliantly upon that stainless throne.
Those established in yoga behold within their own self the Self as the Lord;
indeed, they perceive Him who is of non-dual splendor, peaceful, and auspicious.
They beheld, it is said, that Lord of beings seated upon his throne, from whom the origin of all creatures proceeds and into whom they are dissolved.
They beheld, it is said, that Lord Vāsudeva seated there, within whom all this exists and from whom this entire world is non-different.
Being questioned, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord of sages,
spoke after gazing at the lotus-eyed one [Viṣṇu] regarding his own unsurpassed yoga.
Listen, O sinless ones, with all your minds tranquil, to this knowledge spoken by the Lord as it is being declared by me according to the rule. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.1.53)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Song of the Lord," in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, a compendium of sixty thousand verses. The Lord said:
This knowledge is inexpressible, the eternal secret of the Self, which even the twice-born gods do not fully comprehend despite their striving. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.1)
Relying upon this knowledge, the best of the twice-born, having become Brahman, do not enter into saṃsāra; so too did those who expounded Brahman in the past.
I shall today declare to you, who are devoted and seekers of Brahman, that which is more secret than the secret, to be concealed with effort even from direct perception.
The Self alone exists—absolute, self-abiding, tranquil, subtle, and eternal;
it is the inner witness of all, manifest as pure consciousness, beyond darkness.
"He is the Inner Controller, He is the Puruṣa, He is Prāṇa, He is Maheśvara;
He is Time, He is Fire, He is the Unmanifest—He alone is all this," so says the Śruti.
From this the universe is born, and into this very same place it dissolves.
That wielder of māyā, bound by māyā, creates various bodies.
Nor does this Lord transmigrate, nor cause others to transmigrate;
he is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space.
Neither the vital breath, nor the mind, nor the unmanifest, nor sound, nor even touch; neither form, taste, nor smell; neither am I the agent, nor even speech. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.8)
O best of the twice-born, it has neither hands nor feet, nor anus, nor the organ of generation;
it is neither the agent nor the enjoyer, nor is it primordial nature (prakṛti) or the individual soul (puruṣa);
from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is neither illusion (māyā) nor even pure consciousness (caitanya).
Just as a relationship between light and darkness is not possible,
so too oneness is not a relationship between the phenomenal world and the Supreme Self.
Just as in the world shadow and sunlight are mutually distinct,
so too, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the phenomenal world and the Puruṣa are separate.
If the self were by its very nature impure, unwell, and subject to change, it could not attain liberation even in hundreds of future births. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.12)
The disciplined sages perceive their own self from the perspective of ultimate reality as free from transformation, devoid of suffering, consisting of bliss, and imperishable.
The notion that "I am the doer, happy, miserable, thin, or fat" is projected by people onto the self due to the agency of the ego (ahaṅkāra). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.14)
Those learned in the Vedas declare him to be the witness beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the enjoyer, the imperishable, the pure, and established equally everywhere. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.15)
Therefore, the cycle of existence for all embodied beings is rooted in ignorance;
from ignorance arises false knowledge, and that is conjoined with primordial nature (prakṛti).
The supreme Puruṣa is eternally risen, self-luminous, and all-pervading;
yet, through the non-discrimination of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), he conceives "I am the doer."
The seers, proponents of Brahman, having understood Pradhāna— also called Prakṛti— to be the cause, perceive it as the unmanifest, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being.

For this reason, although this Self is immutable and stainless, being thus associated with [the body], it does not realize its own nature as the imperishable Brahman in accordance with reality. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.19)
The cognition of a self in what is not-self, and from that, suffering and its opposite; all defects such as passion and hatred are rooted in delusion. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.20)
If this [self] were subject to action, there would be the fault of merit and demerit; such is the established rule.
It is solely by the power of that [action] that the arising of all bodies for all beings occurs.
The Self is indeed eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects;
it is one, yet it appears divided through power—that is, through *māyā*—and not by its own nature.
Therefore, the sages declare that non-duality alone is the ultimate reality;
duality, by its very nature, is manifest, and it rests upon the self of Māyā.
Just as the sky does not become soiled by contact with smoke,
the Self is not tainted by the states arising from the internal organ.
Just as a pure crystal shines by its own radiance when alone,
so too does the stainless Self manifest when free from limiting adjuncts.
The wise declare that this world is of the very nature of consciousness;
the ignorant, however, those of perverted vision, perceive it as being of the nature of external objects.
By its very nature, the Self is immutable, devoid of qualities, all-pervading, and of the essence of consciousness;
yet it is perceived by persons of deluded vision in the form of objective objects. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.27)
Just as a pure crystal is perceived by people as being red due to the proximity of a red object such as a hibiscus flower, so too is the Supreme Person perceived.
Therefore, the Self— which is imperishable, pure, eternal, omnipresent, and undecaying—
should be worshipped, reflected upon, and heard by those seeking liberation.
When consciousness shines eternally and universally within the mind,
then it is spontaneously attained by the yogi without obstruction.
When one perceives all beings within one's own self, and one's own self within all beings, then one attains Brahman. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.31)
When one established in samādhi perceives no beings at all,
having become one with the Supreme, then he becomes absolute.
When all the desires that dwell in his heart are completely released,
then this wise man, having become immortal, attains the state of security.
When one perceives the diversity of beings as situated in the One,
and likewise perceives their expansion from that very source, then one attains Brahman.
When one perceives the self as absolute from the perspective of ultimate reality,
and the entire world as mere illusion, then one becomes liberated.
When the exclusive realization of Brahman arises, which is the sole remedy for birth, old age, suffering, and disease, then one becomes Śiva.
Just as in the world rivers and streams attain oneness with the ocean,
so too does this self attain oneness with the partless Imperishable.
Therefore, only consciousness exists; there is neither phenomenal proliferation nor cyclic existence.
The world is shrouded by ignorance, and because of that, consciousness is deluded.
That knowledge which is stainless, subtle, free from conceptual construction, and imperishable is true knowledge;
all else is ignorance—this is my conviction. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.39)
This supreme Sāṃkhya, the highest knowledge, has been declared to you;
for it is the essence of all Vedānta, and Yoga therein is one-pointedness of mind.
From yoga, knowledge is born; from knowledge, yoga proceeds.
For one who is devoted to both yoga and knowledge, there is nothing that cannot be attained anywhere.
That which the practitioners of Yoga attain is reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya as well;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one is a knower of reality. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.42)
Furthermore, other yogis and brahmins whose minds are attached to sovereign power sink right there and then; for such is the Vedic revelation: "The Self does not belong to them. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.43)
That which is all-pervading, divine, sovereign, immovable, and great—
one who is devoted to the yoga of knowledge shall attain it at the end of the body.
This Self is I, the unmanifest, the illusory Lord Supreme;
He is celebrated in all the Vedas as the Soul of All, whose face is turned in every direction.
I am all desires, all tastes, and all fragrances; I am ageless and immortal.
I am he whose hands and feet are everywhere, the eternal inner controller.
Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; dwelling within the heart, though without eyes I see, and likewise, though without ears I hear.
"I know all this, yet no one knows me;
those who perceive the truth call me the one Great Puruṣa. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.48)
The seers, who perceive the subtle, behold the cause of the Self—
that supreme sovereignty which belongs to Him whose form is devoid of qualities and stainless.
"That which the gods do not understand, being deluded by my *māyā*, I shall declare; listen with concentrated minds, O exponents of Brahman. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.50)
"I am not the ruler of all, for by my very nature I transcend illusion;
nevertheless, I impel this [universe]. The wise know this to be the cause."
Those yogins who have entered my most secret body, which is all-pervading for those who perceive reality,
attain my imperishable union (sāyujya).
For those who have come under the power of my illusory energy (*māyā*), which possesses all forms,
they attain supreme purity and *nirvāṇa* together with me.
O lords of yogis, through my grace there is no returning for them even in hundreds of millions of kalpas; this is the instruction of the Vedas.
This knowledge spoken by me, which rests upon Sāṃkhya and Yoga, must not be given by those who discourse on Brahman to anyone other than a son, a disciple, or a yogin. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.2.55)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Īśvaragītā* of the *Uparivibhāga* within the *Śrī Kūrmapurāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses. The Lord said:
From the unmanifest arose time, the primal matter (pradhāna), and the supreme person (puruṣa);
from these all this was born, therefore the world consists of Brahman. (KūrmP 2.3.1)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
and with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading everything.
It manifests as the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all senses;
it is the support of all, eternally blissful, unmanifest, and free from duality.
It is devoid of all comparison, beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition,
free from conceptual construction, without appearance, the abode of all, and the supreme nectar.
The wise know that supreme space to be non-differentiated, yet possessing differentiated forms; eternal, constant, and imperishable; devoid of qualities—that is true knowledge. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.5)
He is the Self of all beings; He is both the external and the internal, the Supreme.
I am He—the omnipresent, peaceful, conscious Self, the Supreme Lord.
By me, whose form is unmanifest, this entire universe is pervaded;
all beings abide in me—he who knows that is a knower of the Veda. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.7)
Pradhāna and Puruṣa are declared to be the two fundamental principles;
Time, which is beginningless, is said to be their supreme uniter.
This triad, which is without beginning or end, is established within the Unmanifest;
it is of that nature, yet distinct from it—know that to be my own form.
That which brings forth the entire universe, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa),
is designated as Prakṛti, the deluder of all embodied beings.
For the Puruṣa, abiding in Prakṛti, experiences the qualities derived from Prakṛti;
because he is free from egoism (ahaṅkāra), he is called the twenty-fifth.

The first transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) is called the Great Self (mahān-ātman); it is indeed the power of consciousness and the knower. From that arises the ego (ahaṅkāra). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.12)
The one and only Great Self is designated as the ego (ahaṃkāra); it is celebrated by those who contemplate reality as the individual soul (jīva) and the inner self (antarātman). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.13)
Through that, he experiences all pleasure and pain throughout his births;
he is of the nature of consciousness, and the mind serves as his instrument.
Therefore, due to that lack of discrimination, the cycle of worldly existence arises for the person;
and that lack of discrimination arose in time from attachment to Prakṛti.
Time creates all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
All are subject to the power of Time; Time is not subject to anyone's power.
That eternal one, the Lord, the omniscient Puruṣottama, who is called Prāṇa, governs all this from within. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.17)
The wise say that the mind is superior to all the senses;
the ego-sense is superior even to the mind, and the Great Principle (mahat) is superior to the ego-sense.
Beyond the Great One is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa;
beyond the Puruṣa is the Blessed Prāṇa, whose this entire world is.
Space is higher than the vital breath; the Lord Agni transcends space.
I am He—the omnipresent, peaceful, omniscient Supreme Lord.
There is no being higher than Me; by knowing Me, one is liberated. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.20)
For there is nothing eternal in this world, whether moving or stationary, except for me alone—the unmanifest Maheśvara, whose form is like space. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.21)
Thus, as a god who is both the wielder of illusion and composed of illusion, united with Time, I create and perpetually withdraw the entire world.
"In my presence, this Time (Kāla) creates the entire universe;
indeed, the Infinite Self (Anantātman) ordains it—this is the teaching of the Vedas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.3.23)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Lord's Song," in the latter section of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, a compendium of sixty thousand verses. The Lord said:
I shall speak; listen with concentrated minds, O exponents of the Veda, to the majesty of the God of gods, by whom this [universe] is set in motion.
For I cannot be known by men through various austerities, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice, except through unsurpassed devotion.
"For I, the all-pervading, abide within all beings;
yet the world does not know me, the witness of all, O lords of sages. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.3)
He within whom all this exists, who indeed is the supreme one within all— he am I,
the supporter and the ordainer, Time, Fire, and the one whose face is in every direction.
Neither do all the sages, nor the inhabitants of the three heavens, nor Brahmā, nor the Manus, nor Śakra, nor any others of renowned power, behold me.
The Vedas constantly proclaim me alone as the Supreme Lord;
the Brāhmaṇas worship Agni with various Vedic sacrifices.
All the worlds pay homage to him; Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, and the yogis meditate upon the God, the Lord, the sovereign of all beings.
For I am indeed the consumer of all oblations and the bestower of their fruits;
having become the body of all the gods, I am the self of all, abiding in everything.
The wise, the righteous, and those who proclaim the Vedas behold me here;
I am eternally present before them who worship me with devotion.
Brahmins, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas who are righteous worship me;
to them I grant that station, the state of supreme bliss. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.10)
Others as well— those of low birth such as Śūdras and so forth who abide in improper occupations—
are liberated through time when they become devoted and united with me.
My devotees do not perish; my devotees are freed from all taint.
This was declared by me at the outset: "My devotee does not come to ruin."
The fool who indeed censures him censures the God of gods;
for he who honors him with devotion always honors me.
Whoever, being self-restrained, offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water for the sake of my worship, that devotee of mine is considered dear to me. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.14)
For at the beginning of the worlds, having created Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, I bestowed upon him all the Vedas issued forth from my own self.
For I alone am the imperishable teacher of all yogins;
I am the protector of the righteous and the slayer of those who hate the Vedas.
I am indeed the liberator from all saṃsāra for yogins here;
yet I am the very cause of saṃsāra, while being myself devoid of all saṃsāra.
For I alone am the destroyer, I am the creator, and I am the protector; I am the wielder of illusion (māyā), whose power is Māyā that deludes the world. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.18)
And my own supreme power, which is celebrated as "Vidyā," I—
abiding in the hearts of yogis— destroy Māyā by means of it.
For I am the initiator and the withdrawer of all powers;
I am the support of them all and the repository of immortality.
The one all-pervading power,
consisting of mind and presided over by me, creates the manifold world by assuming the form of Brahmā.
And another vast power of mine establishes the universe,
having become the infinite Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the world, who consists of the world.
The third is the great power that destroys the entire universe;
it is declared to be my tamasic aspect, known as Time (Kāla), and having the form of Rudra.
Some perceive me through meditation, others through knowledge;
others through the yoga of devotion, and still others through the yoga of action. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.24)
Of all devotees indeed, he who constantly worships me with knowledge and not otherwise is my desired one, my dearest. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.25)
And those other three types of devotees who desire to worship me—
they too certainly attain me and do not return again.
This entire universe, consisting of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), is pervaded by me;
the whole world is established in me alone, and the universe is impelled by me.
"O Brahmins, I am not the impeller; having resorted to the supreme yoga, I impel this entire world. He who knows this is immortal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.28)
I see all this, without exception, existing by its own nature;
the Lord Time himself acts as the Great Master of Yoga.
In the scriptures on Māyā, the wise proclaim that Yoga is the Yogin;
he is the Lord of Yoga, the Blessed One, Mahādeva, the Great Master.
The greatness of all principles is proclaimed as belonging to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) because he is the highest; the Blessed Brahmā is the Great One, consisting of Brahman and stainless.
Whoever knows me thus as the Lord of the Great Lords of Yoga is joined by non-conceptual yoga; of this there is no doubt.
Thus I am the impelling deity, established in supreme bliss;
as a yogi, I dance eternally—he who knows that is a knower of the Veda. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.4.33)
Thus, this most secret knowledge, established in all the Vedas,
should be given to one whose mind is serene, who is righteous, and who maintains the sacred fires.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Īśvaragītā* within the latter section of the glorious *Kūrmapurāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the supreme lord of yogins,
danced, manifesting the supreme state of the Lord.
They beheld that Lord, the supreme treasury of splendors,
Mahādeva, dancing with Viṣṇu in the stainless sky.
The yogis of restrained mind, who know the reality of yoga,
beheld that Lord of all beings in the sky, so it is said.
He whose entire nature consists of illusion, by whom this world is impelled,
the Lord of All, is indeed seen dancing by himself before the Brahmins.
They beheld that Lord of Beings, who was indeed dancing, by remembering whose lotus feet a person abandons the fear born of ignorance. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.5.5)
He whom those who are sleepless, who have conquered their breath, who are tranquil and endowed with devotion perceive as consisting of light— that yogi is indeed seen.
They beheld in the sky that very Rudra, the supreme liberator, who is gracious and affectionate toward his devotees, and who swiftly releases one from ignorance.
The god with a thousand heads, whose form has a thousand feet,
who possesses a thousand arms, who wears matted hair, and who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Wearing a tiger skin, with a great hand resting upon a trident,
holding a staff in his hand, having the three Vedas as his eyes, and possessing the sun, moon, and fire as his eyes.
Enveloping the entire universe with his own splendor, he remained there—
terrible with fangs, invincible, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.

They beheld the Lord, the sovereign Viśvakarman, who was both within the cosmic egg and outside the egg, both external and internal, the supreme one; they saw him dancing, emitting flames of fire and consuming the entire world. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.5.11)
To Mahādeva, the great yogin, the deity even of the gods,
the Lord of creatures, the Sovereign, the imperishable light of lights.
To the wielder of the Pināka bow, the large-eyed one, the medicine for those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence,
the soul of time, the death of Death, the God of gods, Maheśvara.
The Lord of Umā, the three-eyed one, supreme and consisting of the bliss of yoga,
the abode of knowledge and dispassion, the eternal yoga of knowledge.
He possesses eternal sovereignty and glory, is the support of Dharma, and is difficult to approach;
he is bowed to by Mahendra and Upendra, and is worshipped by the hosts of great sages.
The support of all powers, the Lord of the great lords of yoga,
the supreme Brahman of the yogis, praised by the yoga of the yogis,
dwelling in the hearts of the yogis, and enveloped by the illusory power of yoga. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.5.16)
In an instant, the exponents of Brahman beheld Nārāyaṇa, the source of the world and free from affliction, who had attained oneness with Īśvara.
Having beheld that divine form consisting of Rudra and Nārāyaṇa,
the virtuous exponents of Brahman considered themselves to have achieved their life's purpose.
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Bhṛgu, Sanātana, and Sanandana;
Rudra, Aṅgiras, Vāmadeva, and Śukra.
The great seers are Atri, Kapila, and Marīci.
Then, having seen Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, whose left side is occupied by Padmanābha,
and having meditated upon him as residing within the heart, he prostrated with his head.
Having again placed their joined palms upon their own heads.
Having uttered the syllable *oṃ* and beheld the God established within the cave of the body,
they praised him with words consisting of Brahman.
Their minds were fully pervaded by bliss.
The sages said: You alone are the one Lord, the ancient Puruṣa,
the Master of Prāṇa, Rudra, and infinite Yoga.
We all bow to the one who is seated within the heart,
the wise one, consisting of Brahman, and pure.
The sages— self-controlled, tranquil, and stainless— behold you, the source of Brahman, golden-hued and immovable,
abiding within their own bodies through meditation.
The poet [is superior] to others, and he is supreme and even beyond that.
From you is born the progenitor of the universe; you, who have become the self of all, have become the supreme atom—
smaller than the small and greater than the great.
The virtuous declare that you alone are everything.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the inner self of the universe, the ancient Puruṣa, was born from you;
being brought forth by you, he came into existence.
He created everything in its entirety according to the prescribed injunctions.
From you all the Vedas have issued forth;
in you alone they find their final resting place at the end.
We behold you as the cause of the universe.
Dancing within his own heart, he is seated there.
By you alone is this wheel of Brahma set in motion; you are the master of illusion and the sole lord of the worlds.
We bow to you, having come to you for refuge.
The self of yoga, the Lord of Consciousness, the divine dance.
We behold you dancing in the midst of the supreme ether; we remember your majesty,
the self of all, who is established in manifold ways.
Having experienced the bliss of Brahman again and again.
The syllable *oṃ* is your designator; you are the seed of liberation, the imperishable one whose form is hidden within primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
therefore, the virtuous here proclaim you as the Truth.
That radiance of yours is self-luminous.
All the Vedas constantly praise you; the sages, whose defects have been extinguished,
whose souls are tranquil, and who are devoted to truth, bow down to you, the most excellent one.
Ascetics established in Brahman enter into you.
The single Veda, with its many branches and infinite extent,
reveals only You alone in Your singular form; those who have sought refuge in You, the object of all knowledge—
For them there is eternal peace, but not for others.
The Lord of Bhavānī, the beginningless mass of splendor, Brahmā, the Supreme Being, the most excellent of all,
rests, having experienced the bliss of his own self.
He is self-luminous, immovable, and eternally liberated.
You alone are Rudra; you create this universe here, and as the universal form, you protect it in its entirety;
at the end, this world finds its dissolution in you alone.
We bow to you, having fully sought refuge in you.
They call you alone the one Seer, the one Rudra,
the vital breath, the Great One, the Green One, Agni, the Lord,
Indra, Death, the Wind, and the All-knowing.
The creator Āditya, who possesses manifold forms.
You are the supreme imperishable to be known;
you are the ultimate refuge of this universe;
you are the undecaying protector of the eternal dharma.
You are eternal; you are the Supreme Person.
You alone are Viṣṇu, you are the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are Rudra, the Lord and Sovereign;
you are the navel of the universe, primordial nature, and the firm foundation.
You are the Lord of all; you are the Supreme Lord.
They speak of you alone as the one ancient Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun beyond darkness, pure consciousness, unmanifest, and of inconceivable form.
Space is Brahman, the void, primordial nature, and devoid of qualities.
That within which all this shines,
which is imperishable, stainless, and of a single form—
this form of yours is something inconceivable.
That which appears within that interval is the reality.
We all, seeking refuge, bow down to you— the Lord of Yoga, Rudra, of infinite power, the supreme goal, whose body is Brahman, and who is pure.
Be gracious, O Lord of Beings, O Maheśa!
By recollecting your lotus feet,
restraining the mind, and composing the body, the entire seed of saṃsāra goes to destruction.
We propitiate this one Lord alone.
Homage be to you, Bhava, the source of existence, to Kāla, to Sarva, to Hara;
homage be to you, Rudra, the one with matted hair.
Homage to Agni, O God; homage to Śiva! KūrmP_2,5.41.
Then that blessed Lord, the god with matted hair whose vehicle is the bull,
having withdrawn his supreme form, Bhava returned to his natural state.
Having seen the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the master of the past and the future, established there as before, they were struck with wonder and spoke these words.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, whose teaching is marked by the bull,
O Eternal One, having beheld your supreme form, we have attained peace.
By your grace, O stainless Supreme Lord, may there arise within us an unwavering devotion directed toward you alone. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.5.45)
Now we wish to hear, O Śaṅkara,
once again your greatness and the eternal true nature of you, the Supreme Lord.
Having heard the words of those yogins, he who bestows the perfections of yoga looked upon Mādhava and spoke with a profound voice.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Lord's Song," in the latter section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, a compendium of sixty thousand verses. The Lord said:
Listen, all you sages, to the greatness of the Supreme Lord exactly as it is; I shall declare that which those who know the Vedas understand.
I am the eternal Self of all, the sole creator of the entire world, the sole protector of the entire world, and the sole destroyer of the entire world.
I am indeed the inner controller and the father of all things;
everything exists within me, yet I do not abide everywhere.
"O Brahmins, that wonderful form of mine which you have seen is indeed a likeness of me, displayed by me through my illusory power (māyā)."
Abiding within all beings, I impel the entire world; this is my power of action.
That by which this entire universe acts and which follows its own inherent nature—that I am, as Time; I impel the whole world, which consists of the constituent parts (kalās).
"O best of sages, I make the entire world as one part;
I withdraw it in a single form—these two states are indeed my own."
Free from beginning, middle, and end, the instigator of the principle of illusion (māyātattva),
I stir both Pradhāna and Puruṣa at the commencement of creation.
From those two, joined with one another, the universe is born in the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (mahat); thus my splendor unfolds.
For even he who is the witness of the entire world, the setter in motion of the wheel of time,
Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sun— He too was born from my body.
O twice-born ones, at the beginning of the kalpa, he bestowed upon him his own divine sovereignty and the eternal yoga of knowledge, as well as the four Vedas, which are his own offspring.
At my command, the god Brahmā, permeated by my own nature,
himself perpetually bears that divine sovereignty of mine.
That creator of all the worlds, the omniscient one,
having become four-faced by my command, creates the emanation born from himself.
Even Nārāyaṇa, who is Ananta, the source and the imperishable of the worlds, is my own supreme form; he performs the task of protection.
"He who is the ender of all beings, Rudra, the Lord whose nature is Time—
he shall, by my command, constantly withdraw my body."
The Fire-god carries the oblation to the gods and the ancestral offering to the consumers of such offerings;
he also performs the act of cooking, impelled by my power.
And by the command of the Lord, the blessed fire Vaiśvānara digests all kinds of food that have been eaten day and night.
Even Varuṇa, the preeminent among the gods and the source of all waters,
can only revive the entire world by the command of the Lord alone.
That god Prabhajana, who dwells within all beings and without them,
indeed sustains the bodies of beings by my command.
Even that Soma, who restores life to men and is the source of nectar for the gods,
is said to exist impelled by my command.
He who, by his own radiance, eternally illuminates the entire world—
the Sun pours forth rain through the very teaching of the Self-Existent One.
Even he who is the teacher of the entire world, Śakra, the lord of all the immortals,
and the god who bestows the fruits of sacrifices— he exists by my command.
For he who acts here as the punisher of the wicked according to the rules is the god Yama, son of Vivasvat, by the command of the God of gods.
Even he who is the superintendent of all wealth and the bestower of riches— he too,
Kubera, always exists by the command of Īśvara.
He who is the lord of all *rakṣasas* and the bestower of fruits upon those characterized by darkness— that god Nirṛti always remains in office by my command.
The lord of the hosts of Vetālas and Bhūtas, the bestower of the fruits of enjoyment,
Īśāna himself indeed remains here at my command for the sake of his devotees.
He who is Vāmadeva, the disciple of Aṅgiras and the leader of the hosts of Rudras—
he remains as the eternal protector of yogins by my command.
And even he who is worshiped by the entire world, the creator of obstacles,
the leader Vināyaka, the guide of the Dharma— he too, it is said, [shall obey] at my word.
Even he who is the best among the knowers of Brahman, the lord and commander of the divine armies,
Skanda, remains ever present, being himself the Self-born, impelled by the sacred law.
And those lords of creatures, the great seers such as Marīci and others,
create the manifold world by the very command of the Supreme Being.
And she who bestows abundant prosperity upon all beings— she,
the consort of Nārāyaṇa, remains here through my grace.
And that goddess Sarasvatī, who bestows vast speech,
also proceeds when impelled by the command of Īśvara.
The goddess Sāvitrī, who obeys the command of the gods, when remembered, will deliver all men without exception from the terrible hell.
The supreme goddess Pārvatī, the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman,
who is especially meditated upon— she too follows my word.
Even he who possesses infinite majesty, the infinite Śeṣa, the lord of all the immortals,
bears the world upon his head by the command of the God.
That fire which is eternally the Saṃvartaka, existing in the form of the submarine mare (Vaḍavā),
drinks up the entire ocean by the command of the Lord.
And those fourteen Manus of renowned power who protect all the subjects in this world, they too do so by his command.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and likewise the two Aśvins,
as well as all other deities, are established by my teaching alone.
Gandharvas, Garuḍas, bears, Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas, abide in the scripture of the Self-Existent One.
The units of time— kalās, kāṣṭhās, nimeṣas, muhūrtas, days, nights,
seasons, fortnights, and months— are established in the scripture of Prajāpati.
Yugas, manvantaras, and even further periods of time—parārdhas and other such divisions of time—remain within my teaching. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.6.41)
The four kinds of beings, both stationary and moving,
exist solely by the command of the Lord, the Supreme Self.
By the command of the Self-born One, all the netherworlds, all the worlds,
and all the cosmic eggs indeed exist.
By my command, even the countless Brahmāṇḍas of the past proceeded on all sides, accompanied by floods of material objects.
The cosmic eggs, together with the objects contained within them,
shall always carry out the command of the supreme Self.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect,
and likewise the source of the elements— the primordial nature— abide in my command.
Māyā, the source of all worlds and the deluder of all embodied beings, perpetually undergoes transformation by the command of the Lord.
That supreme Puruṣa who is indeed proclaimed as the God of embodied beings is the Self;
he exists eternally by the command of the Lord.
That knowledge by which one perceives that state after shaking off the turbid mire of delusion is itself subject to the command of the Great Lord.
What is the use of saying more here? This entire world, which consists of my own power, is impelled by me alone; it shall go to dissolution in me alone.
For I am the Blessed One, the Lord, the self-luminous, the eternal;
I am the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, and nothing other than me exists.
This supreme knowledge has been declared to you by me;
having known it, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and the cycle of existence. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.6.52)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Lord's Song," in the latter section of the venerable *Kūrma Purāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The Lord said:
Listen, all you sages, to the power of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
knowing which a person, being liberated, shall not fall again into the cycle of worldly existence.
Higher than the highest is Brahman—eternal, partless, and fixed;
it is perpetual bliss, free from conceptual construction; that is my supreme abode. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.7.2)
Among those who know Brahman, I am Brahmā, the self-existent one whose face is turned in every direction;
among masters of illusion, I am the ancient and imperishable Lord Hari.
Among yogis I am Śambhu; among women, the goddess born of the Lord of Mountains;
among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; and among the Vasus I am Pāvaka.
Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among those who fly, I am Garuḍa;
among the lordly elephants, I am Airāvata; and among the wielders of weapons, I am Rāma.
Among the sages I am Vasiṣṭha, and among the gods I am Śatakratu;
among artisans I am Viśvakarman, and among the enemies of the immortals I am Prahlāda.
Among the sages, I am Vyāsa; among the hosts, I am Vināyaka;
among heroes, I am Vīrabhadra; and among the perfected ones, I am the sage Kapila.
Among mountains I am Meru; among the stars I am the moon;
among weapons I am the thunderbolt; and among vows I am truth.
Ananta is the god of the serpent-beings, and Pāvaki is the lord of the army commanders;
the householder’s stage of life is the foremost among the stages of life, and Maheśvara is the lord of all sovereigns.
Among the great eons, I am the Kṛta age; among the ages, I am the Kṛta; among all Yakṣas, I am Kubera; and among the lords of the Gaṇas, I am Vīraka. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.7.10)
Among the Prajāpatis, I am Dakṣa; among all the Rākṣasas, I am Nirṛti;
among the powerful, I am Vāyu; and among the islands, I am Puṣkara.
Among the lords of beasts I am the lion, and among machines I am the bow;
among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda, and among the Yajus formulas I am the Śatarudriya.
Among all that is to be muttered, I am the Sāvitrī; among secret things, I am the Praṇava; among hymns, I am the Puruṣasūkta; and among the Sāmans, I am the Jyeṣṭhasāman. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.7.13)
Among those who know the meaning of all the Vedas, I am Manu Svāyambhuva;
among countries, I am Brahmāvarta; and among sacred fields, I am Avimuktaka.
Among sciences, I am the science of the Self; among forms of knowledge, I am the supreme sovereign wisdom.
Among beings, I am the ether; and among living creatures, I am death itself.
Among snares, I am illusion; among those who reckon time, I am Time;
among goals, I alone am liberation; and among the supreme lords, I am the Supreme Lord.
And whatever other being there may be in this world that possesses superior splendor and strength, recognize all of that as the manifestation of my own power.
"All souls dwelling in the cycle of transmigration are declared to be 'beasts' (paśu);
I am their Lord, O God, and am thus remembered by the wise as Paśupati."
"By my own play, I bind these bound souls (paśus) with the noose of Māyā; the exponents of the Vedas declare me alone to be the liberator of the bound souls. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.7.19)
For those bound by the snare of Māyā, no other liberator is found except me,
the Supreme Self, the imperishable Lord of all beings.
The twenty-four principles—māyā, karma, and the guṇas—are the fetters of Paśupati; they are the afflictions that bind the bound souls (paśus).
Mind, intellect, ego, ether, air, fire, water, and earth—
these are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), as well as the other transformations (vikāras).
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is considered the tenth. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.7.23)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell—
these twenty-three principles (tattvas) are indeed derived from primordial nature (prākṛta).
The unmanifest Pradhāna, characterized by the [three] Guṇas, consists of twenty-four principles;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, and is the supreme cause of the universe.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas). Their state of equilibrium is known as the unmanifest (avyakta) primordial nature (prakṛti).
Sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance, and rajas is declared to be a mixture;
the wise know that the diversity [of the world] arises from the imbalance of these qualities (guṇas) within the intellect (buddhi).
"Dharma and adharma are declared to be the two bonds known as fetters; actions dedicated to me lead to liberation, not to bondage. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.7.28)
They say that ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the clinging to life—
known as the afflictions— are the unshakable nooses that bind the self.
Of these very bonds, Māyā is said to be the cause;
she is the unmanifest root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), that power which abides within me.
He alone is the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), the primary matter (pradhāna), and the person (puruṣa);
he is also the transformations beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), the eternal God of gods.
He alone is bondage, and he is the creator of bondage; he alone is the fetter, and he alone is the bound soul.
He knows everything, yet there is no knower of him.
Him they call the foremost, the ancient Person.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Lord's Song," in the latter section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, a compendium of sixty thousand verses. The Lord said:
O best of Brahmins, I shall declare another most secret knowledge, by which a living being crosses the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.8.1)
"I am composed of Brahman, peaceful, eternal, stainless, and immutable; I am declared to be the solitary Lord, the absolute Supreme Sovereign."
My womb is the Great Brahman; therein I place the seed.
That which is called Māyā is the root, and from it this world is born. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.8.3)
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Ātman, Mahat,
and Bhūtādi likewise gave birth to the subtle elements (tanmātras), the gross elements (mahābhūtas), and the sense organs.
From that, a golden egg arose, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
within it was born Mahābrahmā, empowered by my own Śakti.
And all those other many living beings who consist of my own nature do not see me as their father, being deluded by my illusory power (māyā).
Whatever forms indeed arise in all wombs, Māyā is their supreme source; they know me alone as their father.
He who understands me thus as the seed-giver, the father, and the lord—
that wise man does not fall into delusion in any of the worlds.
I am the Lord of all sciences, the Supreme Lord of all beings, the Blessed One whose form is the syllable Oṃ, Brahmā, the Progenitor of creatures. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.8.9)
He who sees the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings,
remaining undestroyed when they are destroyed— he truly sees.
For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy oneself by means of oneself; therefore, one attains the supreme goal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.8.11)
Having understood the seven subtle elements and Maheśvara with his six limbs,
one who knows the application of the primary cause (pradhāna) attains the supreme Brahman.
Having understood that the All-pervasive One possesses omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal unimpaired power,
and infinite power;
They say there are six limbs of Maheśvara.
The subtle elements, the mind, and the self— these seven, consisting of the principles (tattvas), are said to be subtle;
that which is the cause, Prakṛti, is Pradhāna.
By that [method], the binding (bandha) and the application (viniyoga) are also proclaimed.
That power which is said in the Vedas to be of a latent nature within primordial matter (prakṛti), the cause, the source of Brahman—
beyond that is the one Parameṣṭhin.
Maheśvara is the Puruṣa, whose nature is truth.
Brahmā, the yogi, the Supreme Self, the most exalted, pervading the sky, known through the Vedas, the ancient one;
the one Rudra, death, and the one unmanifest.
The seed is the universe; he alone is the one God.
Others speak of that very one as manifold; some likewise say that the single Self is otherwise.
He is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
He is called Mahādeva by those who know the Vedas.
Thus, he who knows the Supreme Lord dwelling in the cave of the heart— the ancient Puruṣa of universal form,
the golden one, the supreme goal of the wise— [attains Him].
That wise one stands transcending wisdom itself.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Song of the Lord," in the Upper Division of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
The Supreme Lord is partless, stainless, eternal, and actionless;
tell us that, O Mahādeva: how is it that you possess a universal form?
The Lord said:
"I am not the universe, nor does the universe exist apart from me, O twice-born ones. There is here the cause of illusion (māyā), and that rests upon the Self."
Power (śakti) is without beginning or end; it rests upon Māyā and the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Indeed, this phenomenal world (prapañca), caused by that [power], arose from the Unmanifest.
They call the unmanifest the cause, bliss, light, and the imperishable;
I alone am the supreme Brahman, for nothing else exists apart from me.
Therefore, my possession of manifold forms has been ascertained by the exponents of Brahman;
this illustration has been declared regarding both unity and diversity.
"I am that supreme Brahman, the eternal Supreme Self;
O twice-born ones, I am declared to be without cause, for there is no defect in the Self."—Kūrma Purāṇa 2.9.6.
Infinite powers, beginning with Māyā, abide eternally within the Unmanifest;
situated in that celestial realm, the Unmanifest shines forth perpetually as the absolute.
By these [powers], that which is differentiated is perceived, yet it is non-different by its very nature;
through one [of them], there is my eternal union, which is without beginning or end.
For the person, manifestation occurs through one [state] and concealment through another;
indeed, it is said that he who stands without beginning or middle is joined with ignorance.
This is that supreme, manifest [reality], adorned with a circle of light;
it is the imperishable, supreme light, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
In that [Brahman], this entire world is woven as warp and woof;
and by knowing that the whole world is indeed that [Brahman], one is liberated.
When words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind—having known that bliss which is Brahman, one fears nothing whatsoever. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.9.12)
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness;
having realized that, the wise man is completely liberated.
Having become one with Brahman, he becomes eternally blissful.
Since there is nothing beyond it, nothing else whatsoever, that one which is the light of lights situated in heaven—
the wise man, considering himself as that very [light], is then enlightened.
Having become Brahman, he becomes one who rejoices in the Self.
The Brahmins established in Brahman describe it thus: as that which is imperishable, dense, with its body hidden, the immortal bliss of Brahman, and the abode of the universe.
Having gone there, one shall not return again.
In the golden supreme principle of space, that splendor which shines forth as if within its radiance—
that the wise perceive within their own realization.
The stainless, radiant abode of the sky.
Beyond that, the wise perceive the Self within themselves, experiencing it again and again;
he is self-luminous, the supreme abode, the most exalted.
This Lord Īśa is the bliss of Brahman.
The one God is hidden in all beings,
all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
those wise ones who perceive Him as the one alone— [they become immortal].
For them there is eternal peace, but not for others.
The Blessed One has all faces, heads, and necks; he dwells in the secret cave of all beings;
and the Blessed One is all-pervading—nothing else is desired beyond him.
Thus, O best of sages, this divine knowledge has been declared to you;
it must be kept strictly secret, for it is difficult even for yogins to obtain.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Lord's Song," in the upper section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses. The Lord said:
The single, unmanifest, and signless is determined to be Brahman;
it is the supreme reality, self-luminous, established in the highest ether.
That which is the unmanifest cause, the imperishable, the supreme state,
devoid of qualities and pure consciousness— that indeed the wise perceive.
Those who are devoted to that, whose intentions are stilled, and who are constantly permeated by its nature, behold that Supreme Brahman which is the Liṅga; such is the Śruti.
Otherwise, O best of sages, it is indeed impossible to see me;
for that supreme knowledge by which I am known does not exist [among mortals]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.10.4)
This alone is that supreme knowledge which the seers know as absolute;
everything else is ignorance, since the world consists of illusion.
"That knowledge which is stainless, subtle, free from conceptual construction, and imperishable—
wise men declare that this alone is my very self."
Even those who perceive many things also see that Supreme,
having realized the one imperishable reality and being established in the highest consummation.
Furthermore, those who perceive me with devotion as the supreme reality— whether as one or as many, or as the Lord— they should be known as being of that very nature.
They perceive their own self directly as the Supreme Lord—eternal bliss, free from conceptual construction, and the very form of reality; such is the established truth. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.10.9)
Established in their own self, peaceful, and situated in the supreme unmanifest, they partake of that supreme bliss which is all-pervading and of the nature of the Self.
This is my supreme liberation, the highest union;
the wise know it as Nirvāṇa, oneness with Brahman, and absolute isolation (kaivalya). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.10.11)
Therefore, there is one supreme reality, devoid of beginning, middle, or end, which is the most auspicious;
he is Īśvara, the Great God, and by knowing him, one is liberated. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.10.12)
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon, nor the stars; there the lightning does not flash, nor does the fire.
By its light alone, this entire universe shines eternally.
That shines forth as eternally luminous, immovable, and real.
That which shines forth as eternally risen, free from conceptual construction, pure, vast, and supreme—
that is the eternal inner reality for those who know Brahman.
He who perceives the immovable reality is the Lord.
All the Vedas declare that the Puruṣa is eternal bliss, immortal, the embodiment of truth, and pure;
they describe that very Lord as "this is He" by means of the Praṇava.
Those who have ascertained the meaning of the Vedic texts cause others to hold [it] fast.
Neither earth, nor water, nor mind, nor fire;
neither breath, nor wind, nor space, nor even intellect;
neither consciousness nor anything else exists within the midst of the supreme ether.
The Lord shines forth as Śiva alone, the absolute.
Thus has been declared this supreme secret,
the nectar of knowledge hidden within all the Vedas;
the yogi knows it in a solitary place.
One should indeed practice yoga constantly, being self-restrained.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Lord's Song," in the latter section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The Lord said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the yoga that is most difficult to attain, by which they behold the Self as the Lord, resplendent like the sun. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.1)
The fire of yoga quickly burns away the entire cage of evil;
clear knowledge arises, which directly bestows the attainment of nirvāṇa. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.2)
From yoga arises knowledge, and from knowledge yoga proceeds;
for one who is devoted to both yoga and knowledge, Maheśvara becomes gracious.
Those who here apply themselves to my yoga once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or constantly at all times, should be known as Maheśvaras.
Yoga should be known to be of two kinds: the first is considered non-existence (abhāva), while the other is Mahāyoga, the most excellent among all yogas.
That in which one's own nature is contemplated as empty and entirely free from appearances is declared to be the yoga of non-existence, by means of which one perceives the Self.
When one perceives the Self as eternal bliss and stainless,
and [perceives] identity with Me— that is declared by the Supreme Lord to be Mahāyoga.
And whatever other yogas of yogis are heard of in the extensive scriptures,
they are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the yoga of Brahman.
Where they behold the Lord as the universe directly, being liberated—
this is considered the supreme yoga among all yogas.
Those who have been excluded by the Lord, whether by the thousands or by the hundreds—
even those yogins with restrained minds— do not behold me alone.
Breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā),
and absorption (samādhi), O best of sages, as well as restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and posture (āsana).
The practice of one-pointedness of mind toward you occurs through the cessation of other mental fluctuations;
indeed, the eight means for accomplishing that have been taught to you.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—
these are briefly declared to be the restraints (yamas) that bestow purity of mind upon human beings.
The supreme sages have declared that non-violence consists in never causing distress to any living being, at any time, through action, mind, or speech.
There is no dharma higher than non-violence; there is no happiness higher than non-violence.
Indeed, violence that is performed according to the prescribed rule is proclaimed to be non-violence itself.
Through truth one attains everything; everything is established in truth.
Speaking according to reality is what has been declared as truth by the twice-born.
The theft of another's property, whether by stealth or by force, is *steya* (theft);
refraining from that is *asteya*, a means of achieving dharma. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.17)
The renunciation of sexual intercourse in all places, at all times, and in all circumstances—whether by deed, mind, or speech—is declared to be *brahmacarya*. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.18)
The non-acceptance of material objects even when they are encountered at will is called non-possession (aparigraha); one should protect that with great effort.
Austerity, self-study, contentment, purity, and worship of the Lord—
these are briefly declared to be the observances (niyamas) that bestow the perfections of yoga.
Ascetics declare that the emaciation of the body through fasting, the parāka penance, the kṛcchra, the cāndrāyaṇa, and other such rites, constitutes the highest austerity.

The wise declare that the recitation of the Vedānta, the Śatarudrīya, the Praṇava, and so forth, constitutes the study of one's own sacred texts (svādhyāya), which brings about the purification of the inner being for men. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.22)
Those who know the meaning of the Vedas declare that there are three divisions of private Vedic recitation— vocal, whispered, and mental— and that each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
That which clearly generates verbal comprehension for others who listen is declared to be *vācika* (oral) recitation; now follows the definition of *upāṃśu* (whispered).

That which makes another understand the sound through the mere movement of the lips is designated as the "whispered" (upāṃśu) recitation; it is a thousandfold more effective than the vocal (vācika) recitation.
That mental recitation which, through its connection with the syllables of the sacred word, is devoid of physical vibration and consists of the contemplation of all sounds— that they know as *japa*.
The sages have declared that contentment, characterized by happiness, is that disposition of a person which considers what is obtained by chance to be always sufficient.
O best of the twice-born, purity is said to be twofold: external and internal.
External purity is traditionally defined as cleansing with earth and water, while internal purity is the purification of the mind.
Devotion to Śiva that is perfectly steady through the acts of speech, mind, and body— namely, praise, remembrance, and worship— this is the worship of the Lord.
The restraints (yamas) along with the observances (niyamas) have been declared; now learn of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Prāṇa is the wind produced within one's own body, and āyāma is its restraint.
This [practice] has been established as threefold according to whether it is superior, inferior, or middling;
that very same [practice] is declared to be twofold: with embryo (sagarbha) and without embryo (agarbha).
A slow breath-retention consists of twelve *mātrās*, a medium breath-retention consists of twenty-four *mātrās*,
and the best breath-retention consists of thirty-six *mātrās*.

The production of perspiration, trembling, and rising [from the seat] occurs respectively for those who are inferior, middling, and superior; yet that which arises from bliss is the most excellent of all.
The wise say that *sagarbha* (with seed-syllable) is accompanied by recitation (*japa*), while *agarbha* (without seed-syllable) is without recitation (*vijapa*).
This indeed is declared to be the definition of *prāṇāyāma* for yogins.
One should recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyahṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath;
that is called Prāṇāyāma.
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka),
and retention (kumbhaka) are declared in all the scriptures as prāṇāyāma by yogis who strive with disciplined minds.
Recaka is from constant exhalation; pūraka is from its restraint;
that which remains in equilibrium is celebrated as kumbhaka.
O most excellent ones, the wise declare that the restraint of the senses as they naturally roam among their objects is indeed called *pratyāhāra*. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.38)
In the lotus of the heart, at the navel, or on the summit of the head, and in such locations as these, *dhāraṇā* is the binding of the mind. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.39)
The wise know that meditation to be the continuous flow of the activity of the intellect, which, based on its abiding in a single object, remains unmixed with other activities.
Concentration would be of a single form, devoid of place and object;
for the condition consisting of the mere object is the supreme means for achieving yoga. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.41)
Dhāraṇā consists of twelve breath-retentions (āyāmas);
dhyāna consists of twelve dhāraṇās; and when dhyāna reaches twelve [units], it is designated as samādhi.
The postures known as svastika, padma, and likewise ardha-āsana are declared;
among all practices for accomplishment, this is the supreme means of accomplishment. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.43)
O best of Brahmins, having placed both soles of his feet upon his thighs, he sat down;
this is the supreme lotus-seat of the Self.
Then, O best of beings, placing one foot upon the other thigh, one should sit;
this is the "half-seat" posture, the supreme means for achieving yoga.
Having placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, one should sit; this is declared to be the supreme *svastika* posture for oneself.
Indeed, the visualization of yoga is not possible at an improper place or time,
whether near fire, in water, or likewise upon a heap of dry leaves.

In a cremation ground infested with creatures, in a dilapidated cow-pen, at a crossroads, or in a place that is noisy or terrifying, or at a shrine, an anthill, or a heap of refuse; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.48.

One should not practice in an impure place, one infested by wicked people, or one filled with mosquitoes and the like; nor when there is physical affliction, or when mental distress and the like arise.
In a well-concealed and very beautiful place, such as a mountain cave,
on the bank of a river in a sacred region, or likewise in a temple of the gods.
In a house that is very beautiful and delightful, or in a secluded place free from living beings,
the yogi, devoted to me, should constantly apply himself to yoga.
Having paid homage to the lords of yogis along with their disciples, to Vināyaka,
and to his own guru as well as to me, the yogi should then practice yoga with a well-composed mind.
Having assumed the *svastika*, the *padma*, or even the *ardha* posture,
one should fix the gaze evenly on the tip of the nose with the eyes slightly opened.
Then, having become fearless and tranquil, and having abandoned the world consisting of illusion,
one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, the God who is established within one's own self.
Then, having visualized a lotus at the tip of the crest-lock twelve finger-breadths long— a beautiful lotus with the Dharma as its root and wisdom as its stalk— KūrmP_2,11.55.

One should meditate upon the supreme treasure-chest, white and possessing eight petals of sovereignty, with supreme detachment as its pericarp; within that pericarp, one should contemplate the golden [chest].
They call him directly the embodiment of all power, divine and imperishable;
he is the unmanifest denoted by the syllable Om, pervaded by a network of rays.
Therein, one should contemplate the stainless, supreme, imperishable light;
having placed one's own self within that light through non-duality with it.
One should meditate upon the Lord, the supreme cause, situated in the midst of space;
then, having become that Self which pervades all, one should not think of anything at all.
This is the most secret meditation; now the intermediate meditation is described:
having contemplated the previously mentioned supreme lotus within the heart.
Then, one should perceive the Self as the agent therein, possessing a brilliance equal to fire,
appearing in the midst like a flame of fire— the twenty-fifth Puruṣa.
One should contemplate the Supreme Self within that [space], as the supreme sky, the reality awakened by the syllable Oṃ—eternal, auspicious, and immutable. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.62)
The unmanifest, merged within primordial nature (prakṛti), is the supreme, unsurpassed light;
within that is the ultimate reality, the stainless support of the self.
Having purified all the principles (tattvas), one should constantly meditate, becoming absorbed in that single form of Maheśvara, or alternatively, by means of the syllable *praṇava*.
Having established the self within me, in the stainless, supreme state,
and having bathed one's own body with that very water of knowledge— Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.65.
Having become identified with me and absorbed in me, one should take the ashes produced from the *agnihotra* sacrifice;

then, having smeared all the limbs with them while reciting the mantra beginning with "Agniriti," one should contemplate within one's own self the Lord (*Īśāna*), whose nature is the supreme light. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.66)
This is the Pāśupata Yoga for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu);
this is the essence of all Vedāntas, according to the Śruti which calls it "the state beyond the stages of life" (atyāśrama).
This most supreme secret, which brings about union with me,
has been declared for the twice-born who are devoted and observe the vow of celibacy.
Celibacy, non-violence, forbearance, purity, austerity, self-control,
contentment, truthfulness, and faith— these are especially the constituent parts of the vow.
If even one [of these] is lacking, his vow is violated;
therefore, only one endowed with personal virtues is fit to bear my vow.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me,
many have been purified by this yoga and have attained my own state.
"In whatever way people approach me, in that same way do I reward them;
therefore, one should worship the Supreme Lord through the yoga of knowledge. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.72)
Alternatively, being ever pure, one should worship me with the yoga of devotion, with supreme detachment, and with a mind endowed with awakening.
Having renounced all actions, subsisting on alms and free from possessions, one attains union with me; this secret has been declared by me.
He who is free from hatred toward all beings, who is friendly and compassionate,
devoid of the sense of "mine" and free from egoism— he who is my devotee is dear to me.
The yogi who is always contented, self-controlled, and firm in resolve;
he whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me.
He by whom the world is not agitated and who is not agitated by the world, who is free from joy, envy, fear, and anxiety— he indeed is dear to Me.
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, indifferent, devoid of distress,
who has renounced all undertakings, and who is full of devotion— he is dear to me.
One who regards praise and blame as equal, who observes silence, who is content with whatever comes,
who has no fixed abode, whose mind is steady, and who is devoted to me— that devotee shall come to me.
Even while constantly performing all actions, one who has me as their supreme refuge attains,
through my grace, the eternal, highest state.

Having surrendered all actions to Me with the mind, regarding Me as the Supreme, and becoming free from desire and free from the sense of "mine," one should take refuge in Me alone. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.81)
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent,
one is not bound at all by action even while fully engaged in it.
With the mind and self free from desire, having renounced all possessions,
and performing action solely for the sake of the body, one attains that state.
For one who is content with what is obtained by chance and has indeed transcended the pairs of opposites,
performing action for the sake of my grace brings about the destruction of saṃsāra.

With mind fixed on me, offering salutations to me, sacrificing to me, and having me as his supreme goal—knowing me to be the Supreme Lord, that yogi shall come unto me, the Lord of Yoga. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.85)
Those whose intellects are fixed on me, constantly awakening one another regarding me and always speaking of me, shall attain union with me.
Thus, for those who are constantly devoted, I destroy this entire darkness consisting of the succession of karma through the radiant lamp of knowledge.
Those people here who, with their minds fixed on me, constantly worship me—
for those who are ever-devoted, I provide for their acquisition and preservation.
And those others who sacrifice to other deities for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures— for them,
that fruit which follows from the deity should be known as finite.
And those who are devotees of other deities and worship the gods here,
if they are endowed with the contemplation of me, they too are liberated through their inner disposition.
Therefore, having completely abandoned all other gods who are not the Supreme Lord, one should take refuge in me alone as the Lord; he goes to the supreme state.
Having abandoned affection for sons and others, free from sorrow and without possessions,
one who is dispassionate should worship the Supreme Lord at the *liṅga* until death.
To those who always worship the *liṅga*, having renounced all enjoyments without exception,
I grant supreme sovereignty within a single lifetime.
The Liṅga, which consists of supreme bliss, is absolute, stainless, composed of knowledge, all-pervading, and resides in the hearts of yogins. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.94)
And those other devoted ones who are fixed [in their resolve], having meditated according to the prescribed rule,
worship Maheśvara with that very liṅga wherever it may be.
Whether in water, in the midst of fire, in the sky, in the sun, or elsewhere,
such as in a gemstone, one should meditate upon the Lord and worship the Īśvara-liṅga.
For all this is indeed composed of the *liṅga*, and all is established within the *liṅga*;
therefore, one should worship the Lord in the *liṅga* eternally, wherever it may be.
For those who perform ritual actions, [the Liṅga] is in fire; for the wise, in water, in the sky, or in the sun;
for the ignorant, in wood and such things; but for yogis, the Liṅga is in the heart.
If one whose consciousness is unarisen is dispassionate and endowed with joy, he should,
being disciplined, recite the Praṇava— the very body of Brahman— for as long as life lasts.
Alternatively, a twice-born man who, solitary and with his mind and self restrained, recites the Śatarudrīya until death, attains the supreme state.
If a Brahmin dwells with a concentrated mind in Vārāṇasī until death,
he too, by the grace of the Lord, goes to that supreme state.
For at the time of departure from this world, [the Lord] bestows that supreme knowledge upon all embodied beings, by which they may be liberated from bondage.
One who, being devoted to Me, performs the entire code of duties pertaining to the social classes and stages of life,
attains knowledge in that very birth and goes to the auspicious state.
O twice-born ones, even those who dwell there— whether they be lowly or of sinful birth— all cross over saṃsāra through the grace of the Lord.
But obstacles will arise for those whose minds are afflicted by sin;
therefore, O twice-born ones, one should certainly take refuge in Dharma for the sake of liberation.
This secret of the Vedas must not be given to just anyone;
it should be imparted only to one who is righteous, devoted, and a celibate student.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One [Brahmā] declared his unsurpassed self-yoga to the seated Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction.
This knowledge has been spoken by me for the benefit of those who discourse on Brahman;
may you bestow this auspiciousness upon disciples whose minds are tranquil.
Having spoken thus to the lords of yogins, O best of the twice-born, the unborn Lord then spoke for the benefit of all his devotees among the twice-born.
"Indeed, by my command, you all shall also impart my knowledge to your devoted disciples according to the prescribed ritual."
"This Nārāyaṇa is I, the Lord; there is no doubt about this.
This supreme [teaching] should be given to those who perceive no difference between us. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.111)
This is my supreme form, called Nārāyaṇa;
it abides as the self of all beings, peaceful, and designated as the Imperishable (akṣara).
But those people in the world who perceive otherwise, possessing a vision of duality, do not truly see me; they are born again and again.
But those who behold this Viṣṇu, the unmanifest, or me, the god Maheśvara, as being one in essence— for them there is no further rebirth.
Therefore, behold me alone as Viṣṇu, the imperishable Self, without beginning or end; and likewise, worship me indeed.
Those who perceive me otherwise, thinking me to be a separate deity, go to terrible hells; I am not established among them.
Whether he be a fool or a scholar, a Brahmin or one who takes refuge in me, even an outcaste dog-cooker—I liberate him; but not the reviler of Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, this great yogi, the supreme person, should indeed be worshipped and saluted by my devotees for the sake of generating my pleasure.
Having spoken thus and embraced Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow vanished even as all of them were looking on.
The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa also assumed the supreme garb of an ascetic,
having indeed cast aside his own transcendent form for the sake of all yogins.
By the grace of the Supreme Lord, you have directly realized that stainless knowledge of Maheśvara which destroys the cycle of worldly existence.
Go forth, all of you, free from fever; O lords of sages, cause the supreme knowledge of the Parameṣṭhin to be imparted to your righteous disciples.
This divine knowledge should be given to one who is devoted, tranquil, righteous, and maintains the sacred fires— especially to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having spoken thus, that Soul of the Universe, Nārāyaṇa, the great yogi and the foremost among yogis who know yoga, himself vanished from sight.
Having paid homage to Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods,
and to Nārāyaṇa, the source of all beings, they also returned to their own respective abodes.
The blessed Sanatkumāra, the great sage Saṃvarta, imparted the sovereign knowledge; he, in turn, gave it to Satyavrata.
Sanandana, the lord of yogis, gave it to the great seer Pulaha;
then Pulaha, the progenitor, gave it to Gautama.
Aṅgiras gave it to Bharadvāja, who was learned in the Vedas;
likewise, Kapila gave it to Jaigīṣavya and to Pañcaśikha.
Parāśara, my father, who perceives all principles, obtained this supreme knowledge from Sanaka; from him, Vālmīki received it.
Long ago, the god Vāmadeva—the great yogi, Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who was born from the body of Satī—spoke to me. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.130)
The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the son of Devakī,
himself personally bestowed this supreme [teaching] upon Arjuna.
