Since I obtained from Rudra Vāmadeva this unsurpassed [teaching],
from that time forth I have possessed a special devotion toward Giriśa.
I have especially sought refuge in Rudra, the protector worthy of refuge—
the Lord of Beings, the one praised by speech, the immovable Sthāṇu, the God of gods, who bears the trident.
Therefore, you too, along with your wives and sons, should take refuge in that auspicious god Śambhu, who has the bull as his vehicle.
By his grace, proceed through the yoga of action;
worship Śaṅkara, Mahādeva, the Lord of Cows, who is adorned with ashes.
When this had been said, the sages headed by Śaunaka bowed down to Maheśvara,
the eternal Sthāṇu, and to Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
With joyful minds, they spoke to the lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
who was Hṛṣīkeśa himself, the great sovereign of all the worlds.
O refuge of all, O you who have the bull as your emblem, by your grace there now arises an unwavering devotion that is difficult even for the gods to attain. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.11.138)
O best of sages, tell me of the unsurpassed yoga of action (karmayoga),
by which that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, is to be propitiated by those seeking liberation.
"In your presence, let this Sūta hear the words of the Blessed One;
speak that which is the protection of all worlds and the compendium of Dharma."

As was previously spoken by Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who had assumed the form of a tortoise, when questioned by the sages and by Śakra during the churning for the nectar of immortality. (Kūrmaka Purāṇa 2.11.141)
Having heard the eternal yoga of action as spoken by the sages, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī, spoke with a well-composed mind.
Whoever constantly recites this dialogue between the wearer of the animal skin (Śiva) and those headed by Sanatkumāra is liberated from all sins.
Or one may cause pure twice-born men, devoted to celibacy, to hear it;
whoever contemplates its meaning attains the supreme goal.
And whoever should hear this constantly, endowed with devotion and firm in their vows,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Therefore, it should be recited with every effort by the wise;
moreover, it should always be heard and reflected upon, especially by Brahmins.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Song of the Lord," in the latter section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, a compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, all you sages, to this eternal *karmayoga* about to be described, which bestows the ultimate fruit upon the Brahmins.
All that is established by tradition and revealed by Brahmā,
Manu, the Lord of Creatures, spoke of old while the sages were listening.
"Listen with concentrated minds as I speak of that which removes all sins, brings merit, and is practiced by the assembly of sages. KūrmP_2,12.3.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the best of the twice-born should study the Vedas,
either in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth], according to the procedure prescribed in their own *sūtra*.
Carrying a staff, a girdle, and the sacred thread, wearing a black antelope skin,
the sage should subsist on alms, be devoted to his guru, and gaze upon the face of his guru.
In ancient times, Brahmā fashioned from cotton the three-stranded sacred thread for Brāhmaṇas; it may be made of kuśa grass or even of cloth.
A twice-born man should always wear the sacred thread and always have his topknot tied;
otherwise, whatever rite he performs becomes as if unperformed.
He should wear an unaltered garment made of cotton or dyed with astringent decoctions; that same garment should be worn as an undergarment—white, without holes, and of the highest quality.
But the upper garment is declared to be an auspicious black antelope skin;
in its absence, a cowhide or a Ruru deer skin is prescribed.
Having lifted the right arm and placed the sacred thread upon the left arm, it is always the *upavīta*; when it hangs from the neck, it is the *nivīta*.
O twice-born ones, having raised the left arm and holding [the sacred thread] over the right shoulder, it is called *prācīnāvīta*; one should employ this at rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*).

In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, during a burnt offering, during the muttering of prayers, likewise during Vedic study, while eating, and always in the presence of Brahmins. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.12.12)
In the service of gurus, at the two twilights, and in the company of the virtuous, one should always wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder;
this is the eternal rule.
The girdle of a Brahmin should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
in the absence of muñja, they say it may be made of kuśa grass with one or three knots.
A twice-born man should carry a staff made of bilva or palāśa wood reaching to the hairline,
or one made from a tree suitable for sacrifice, which is pleasing and free of blemishes.
A twice-born man should perform the twilight devotions with a concentrated mind both morning and evening;
by abandoning them out of desire, greed, fear, or delusion, he becomes fallen.
Then, with a serene mind, one should perform the fire-ritual in the evening and in the morning;
having bathed, one should likewise satisfy the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
One should perform the worship of the deities with flowers, leaves, or water;
one should always be habituated to saluting elders in accordance with dharma.
"O sir, I am so-and-so by name," he should say with a perfect prostration, free from sloth and other such faults, for the sake of attaining long life and health. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.12.19)
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you live long, O gentle one.
At the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as a protracted (*pluta*) sound.
That twice-born man who does not offer a return salutation to one who has greeted him should not be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
The salutation to the teacher should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot should be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge,
one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received.
One should not carry water, alms-food, flowers, or sacrificial fuel,
nor other such items, during rites dedicated to the gods and similar ceremonies.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, about his health; a Vaiśya, about his prosperity; and a Śūdra, indeed, about his freedom from illness.
The preceptor, the father, the elder brother, the sovereign,

the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, the maternal grandfather, the paternal grandfather, one of superior caste, and the paternal uncle— these are remembered as the gurus for a man. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.12.26)
The mother, the maternal grandmother, the teacher, the paternal and maternal uncles,
the mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, the elder sister, and the nurse— these women are to be regarded as gurus.
Thus, O twice-born ones, has this group of gurus, beginning with the mother and the father, been described;
one should follow them through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Upon seeing his guru, he should rise and salute him with palms joined;
he should not sit together with these [other disciples], nor should he dispute with them for his own sake.
One should never speak ill of one's gurus even for the sake of one's life;
for one who hates their guru falls downward, even if endowed with other virtues.
Of all gurus as well, five are especially worthy of worship;
among them, the first three are the most excellent, and of those, the mother is most highly honored.
He who imparts instruction, she who gives birth, he by whom one's knowledge is taught,
the elder brother, and the husband— these five are remembered as gurus.
One who desires prosperity must especially honor these five with every effort, even at the cost of one's own life.
As long as both father and mother remain free from change,
so long should the son renounce everything else and be devoted solely to them.
If both father and mother are well-pleased by the virtues of their son,
that son shall, through that deed, attain the entirety of dharma.
There is no deity equal to a mother; there is no teacher equal to a father. No recompense whatsoever can ever exist for them.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two through action, mind, and speech;
without being permitted by them, one should not perform any other religious duty.
Excluding the fruit of liberation, as well as the constant and occasional rites,
the essence of Dharma is declared to bestow infinite fruit after death.
Having properly propitiated the teacher and being dismissed by his permission,
the disciple enjoys the fruit of the knowledge after death and attains heaven.
The fool who disregards his eldest brother, who is like a father,
goes to a terrible hell after death because of that transgression.
A husband must always be honored by a man who has entered upon the path of worldly life;
for in this world, one gains respect through the act of giving and through the benefit one provides.
Indeed, for those men who sacrifice their own lives for the sake of their master's sustenance,
the Blessed Manu has declared inexhaustible worlds.
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "I am so-and-so."
One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name, even if he is younger; however, he should speak to him using the honorifics *bhoḥ* or *bhavat* as prefixes.
A Brāhmaṇa should always be saluted, honored, and bowed to with the head by those seeking prosperity— namely, by Kṣatriyas and others— with due respect.
A Brahmin must never, under any circumstances, salute those of the Kṣatriya and other lower castes,
even if they are endowed with knowledge, ritual action, and virtues, and are highly learned.
It is the established rule that a Brāhmaṇa should bestow blessings upon all castes;
however, among those of equal caste, the act of salutation must indeed be performed by equals toward one another.
The teacher is the fire for the twice-born; among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the teacher;
the husband alone is the teacher of women; and everywhere, the guest is a teacher.
Knowledge, ritual action, age, kinship, and fifthly, wealth—these they call the five grounds for respect; each preceding one is weightier than the one following. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.12.49)

Among the five [classes], those who are numerous and powerful within the three [upper] castes are worthy of honor here; even a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage [of life] is worthy of honor in this regard.
The path must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, to a woman, to a king, to one who is sightless,
to an elder, to one burdened by a load, to a sick person, and to one who is weak.
Having collected alms daily from the houses of the learned while remaining pure,
he should offer them to his teacher and eat them with speech restrained, according to the teacher's permission.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class (a Brāhmaṇa) should go about for alms using "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, at the end.
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt—whichever of these would not treat him with contempt. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.12.54)
The practice of wandering for alms is prescribed as being among those of the same caste, or even among all castes, while avoiding those who have fallen from their status (patita) and the like.
From the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praised for their own duties,
let the self-restrained student daily collect alms while practicing celibacy.
One should not beg for alms within the family of the guru, nor among one's own paternal or maternal kin.
If alms are not obtained from other houses, one should avoid each preceding house in favor of the next.
Or, if those previously mentioned places are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech with self-control and not looking toward the cardinal directions.
Having collected that alms-food according to his needs without guile,
he should always eat it with self-restraint, silent, and with a mind focused on nothing else.
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the subsistence of a vow-holder on alms is equal to fasting.
One should always worship food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven;
it is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
One should eat food facing the east or indeed facing the sun;
one should never eat facing the north—this is the eternal rule.
Having washed his hands and feet, one who is about to eat should sip water twice;
seated in a clean place, and having finished eating, one should likewise sip water twice.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the upper division of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
"Having eaten, having drunk, having slept, having bathed, or upon approaching a carriage road..."
Having touched the corners of the lips and having put on the garment, one should perform the rite.
Upon the voiding of feces, urine, or excrement; during improper speech;
after spitting; at the commencement of Vedic study; and likewise upon the onset of coughing or labored breathing.
Having stepped upon a crossroads or a cremation ground at either of the two twilights, the best of the twice-born, even if he has already sipped water for purification, should sip water again.

Upon conversing with a Caṇḍāla or a Mleccha, upon speaking with a woman or a Śūdra while they are left-over from a meal, upon touching a person who is impure from food remnants, or likewise upon touching food that is in such a state,
or when tears are shed, or similarly when blood [is shed], one should sip water for purification (ācamana).

After eating, at the two twilights, after bathing, after drinking, after voiding urine or excrement, and even after sipping water, one should sip water again after sleeping; furthermore, one should do so once after each of the other [activities].
Upon touching fire, or cows, or one who is already pure,
or upon touching women, or oneself, or after adjusting the knot of one's lower garment (nīvī), one should sip water.
One should touch water, or moist grass, or even the earth,
upon touching one's own hair or an unwashed garment.
One who desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy and free from impurities, in accordance with the Dharma, while seated and facing either the east or the north.
Having covered one's head or neck, or with the lower garment or the topknot loosened,
or without having washed the feet— even if one has sipped water for purification, one remains impure.
A wise man should not recite while wearing shoes, nor while standing in water, nor without a turban; nor indeed under rain-showers, nor while standing, nor with water drawn up from a source.
Nor [should one offer] with water held in only one hand, nor without a thread,
nor while standing on sandals or a seat, nor with the knees outside [the hands].
Neither while talking, nor laughing, nor looking about, nor lying down, nor even while bent over;
nor with water that is not inspected, or that is mixed with foam and the like.
One should not [use water] released from a Śūdra or an impure person, nor likewise that which is alkaline;
nor with the fingers, nor making noise, nor with a distracted mind.
Nor with water corrupted by color or taste, nor with water from fissures in the ground;
nor with water stirred by the hand, nor even with that which has been drawn outside the armpit.
A Brahmin is purified by [the water] reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya becomes pure by [the water] reaching the throat;
likewise, a Vaiśya by [the water] being swallowed; and women and Śūdras by contact at the very end.
The space between the base of the thumb and the line is called the Brāhma-tīrtha;
the area between the thumb and the forefinger is the supreme tīrtha of the ancestors (pitṛs).
Behind the base of the little finger, they declare the Prājāpatya;
at the tips of the fingers, the Daiva is remembered, and that same [place] is proclaimed as the Ārṣa.
At the root [of the hand] is the divine (daiva) and the ṛṣi-tīrtha; the āgneya is remembered to be in the middle;
that very same [place] is the saumika tīrtha—knowing this, one is not deluded.
A twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha;
or, O twice-born ones, he may do so with the Kāya, the Daiva, or the Pitrya-tīrtha.
First, a self-restrained Brāhmaṇa should sip water three times;
then, having wiped his mouth with the base of his thumb, he should touch his face.
Then, one should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger;
next, one should touch both sides of the bridge of the nose using the combination of the index finger and the thumb.
One should touch the ears by joining the little finger with the thumb;
then, by the union of all fingers, one should touch the heart, or else with the palm; or likewise, one should touch the head, or else both [the heart and head] with the thumb.
One should drink three mouthfuls of water; by that, the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa become well-pleased—so we have heard.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are pleased by the cleansing [of the eyes],
and the Moon and the Sun are pleased when the two eyes are touched.
When both nostril passages are touched, the two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins) are pleased;
likewise, when the two ears are touched, Vāyu and Agni are pleased.
When his heart is touched, all the deities are pleased;
by touching him on the head, that single person becomes delighted.
The principal [sages] do not consider those droplets that fall upon the body to be "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa);
things stuck between the teeth are like the teeth themselves, but one becomes impure if the tongue touches them.
Those drops which touch the feet of one who is rinsing the mouth for others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
Manu has declared that there is no fault in the case of the madhuparka offering, the soma juice, the chewing of betel, or the consumption of fruits, roots, and sugarcane stalks.
If a man, while moving among food and drink, should have an object in his hand,
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then sprinkle it with water.
If a twice-born man should become impure while holding something made of metal,
he should set that object down on the ground, sip water for purification, and then sprinkle it with water.
If one should take up a vessel and become possessed of food remnants,
one attains purity by sipping water (ācamana) even without setting that object down; however,
regarding clothes and such, there may be an option, for here one becomes pure after touching them.
In a forest, in a waterless place, at night, or on a path infested with thieves and tigers,
one who has urine or feces in hand does not incur fault after voiding them.
Having placed the sacred thread over his right ear, he should void excrement and urine facing north during the day; if at night, he should face south.
Having covered the ground with wood, leaves, clods of earth, or grass, and having veiled his head, he should perform the voiding of excrement and urine. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.13.35)

One should not perform [the ritual] in a shadow, in a well, in a river, in a cow-pen, at a shrine, in water, on a path, on ashes, in fire, in a cremation ground, or in feces and urine. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.13.36)
Neither on cow dung nor on ploughed ground, nor at a great tree, nor in a grassy spot; neither while standing, nor naked, nor on the peak of a mountain. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.13.37)
One should never perform it in a dilapidated temple, nor on an anthill,
nor in pits containing living creatures, nor while walking.
Nor on husks, charcoal, or potsherds, nor likewise on the royal highway; neither in a field, nor in a pit, nor at a sacred bathing place, nor at a crossroads.
Nor near a garden or a reservoir, nor on saline soil, nor where there is great impurity;
nor wearing sandals or shoes, nor holding an umbrella, nor in the open air.
Nor indeed should one ever do so in the presence of women, teachers, Brahmins, or cows,
nor in the vicinity of temples of the gods or of water.
Nor should one look at the luminaries, nor face the twilight, nor likewise face the sun, the fire, or the moon.
Having taken earth from the riverbank, one should untiringly perform purification with pure, drawn-up water to remove any remaining smear or odor.
A Brahmin should not take earth from a dusty place, nor from mud,
nor from a road, nor from saline ground, nor from a spot already used for purification, nor from that belonging to another.
One should never perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) from a temple, a well, a village, or from water [in such places], but rather always according to the previously stated rule.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Upper Division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, endowed with the staff and other [emblems], and possessed of purity and right conduct, [the king should rule].
Being called upon, he should engage in study while gazing at the face of his teacher.
One should always have one's hands ready for service, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," one should sit facing the teacher.
One should not engage in responding or conversing while lying down, nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.3)
In the presence of his teacher, he should always use a low bed and seat;
within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name even in his absence alone,
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever slander or even censure of the guru occurs,
one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.

One should not worship him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; one should not speak back to him, nor sit while he is standing, nor remain seated in his immediate proximity.
He should always fetch a water-pot, kusha grass, flowers, and sacrificial fuel;
he should indeed perform the daily sprinkling and the smearing of his limbs.
One should never step upon his discarded flower offerings, his bed, his wooden sandals, or his shoes; nor should one ever step upon his seat or his shadow.
He should prepare the tooth-stick and other necessities, and whatever he has obtained, he should present it to him;
he should not depart without asking permission, and he should remain devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial.
One should never stretch out one's feet in his presence; likewise,
one should always avoid yawning, laughing, covering the neck, and spitting in his vicinity.
One should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not troubled in mind;
one should sit with a concentrated mind on a low seat made of grass or a wooden plank below the teacher.
He should never remain stationary while [the teacher] is sitting, lying down, or traveling;
he should run after him when he runs and follow him when he walks. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.13)
One may sit together with one's teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on palaces, on stone slabs, on mats, and on rocks, wooden planks, or boats.
One should always have the senses conquered, be self-controlled, free from anger, and pure;
one should always employ speech that is sweet and speaks what is beneficial. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.15)
Perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, fermented liquids, sour gruel, the harming of living beings, anointing the body, and likewise the wearing of ointments, shoes, and umbrellas; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.16.

One should diligently avoid desire, greed, fear, sleep, singing, instrumental music, dancing, threats, slander, looking at or touching women, as well as harming others and backbiting. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.17)
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, clay, and *kuśa* grass, as much as required; and he should go out for alms every day.
One should always avoid all salt that has been prepared and anything that is stale;
one should never watch dances and remain free from longing for songs and the like.
One should not look at the sun, nor should one practice the cleaning of the teeth;
one should avoid seclusion with impure women and conversation with Śūdras or those of the lowest castes.
One should employ the remains of the Guru's food for medicinal purposes, and not out of desire;
one should never perform the ritual bath of extracting the *kalāpa*.
A Brahmin should never entertain the thought of abandoning his guru, whether out of delusion or greed; by abandoning him, he becomes fallen.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic,
or even spiritual knowledge, one should never bear malice toward anyone from whom one receives it.
Manu has declared that even a guru— one who is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, and who has set out upon a wrong path— should be abandoned.
When the teacher's teacher is present, one should practice devotion toward him as toward one's own teacher;
however, unless permitted by one's teacher, one should not offer salutations to one's own teachers.
This same constant conduct is due toward teachers of knowledge as toward one's own parents,
and likewise toward those who forbid unrighteousness and those who impart what is beneficial.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one would toward the guru—
toward the guru’s sons, his wives, and indeed his own kinsmen.
Whether he be of equal age, a child, or a disciple,
the son of the guru who teaches during a sacrificial rite deserves honor just like the guru himself.
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing, or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one perform the washing of his feet. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.29)
The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the gurus themselves;
those who are of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs, and the dressing of the hair—these should not be performed for the wife of one's guru. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.31)
A young wife of the guru, however, should not be saluted by touching her feet;
one should instead perform a prostration on the ground, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher's wives every day and offer salutations,
remembering the dharma of the virtuous.
A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, and a paternal aunt are to be honored like the wife of one's guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
The wife of one's brother, if she is of the same caste, should be saluted day after day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the wives of kinsmen and relatives should be saluted.
One should behave toward one's father's sister and one's mother's elder sister as toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they.
One should constantly teach the Veda, the Dharma, and the Purāṇas along with their auxiliary limbs to one who is thus perfected in conduct, self-possessed, and free from pride and hypocrisy.
If a teacher does not impart knowledge to a disciple who has resided with him for a year,
that teacher takes upon himself the misdeeds of that disciple living with him.

The son of a teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, capable, a provider of food, wealthy, a kinsman, and a virtuous person— these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma.
A man who is grateful, free from malice, intelligent, and a doer of good, as well as one who is trustworthy and dear— these six types of twice-born men should be taught according to the rule;
to them the Veda may be given, but not to others except as previously stated.
Having sipped water and being self-restrained, he should always study while facing north;
having clasped the teacher's feet and gazing at the teacher's face, he should say, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude with the words, "May there be a pause."
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by sacred purifiers (pavitra),
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Oṃ.
A twice-born Brāhmaṇa should utter the syllable *praṇava* at the end according to the rule;
he should always perform his study preceded by the *brahmāñjali* gesture.
The Veda is the eternal eye for all beings;
one should study it constantly, otherwise one falls from the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever constantly recites the Ṛgvedic verses satisfies the deities with an oblation of milk;
being satisfied, they indeed always gratify him with his desires.
One who regularly studies the Yajus-sacrificial formulas gratifies the deities with curd;
one who studies the Sāmans gratifies them daily with oblations of clarified butter.
He constantly gratifies the deities with the Atharva-Āngirasas as if with honey;
he satisfies the gods with the ancient limbs of Dharma as if with meats.
Restrained and having resorted to the daily rite, one should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Gāyatrī near water.
One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī, which has a maximum of one thousand, a middle of a hundred, and a minimum of ten; this is proclaimed as the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
The Lord weighed the Gāyatrī and the Vedas on a scale:
the four Vedas on one side, and the Gāyatrī likewise on the other.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, and immediately thereafter the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should then recite the *Sāvitrī* with single-minded focus and endowed with faith.
In a former age, the three eternal Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti)—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—arose; they are the destroyers of all that is inauspicious.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Kāla; Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara;
and the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are traditionally known as the three vyāhṛtis respectively.
The syllable *oṃ* is that supreme Brahman; the Sāvitrī is its imperishable letter.
This mantra is the great yoga, declared to be the essence of essences.
The student who studies this Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, day after day,
having understood its meaning, attains the supreme goal.
Gāyatrī is the mother of the Vedas; Gāyatrī is the purifier of the worlds.
Knowing that there is no recitation higher than Gāyatrī, one is liberated. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.56)
O best of the twice-born, the commencement of Vedic study (vedopākaraṇa) is traditionally prescribed for the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
or for the full moons of Āṣāḍha or Bhādrapada.
Having left behind villages and cities, for four and a half months,
the Brahmin should study in a pure place, observing celibacy and remaining concentrated.
Under the Puṣya asterism, the twice-born should perform the external dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarjana),
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon.
A twice-born man should indeed study the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights, both in the morning and in the evening;
he should study the Vedāṅgas and the Purāṇas during the dark fortnights, as well as the Mānava-dharmaśāstra.
One who teaches and one who practices diligently should always avoid these occasions when study is prohibited.
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, when there is a rising of dust by day,
during lightning, thunder, and rain, and upon the falling of great meteors—
Prajāpati has declared that in these cases there shall be no study for the remainder of the day.
One should know that when these [omens] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, so too when clouds are seen out of season.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the celestial bodies,
one should know these to be occasions for non-study (*anadhyāya*) that last until the same time the following day, even during the rainy season.
But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder,
there shall be a suspension of study for the remainder of the night with the light still present, just as during the day.
For those who desire proficiency in dharma, there shall always be a suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as whenever a foul odor is present.
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a *vṛṣala*,
nor while there is weeping, nor in a crowd of people.
In water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine, while impure from food, or during a funeral rite (śrāddha), one should not even mentally contemplate [forbidden things]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.68)
Having accepted an invitation for an ekoddiṣṭa rite,
a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the impurity caused by a king or by Rāhu (an eclipse).
As long as even a single drop of the consecrated oil remains on the body of a learned Brahmin, one should not recite the Veda.
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food from a house where birth-impurity (sūtaka) has occurred.
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon day, the fourteenth, the full moon, and the eighth lunar days; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.72.
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga, a fast of three nights is prescribed;
at the Aṣṭakās, however, it is a day and night, as well as on the final nights of the seasons.
Likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and similarly in the month of Māgha—
the three Aṣṭakās are proclaimed by the wise as occurring in the dark fortnight.
One should never study under the shade of the Śleṣmātaka, the Śālmali, the Madhuka, the Kovidāra, or the Kapittha trees.
Likewise, when one who shares the same sacred knowledge has died, or a fellow student,
or even when a teacher has passed away, a fast of three nights is prescribed.
These are the vulnerabilities of Brahmins that are proclaimed as times unfit for study;
Rākṣasas strike them during those times, therefore one should avoid them.

In the case of daily rites, there is no suspension of study, nor in the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), nor indeed at the commencement of the ritual (upākarma), nor at the conclusion of the rite, nor in the mantras for the fire-oblation (homa). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.78)
Furthermore, during the Aṣṭakā and other such occasions, one should recite a single Ṛg-verse, or a single Yajus-formula, or even a Sāman, while the Marut wind blows intensely.

But there is no suspension of study regarding the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), nor for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, nor for the other Dharmaśāstras; one should avoid these [specific] festival days (parvan) [only] in those cases.
This dharma of those practicing celibacy has been proclaimed in brief;
it was previously declared by Brahmā to the sages of purified souls.
That twice-born man who exerts effort in other matters without having studied the Veda is utterly deluded; he is outside the Veda and should not be conversed with by those of the twice-born caste.
A twice-born man should certainly not be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Vedas;
for one who rests content with recitation alone sinks like a cow in the mud. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.14.83)

He who, having studied the Veda according to the prescribed rules, does not investigate the meaning of the Veda, is like a Śūdra together with his lineage; he does not attain the status of a worthy recipient.
If, however, he indeed desires to dwell with his guru for the rest of his life,
he should serve him diligently until the liberation of the body.
Or, having gone to the forest, he should duly offer oblations into the sacred fire;
he should always study the Veda, being ever devoted to Brahman and composed in mind.
Devoted to the practice of bathing with ashes, one should constantly and with focused discipline study the Sāvitrī, the Śatarudrīya, and especially the Vedāntas.
This supreme and ancient ordinance, correctly proclaimed here in the Vedic tradition,
was formerly requested by the most eminent of great sages.
As the god Manu, the son of the Self-existent (Svāyambhuva), has declared.
Thus, he who knows the injunction and performs it with his inner self surrendered to the Lord,
having cast off the net of delusion, becomes immortal.
He goes to that auspicious state which is free from all affliction.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
"O twice-born ones, [one may study] one Veda, two Vedas, or likewise all four Vedas."
Having studied and understood the meaning, the best of the twice-born should then perform the ceremonial bath.
Having given a boon to the guru, he should bathe with his permission;
then, having fulfilled his vows, being self-disciplined and capable, he is fit to perform the ritual bath (snāna).
He should carry a bamboo staff, an inner garment, and likewise an upper garment;
two sacred threads, and a water-pot containing water.
A parasol, a stainless turban, two sandals and shoes, and two golden earrings; [he should offer these] while pure, with his hair and nails clipped, and having studied the Veda.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas; he should not wear garlands outdoors, except for those made of gold, nor should a Brahmin wear a wreath that is red.
He should always wear white garments, be fragrant, and be pleasant to behold;
indeed, when he has the means, he should never wear worn-out or dirty clothes.
One should not use clothing that is dyed red, ostentatious, or worn by another;
nor should one use a water-pot, sandals, a garland, or wooden shoes.
One should not wear the sacrificial thread, ornaments, darbha grass, or black antelope skins over the right shoulder; nor should one wear clothing that is discolored or torn.
One should duly take a wife who is auspicious, similar to oneself,
endowed with beauty and auspicious marks, and free from defects of lineage.
A Brāhmaṇa should take as his wife one who is not born of his mother’s lineage, who does not belong to the same ṛṣi-lineage, and who is endowed with good character and purity.
He should approach his wife during her fertile season until a son is born,
but he must carefully avoid those days that are prohibited.
On the sixth, eighth, fifteenth, twelfth, and fourteenth [lunar days],
as well as on the anniversary of one's birth, one should always remain celibate.
One should establish the domestic fire (āvasathya) and offer oblations to Jātavedas;
the Snātaka should always observe his vows and maintain those purifications.
One should constantly perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas without sloth;
by failing to do so, one quickly falls into most terrifying hells.
Being self-restrained, he should practice the Veda, not neglect the great sacrifices,
perform the domestic rites, and likewise observe the twilight devotions.
One should cultivate friendship with those who are concentrated in mind, always approach the Lord,
visit the deities as well, and provide for the maintenance of one's wife.
A wise man should not proclaim his own righteousness, nor should he conceal his faults;
rather, being compassionate toward all beings, he should constantly perform what is beneficial for himself.
One should always conduct oneself by practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.15.18)
One should practice that conduct which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti and which is properly followed by the virtuous; one should never seek to follow anything else.
By that path by which his fathers have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone, let him travel the way of the virtuous; going by that path, he does not come to harm.

One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, always wearing the sacred thread, truthful in speech, and having conquered anger; such a person is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Constantly devoted to the twilight ablutions and dedicated to the sacrifice to Brahman,
free from malice, gentle, and self-controlled, the householder prospers after death.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, devoid of greed and delusion,
devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra and performing ancestral rites, the householder is liberated.
One who is intent on the welfare of his mother and father, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins,
self-controlled, a performer of sacrifices, and a devotee of the gods, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One who pursues the three aims of life should constantly perform the worship of the deities;
he should daily and perpetually pay homage to the gods with a disciplined mind.
One who is constantly disposed toward renunciation, endowed with patience, and compassionate is declared a true householder; one does not become a householder merely by means of a physical dwelling.
Forbearance, compassion, discernment, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility,
and knowledge devoted to the inner self— this is the characteristic of a brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, the best of the twice-born should not be negligent, especially while performing his duties according to his capacity; he should avoid those actions that are censured.
Having shaken off the mire of delusion and attained the unsurpassed yoga, even a householder is liberated from bondage; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.15.29)
Forgiveness is the endurance of faults arising from the anger of others—such as reproach, transgression, insult, injury, binding, and killing. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.15.30)
"Out of affection for the suffering of others, as if it were their own, the sages declare that compassion is the direct means for accomplishing dharma."— Kūrma Purāṇa 2.15.31.
One should know that true knowledge (*vijñāna*) is the retention of the fourteen branches of learning according to their actual meaning—that by which the Dharma increases. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.15.32)
Having studied the sciences according to the rules and having indeed understood their meaning,
if one desists from performing dharma, that is not considered true knowledge.
One conquers the worlds through truth; truth is that supreme state.
The wise declare that truth is speech in accordance with reality as it is.
Self-restraint is the cessation of bodily activity, and tranquility arises from the clarity of wisdom;
one should know the imperishable inner self, having attained which one no longer grieves.
That knowledge by which the supreme Lord, the Blessed One, the Great God himself, is directly known—that is celebrated as true knowledge. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.15.36)
The learned Brahmin who is devoted to that, intent on that, ever free from anger, pure,
and dedicated to the great sacrifices, attains that unsurpassed state.
One should diligently protect the body, for it is the abode of Dharma;
indeed, without the body, the Supreme Rudra cannot be realized by men.
A twice-born man, being self-restrained, should apply himself constantly to virtue, wealth, and pleasure;
he should not even mentally contemplate pleasure or wealth that is devoid of virtue.
For even when suffering, one should not practice unrighteousness according to dharma;
for the Blessed Lord Dharma is the refuge for all living beings.
One should act for the benefit of living beings and not have a mind intent on deeds of malice toward others;
one should not engage in the censure of the Vedas or the deities, nor should one dwell with those who do so.
But that pure Brahmin who reads this definitive chapter on Dharma,
or teaches it, or causes others to hear it, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
One should not harm any living beings, nor should one ever speak an untruth.
One should never speak words that are harmful or unpleasant, nor should one ever be a thief.
Whether it be grass, or vegetables, or earth, or even water,
a living being who takes these from another falls into hell.
A wise man should not accept gifts from a king, nor from a Śūdra or an outcast; he should not accept from others if he is unable [to subsist otherwise], and he should avoid those who are censured.
One should never be a beggar, nor should one ever beg from him again;
for such a foolish beggar takes away his very life.
One should not be a stealer of the property of the gods, especially so for the best of the twice-born;
nor should one ever seize the property of a Brahmin, even in times of distress.
They say that poison is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brahmin that is called poison.
Therefore, one should always take great care to avoid the property of the gods as well.
Regarding flowers, vegetables, water, wood, as well as roots, fruits, and grass, the taking of what is not given is theft; Manu, the Lord of Creatures, has declared that non-stealing is its opposite.
O twice-born ones, flowers for the ritual of worshipping the gods should be gathered from more than one source,
provided they have not been specifically forbidden.
A wise man may indeed take grass, wood, fruit, flowers, or light solely for the sake of dharma, O brahmins; otherwise, he would become fallen.

O Brahmins, it is the established rule that those standing on the road who are afflicted by hunger may take a handful of sesame, mung beans, barley, and so forth; not otherwise, for they are knowers of the Dharma.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing one's sin with a vow, one merely practices deception upon women and śūdras.
Such a Brahmin is censured both in this world and after death by those who discourse upon the Veda;
and whatever vow is practiced through deceit goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, being without the marks [of his order], subsists by the dress of one who bears the marks,
incurs the sin of those who bear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.
Those wicked ones who follow the "vow of the cat" are destroyers of dharma in this world;
they fall immediately into sins, for that is the fruit of such action.
One should not honor, even with a mere word, heretics, those engaged in improper occupations, those who follow left-handed practices, nor the Pañcarātras and Pāśupatas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.15)
One should not even mentally contemplate those mortals who delight in reviling the Vedas, likewise those who delight in reviling the gods, or those who delight in reviling the twice-born.

A living being falls [into degradation] by performing sacrifices for them, forming matrimonial alliances with them, dwelling together with them, or conversing with them; therefore, one should avoid these with great effort. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.17)
Betrayal of one's guru is ten million times more grievous than betrayal of the gods;
and atheism and the reviling of knowledge are ten million times more grievous than that. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.18)
Families that have fallen away from righteousness through [the pursuit of] cattle, gods, Brahmins, agriculture, or service to kings, descend to the state of being non-families.
Through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas,
and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble lineages fall into a state of ignobility.
Through falsehood, adultery, the eating of forbidden food, and the practice of non-Vedic dharma, a family indeed perishes quickly. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.21)
Indeed, by giving to those who are not learned in the Vedas, as well as to the low-born (vṛṣala) and to those devoid of prescribed conduct,
the family quickly perishes.
One should not dwell in a village surrounded by unrighteous people, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not live in a kingdom ruled by Śūdras, nor in one crowded with heretics.
A twice-born man should not dwell anywhere other than in the auspicious region between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, extending from east to west, excluding the lands bordering the two oceans.
Or where the black antelope always roams by its very nature,
or where there are famous and sacred rivers— there a twice-born man should dwell.
Having avoided the riverbank within half a krośa, the best of the twice-born should not dwell elsewhere,
nor near a village of outcastes.
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their status, nor with Caṇḍālas, nor with Pukkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with outcastes, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society.

Sharing a bed or a seat, sitting in the same row, mixing vessels or cooked food, officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching one another, being of the same lineage, and likewise eating together— these are [grounds for loss of caste].
Studying together is the tenth, and officiating at sacrifices together is indeed the eleventh;
these are declared to be the defects known as "intermixture" (sāṅkarya).
Sin is transmitted to men through proximity;
therefore, with every effort, one should avoid intermixture.
Those who sit in a single row without touching one another,
having established a boundary with ashes, for them there shall be no confusion of castes.
By fire, by ashes, by sprinkling with water,
by a door, and by a pillar-path— by these six, the row is divided.
One should not engage in groundless enmities, nor in disputes or slander. One should not report to anyone a cow suckling her calf in another's field.
One should not converse during a period of birth-impurity, nor should one touch anyone at their vulnerable point. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.33)
A wise man should never describe to another a halo around the sun, a rainbow, a funeral pyre, or the moon.
One should not engage in conflict with many people, nor likewise with one's kinsmen;
one should not do unto others what is disagreeable to oneself.
The best of the twice-born should not mention the lunar day of the fortnight, nor should he point out the constellations; he should not speak with a woman in her courses, nor with one who is impure.
One should not prevent what is being given to the gods, gurus, or brahmins;
one should not praise oneself, and one should avoid censuring others. One should diligently avoid reviling the Vedas and reviling the gods. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.37)
O lords of sages, for that twice-born man who reviles the gods, the ṛṣis, the brahmins, or the Vedas,
no expiation is seen in the scriptures here on earth.
A man who indeed reviles his guru, the deity, or the Veda along with its auxiliary texts,
is cooked in the Raurava hell for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
One should remain silent during slander and should not utter any reply; one should depart after covering the ears and should not even look at those who revile. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.40)
A wise man should indeed avoid the secrets of others and keep them hidden;
he should never engage in disputes with his own kinsmen.

O best of the twice-born, one should not speak of sin to the sinful, nor of sinlessness to them; by speaking falsely, one incurs a fault equal to theirs, but by speaking the truth, one becomes free from fault.
The tears that fall from the weeping of those who have been falsely accused destroy the children and livestock of those false accusers.

For the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife, a means of purification has been seen by the elders; however, there is none for making a false accusation.
One should not look at the rising sun or the moon without a specific reason; nor should one look at them when setting, nor reflected in water, nor eclipsed, nor passing through the meridian,
nor obscured by a cloth, nor entering into a mirror.

A wise man should never look at a naked woman or a naked man; nor should he look at urine or feces, nor at one who has engaged in sexual intercourse. Being impure, he should not gaze upon the sun, the moon, or other celestial bodies.
One should not look at those who have fallen from their caste, those with missing limbs, Caṇḍālas, or those who are impure from eating leftovers;
nor should one speak to another while oneself is impure from leftovers or with one's head covered.
One should not look upon the touch of a hungry ghost (preta), nor the face of an angry teacher,

nor one's own reflection in oil or water, nor one's wife while she is eating, nor a woman whose limbs are not yet released from their bonds, nor one who is insane, nor one who is intoxicated. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.48)
One should not eat together with one's wife, nor should one look at her while she is eating,
or while she is sneezing or yawning, nor when she is seated comfortably as she pleases.
One should not look at one's own reflection in water, nor at a riverbank or a chasm;
one should never step over urine, nor stand upon it at any time. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.50)
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor kṛśara, milk-rice, or curd;
nor should one give him leavings, honey, ghee, a black antelope skin, or sacrificial oblation.
A wise man should not impose a vow upon him, nor should he preach the Dharma to him;
he should not fall under the sway of anger, and he should avoid both hatred and attachment. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.52)
One should diligently avoid greed, hypocrisy, malice, disparagement of knowledge, envy, pride, as well as sorrow and delusion. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.53)
One should not cause pain to anyone; one may strike a son or a disciple [only for correction].
One should never serve those who are base, nor ever those who are of sharp (or cruel) intellect.
A wise man should not despise himself; he should avoid despondency with effort. He should not treat those who are superior with disrespect, nor should he revile himself.
One should not scratch the earth with one's nails, nor should one cause a cow to lie down;
one should not speak of a river when among rivers, nor of mountains when among mountains.
One should not abandon a companion in a dwelling or at a meal;
one should not enter water naked, nor should one step over a fire with one's feet.
One should not smear the body with oil remaining after anointing the head;

one should not play with snakes or weapons, nor touch one's own bodily orifices; one should not touch the hair of the private parts, and one should not walk with an unrefined person. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.58)
One should not resort to fickleness of hand, foot, speech, or eyes;
nor to fickleness of the genitals or the belly, nor ever to that of the ears.
One should never engage in conversation regarding women or fingernails, nor drink from one's cupped hands;
nor should one ever strike water with one's feet or with one's hands.
One should not break fruits with bricks, nor [crush] a fruit with another fruit;
one should not learn the speech of barbarians, nor should one drag a seat with the foot.
A wise person should not perform piercing, cracking, cutting, or scraping; nor should he perform rubbing down without cause or to no purpose.
One should not eat food from one's lap, nor should one engage in useless exertion;
one should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one propitiate the gods with worldly hymns, even those originating from outside [the Vedic tradition].
One should not play with dice, nor run about, nor void excrement or urine in water;
one should never lie down while still impure from food, nor perform a bath naked.
One should not walk, nor read, nor touch one's own head; one should not bite off one's nails or hair with the teeth, nor awaken one who is asleep. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.66)
One should not expose oneself to the morning sun, one should avoid the smoke from a funeral pyre,
one should not sleep alone in a deserted house, and one should not remove one's own sandals.
One should not spit without cause, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms;
nor should one ever wash one's feet with the very foot itself.
A wise man should not warm his feet over a fire, nor should he wash them in a vessel of bell-metal;
nor should he point his feet toward a deity, a Brāhmaṇa,
or a cow, nor toward the wind, fire, a guru, a learned Brahmin, the sun, or the moon.
One who is impure should by no means engage in sleeping, traveling, Vedic recitation, bathing, riding a vehicle, or going outside.
One should always avoid sleeping, studying, bathing, anointing the body with unguents, eating,
and walking during both twilights as well as at midday.
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor should he touch a seat with his foot, nor should he touch an image of a deity.
One who is impure should not tend the sacred fire, nor should he praise the gods or the ṛṣis;
he should not plunge into unfathomable water, nor should he hold his breath without a specific reason.
One should not lift water with the left hand nor drink it from the mouth;
one should not cross over [water] without having sipped water for purification, nor should one discharge semen into the waters.

One should not step over anything smeared with impurity, nor blood, nor poisons; one should not cross a flowing river, nor engage in sexual intercourse in water. One should certainly not cut down a sacred tree, nor should one discharge phlegm into the water. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.16.75)
One should never step upon bones, ashes, or skulls, nor upon hair or thorns,
nor upon husks, charcoal, or dried cow-dung.
A wise man should not leap over fire, nor should he ever place it beneath anything;
a learned man should not treat it with his feet, nor should he blow upon it with his mouth.
One should not descend into a well, nor should one ever look down while impure;
one should not cast fire into fire, nor likewise extinguish it with water.
One should not personally inform others of the death or suffering of a friend;
nor should one employ non-saleable goods or counterfeit merchandise for the purpose of selling.
A wise person, being impure, should not fan a fire with breaths from the mouth,
nor should he plow a sacred site, a reservoir of water, or a boundary line.
One should never violate a previously accepted agreement;
one should not cause animals, beasts of prey, or birds to perceive one another.
One should not cause obstruction to others by means of water, wind, heat, and so forth.
Having caused artisans to perform their work, one should not deceive them afterwards.
One should not keep the doors of one's house closed in the evening or morning for the sake of preventing alms-seekers from entering.
One should avoid wearing garlands or applying perfumes outside [the house], eating together with one's wife, engaging in contentious debate, and entering through a side door.
A wise Brahmin should not stand while eating, nor should he speak or laugh;
he should never touch his own sacred fire with his hand, nor should he remain in water for a long time.
One should not blow on the fire with the breath of the mouth, nor with a winnowing basket, nor with the hand;
one should certainly not blow on the fire with the mouth, for fire was born from the mouth.
A twice-born man should not converse with another's wife, nor should he officiate at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice;
a Brahmin should not frequent an assembly alone, and he should avoid large gatherings.
One should never go around a temple in a counter-clockwise direction;
one should not fan it with a garment, nor should one sleep within a temple.
One should not set out on a journey alone, nor with unrighteous people,
nor with those afflicted by disease, nor with Śūdras, nor with one who has fallen from his caste.
One should not go out without sandals, nor likewise without water and other necessities;
one should not travel at night, nor with a woman, nor without a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu);
and one should never pass between fire, cows, Brahmins, or others.
A twice-born man should never step over a stretched-out calf-rope anywhere;
nor should he revile yogins, perfected beings (siddhas), or those observing vows who are traveling.
A wise person should not intentionally step upon the shadow of a temple, of deities, or of those performing a sacrificial session, nor that of Brahmins or even a cow.
One should not allow one's own shadow to be stepped upon by outcasts and the like, nor by those afflicted with disease;
nor should one ever stand upon charcoal, ashes, hair, or similar substances.
A twice-born man should avoid the dust raised by a broom, the water used for bathing or washing clothes,
he should not eat what is unfit to be eaten, nor should he drink what is unfit to be drunk.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
A Brāhmaṇa should not eat the food of a Śūdra, whether out of delusion or for any other reason.
He who eats [forbidden food] when there is no distress indeed goes to a Śūdra womb.
The twice-born who eats the censurable food of a Śūdra for six months becomes a Śūdra while still alive and,
after death, is reborn as a dog.
O lords of sages, for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra,
he whose food remains in the stomach after death shall attain the womb of that [person].
One should avoid the food of a king, the food of a dancer, the food of a carpenter, the food of a leather-worker, the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, and likewise the food of a eunuch.
One should likewise avoid the food of those who live by chariots, washermen, thieves, and soldiers, as well as the food of musicians, ironworkers, and those in a state of birth-impurity.
The food of a potter, of one engaged in painting, of a usurer, of an outcast, of the son of a remarried woman,
of a seller of umbrellas, and indeed of one who is accused of a grave crime— these are forbidden.
The food of a goldsmith, an actor, a hunter, a prisoner, a physician, a harlot, and a staff-bearer [is forbidden].
The food of a thief, an atheist, and one who reviles the deities;
the food of a seller of soma, and especially that of a dog-cooker (outcaste).
The food of one who is conquered by his wife, of one in whose house there is a paramour, of one who has renounced worldly life, of a miser, and likewise of one who eats the leavings of others;
One should avoid the food of those unworthy of the company at a meal, the food of a group, and indeed the food of one who lives by weapons;

likewise the food of a eunuch, of a renunciant, of one intoxicated, of one insane, of one who is afraid, of one who weeps, and that which is defiled by being sneezed upon or spat over. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.10)
The food of one who hates Brahmins, of one who delights in sin, of one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka),
of one who cooks in vain, of one in a state of death-impurity (śāva), and of a father-in-law [should not be eaten].
Likewise, [the food] of childless women, of a hired servant,
and especially the food of artisans and of those who sell weapons, [is forbidden].

The food of a drunkard, the food of a publican, the food of physicians, the food of one whose offspring has been aborted, and the food of a younger brother who marries before his elder brother; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.13.
Furthermore, one should especially not eat the food of a remarried woman, nor likewise that of the husband of a younger sister married before her elder;

nor should one eat the food of one who has been treated with contempt, or of one who has been cast off, or of one full of wrath, or of one filled with wonder; nor should one eat the food of even a guru if it is devoid of ritual consecration.
For all the evil deeds of a person reside in his food;
whoever eats another's food, he indeed consumes that person's sin. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.15)
A partner in a business, a family friend, one's own cowherd, a barber, and he who offers himself—these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.16)
An actor, a potter, and one who works the fields—
these among Śūdras may have their food eaten by the wise after giving a small fee.
Milk-rice cooked with oil, cow's milk,
barley meal, oil-cake, and oil may be accepted from a Śūdra by the twice-born.
One should avoid eggplant, the nālikā vegetable, safflower, and aśmantaka; likewise, one should avoid onion, garlic, fermented gruel, and resinous exudations.
One should avoid mushrooms, the excrement of a wild boar, *śelū*, colostrum, *vilaya*, *sumukha*, and fungi. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.20)
By eating gṛñjana, kiṃśuka, kakubhāṇḍa,
as well as udumbara and alābu, a twice-born man indeed falls from his status.
One should not eat kṛśara, saṃyāva, milk-rice (pāyasa), or cakes (apūpa) in vain,
nor meat that has not been consecrated, nor the food of the gods or sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi).
One should carefully avoid barley gruel, citron, even fish that have not been consecrated, as well as the *nīpa*, the *kapittha*, and the *plakṣa* fruit. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.23)
One should carefully avoid oil-cakes from which the oil has been extracted, as well as divine grains (devadhānya), sesame seeds at night, and curd. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.24)

One should not eat buttermilk with milk, nor should one subsist on seeds; one should avoid that which is defiled by its preparation, defiled by its nature, or associated with the unrighteous. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.25)
Food contaminated by hair or insects, that which is mixed with saliva,
that which has been smelled by a dog, that which has been prepared again [after being left over], and likewise that which has been looked upon by a Caṇḍāla— [these must always be avoided].
Nor should one ever eat food that has been smelled by a woman in her courses, by outcasts, or by a cow; nor food that is unhonored, stale, or the remnants of a meal.
That which has been touched by a crow or a cock, or is infested with worms, or even smelled by humans, or touched by one afflicted with leprosy; (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.28).

One should not accept food given by a woman in her menses, nor by one who is menstruating, nor by one who is angry, nor by one wearing soiled clothes; furthermore, one should avoid clothing belonging to another.

Manu has declared that the milk of a cow whose calf has died, the milk of a camel, the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, the milk of a sheep, and the milk of a *sandhinī* cow are unfit for drinking.
The crane, the swan, the gallinule, the sparrow, as well as the parrot, the osprey, the Greek partridge, the web-footed bird, and the cuckoo. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.31)
The crow, the wagtail, the hawk, and likewise the vulture;
the owl, the ruddy goose, the bearded vulture, and also the pigeons;
the dove, the lapwing, and indeed the village cock. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.32)
One should not eat the meat of a lion, a tiger, a cat, a dog, a boar, a jackal, a monkey, or a donkey. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.33)
One should not eat any wild animals, other birds that roam the forest, nor creatures that move in water or on land; such is the established rule. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.34)
The iguana, the tortoise, the hare, the porcupine, and the hedgehog—these five-clawed animals are always fit for consumption; so Manu, the Lord of Creatures, has declared. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.35)
One may eat fish with scales and the meat of the ruru deer only after having offered them to the deities and to the Brahmins, and not otherwise. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.36)
The peacock, the partridge, the pigeon, the francolin,
the vādhrīṇasa crane, the heron, fish, and the haṃsa and parājita birds are edible.
The śaphara, the siṃhatuṇḍa, as well as the pāṭhīna and the rohit—
these fish, O best of the twice-born, are prescribed for consumption.

One may eat the meat of these animals when it has been consecrated by sprinkling, when requested by a twice-born, when one is enjoined according to the rules, or when there is a danger to one's life. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.39)

One should never eat meat; one who eats only what remains [of a sacrifice] is not defiled, except for the purpose of medicine, in cases of incapacity, by command, or for the sake of a sacrifice. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.40)
But he who, having been invited to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods, should reject meat, shall go to as many hells as there are hairs on the body of that animal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.17.41)
It is the established rule that liquor is always unfit to be given, unfit to be drunk, and likewise unfit to be touched; it must never even be looked upon by the twice-born.
Therefore, one should always avoid liquor in every possible way;
for by drinking it, a twice-born man falls from his religious duties and becomes unfit for conversation.

For having consumed what is unfit for consumption and having drunk what is unfit for drinking, a twice-born man shall not be qualified [for ritual acts] as long as that [impurity] has not been cast down.
Therefore, a Brahmin should always diligently avoid foods that ought not to be eaten and drinks that ought not to be drunk; for if he does so, he goes to the Raurava hell.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"O great sage, what should be performed by Brahmins day after day?"
Therefore, explain in its entirety that action by which one may be liberated from bondage.
Vyāsa said:
"I shall speak; listen with concentrated minds as I declare to you the ritual procedure for Brāhmaṇas that must be performed day by day in its proper sequence."
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate *dharma* and *artha*;
then, through mental discipline, one should meditate upon the Lord who arises from that [contemplation], while reflecting on the exhaustion of the body.
Then, when the time of dawn has arrived, the wise man, having performed his necessary duties and having purified himself according to the rules,
should bathe in pure rivers.
Even those people who are doers of evil are purified by the morning bath;
therefore, one should perform the morning bath with every effort.
The sages praise the morning bath as auspicious, bringing both visible and invisible benefits;
there is no doubt that the constant sagehood of the seers arises from the morning bath.
Indeed, saliva constantly flows from the mouth of one who sleeps;
therefore, one should not perform any ritual action without first bathing.
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—all such sins are purified by bathing at dawn; of this there is no doubt.
And no purifying rite for men is well-remembered as being effective without bathing, especially in the case of fire-offerings and recitation; therefore, one should perform the bath.
In case of inability, bathing for him is prescribed either without the head or by wiping with a wet cloth; this is remembered as the Kapila method.
When incapacity has arisen, one should perform an ablution in this manner;
the wise have declared that the Brāhma and other types of ablutions are to be performed according to one's ability.
The Brahma, Āgneya, Vāyavya, Divya, Vāruṇa, and likewise the Yaugika—thus the sixfold bath is proclaimed. (KūrmP 2.18.12)
The *brāhma* purification consists of sprinkling water drops with *kuśa* grass while reciting mantras;
the *āgneya* purification is the smearing of the body from head to foot with ashes. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.13)
Indeed, bathing with the dust raised by cows is declared to be the supreme Vāyavya bath;
that which is performed during rain while the sun is shining is called the Divya bath.

Immersing oneself in water is the Vāruṇa bath; the realization of the Self is the Mānasa bath; and the Yogic bath is declared to be the contemplation of Viṣṇu, for yoga is the meditation upon Viṣṇu. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.15)
Known as the "ford of the self" (ātmatīrtha) and frequented by those who discourse on Brahman,
one should constantly perform that bath which purifies the mind for men.
If capable, one who knows the Vāruṇa and likewise the Prājāpatya [mantras],
having washed the tooth-stick and chewed it according to the rule, [should proceed].
Having sipped water and being purified, one should always perform the morning bath;
[the tooth-stick] should be as thick as the middle finger and twelve finger-breadths in length.
The tooth-stick should have its bark intact; one should brush with its tip.
It may be produced from a milk-tree, or auspiciously from *mālatī*, and especially from *apāmārga*, *bilva*, or *karavīra*.
Having avoided the forbidden items and having taken one [fruit] as prescribed,
the knower of the rules should indeed eat it after avoiding the sinful day.
One should not tear off the tooth-stick with one's fingers, nor should one ever clean the teeth with them;
having rinsed and broken it, one should discard it in a clean place with a concentrated mind.
Having bathed, he should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the mantra, he should always sip water again while remaining silent.
Having purified oneself with mantras using *kuśa* grass and drops of water— with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and auspicious *vāruṇa* verses— KūrmP 2.18.23.
Having recited the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, together with the syllable *oṃ* and the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should offer handfuls of water toward the Sun with the mind fixed upon Him.

Seated upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, well-composed in mind, and having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should meditate upon the *saṃdhyā*; such is the sacred revelation (*śruti*).

That which is the twilight (saṃdhyā) is the source of the world; indeed, she is beyond illusion (māyā), partless, the sovereign supreme power (parāśakti), and the origin of the three principles (tattva). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.26)
Having meditated upon Sāvitrī situated within the orb of the sun, the wise Brahmin, facing the east, should constantly perform the twilight worship while reciting [the mantra]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.27)
One who neglects the twilight prayers is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever else he may perform, he shall not obtain its fruit. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.28)
With undistracted minds and tranquil, those Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas attained the supreme goal in former times after worshipping the twilight devotions according to the prescribed rites.
O best of the twice-born, that foremost of brahmins who exerts effort in other religious duties while neglecting the salutation at the twilight devotions goes to ten thousand hells.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
By that, the supreme Lord whose body is yoga becomes worshipped.
A wise man, purified and standing facing the east, should constantly recite the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times at most, a hundred times in the middle, or ten times as the minimum.
Then, being composed in mind, he should worship the rising sun with various solar mantras derived from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having approached the Sun, the God of gods and the Great Yoga,
one should perform prostration upon the ground with the head, using that very mantra.
Oṃ! To Khakholka, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes;
I offer myself to you, whose form is knowledge.
Homage to you, the compassionate one, to Sūrya, whose form is Brahman. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.35)
You alone are the supreme Brahman, the waters, light, essence, and the immortal;
you are Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, and the syllable Om; you are all the eternal Rudras;
you are the Puruṣa, the True, and the Great; therefore, I bow to you, O Kapardin.
You alone bring forth the universe in its many forms, both the existent and the non-existent;
salutations to Rudra, to Sūrya—I have come to you for refuge.
Salutations to you, O Pracetas; salutations to you, the most bountiful giver.
Salutations, salutations to you, Rudra; I have come to you for refuge.
Salutations to you, the golden-armed one; salutations to you, the lord of gold.
Salutations to you, the husband of Ambikā; salutations to you, the husband of Umā.
Homage be to the blue-necked one; homage to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
homage to you, the deep-red Bharga, the thousand-eyed one.
Salutations always to you, the Swan; let there be salutations to you, the Sun.
Salutations to you who hold the thunderbolt in hand; let there be salutations to you, the Three-Eyed One. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.41)
I take refuge in you, the three-eyed one, the Great Supreme Lord,
the golden self hidden within the house of all embodied beings.
I pay homage to you, the supreme light, the Brahman, the ultimate goal;
to Viśva, Paśupati, the formidable one, who possesses the bodies of both man and woman.
Salutations to Sūrya, to Rudra, to the radiant Parameṣṭhin, to the fierce one who is the portion of all; I indeed take refuge in you forever. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.44)
Having recited this unsurpassed hymn, the Sūryahṛdaya,
one should pay homage to the Sun at both morning and midday.
This *Sūryahṛdaya*, revealed by Brahmā, is to be imparted to a son, a disciple, or a righteous twice-born man.
It pacifies all sins, originates from the essence of the Vedas,
is beneficial to brahmins, meritorious, and practiced by hosts of sages.
Then, having returned home, the brahmin, having sipped water according to the rule,
and having duly kindled the fire, should offer oblations into the Jātavedas fire according to the prescribed rite.
Then the officiating priest, the son, the wife, the disciple, or even a uterine brother—
having obtained special permission— should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rule.
With the sacred grass in hand, his soul purified, wearing white garments as his upper cloth,
with a single-minded focus and senses restrained, he should offer oblations into the fire.
Whatever rite is performed without *darbha* grass or without the sacred thread (*sūtra*), all that becomes demonic; it yields no fruit, neither in the hereafter nor in this world.
One should pay homage to the deities, offer them the best of what is to be given, present flowers and other such offerings to them, and likewise salute the elders. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.52)
He should also attend upon his guru and practice what is beneficial for him;
thereafter, the twice-born man should diligently study the Vedas according to his ability.

The best of the twice-born should recite [the mantra], teach his disciples, retain it in memory, and reflect upon it; he should also examine the scriptures concerning dharma and other matters, as well as the Vedic collections and especially the Vedāṅgas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.54)
