Then, for the sake of securing his well-being and protection, the twice-born man should approach a lord; thereafter, he should accomplish various aims for the sake of his family.
Then, at the time of midday, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing,
as well as flowers, unbroken grains of rice, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and pure cow dung.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in mountain clefts and springs.
One should never bathe at water-reservoirs belonging to others;
however, if no other option exists, one may bathe after removing five lumps of earth [from the bottom].
The head should be washed with one application of clay; likewise, the area above the navel with two;
the body below that with three; and the feet likewise with six.
And clay is prescribed to be the size of a fresh āmalaka fruit;
that is the measure for the cow dung, with which one should then smear the limbs.
Having smeared [the body] while standing on the bank with those very [ashes] according to the mantra,
and having washed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule, one should then bathe with a concentrated mind.
Having consecrated the water with auspicious mantras related to Varuṇa or those bearing his characteristics,
one who is purified in heart should indeed meditate upon the unmanifest, immutable Viṣṇu.
The waters were produced from Nārāyaṇa, and they alone are his place of rest;
therefore, at the time of bathing, a wise person should remember the divine Nārāyaṇa.
Having uttered the syllable *oṃ* toward the sun, one who knows the mantras should immerse himself three times in a body of water;
having sipped water, he should sip again with this mantra.
You move within all beings, facing every direction in the secret cave of the heart;
you are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*, you are the waters, light, essence, and immortality.
Or the wise man should recite the Drupadā verse three times, accompanied by the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava; or he should mutter the Sāvitrī, or likewise the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Then one should perform the sweeping with the verses "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" and likewise with the verse "idam āpaḥ pravahata," as well as with the vyāhṛtis.
Then, having consecrated that sacred bathing place with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should enter the water, remain submerged, and recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Or one should repeat the three-footed Sāvitrī, or the verse "tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam," or the Praṇava, or one should meditate upon Hari, the God.
The mantra beginning with "drupadādiva," which is established in the Yajurveda—
by reciting it three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sins.
Having taken water in the hand, having recited [the mantra], and having performed the sprinkling (mārjana), one who places that water upon the head is liberated from all sins. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.71)
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
Then, placing his hands joined with flowers upon his head,
he should worship the Sun and gaze at the deity while reciting the mantra "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari."
With the hymns "ud u tyam" and "citram," with the mantra "taccakṣuḥ," with the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," and especially with the Sāvitrī; KūrmP_2,18.74.
Furthermore, one should recite other Vedic mantras dedicated to the Sun that destroy sin, and subsequently recite the Sāvitrī; that indeed is remembered as the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
Various purificatory rites and likewise secret sciences,
the Śatarudrīya, the Atharvaśiras, and the Saura hymns, according to one's ability.

Seated upon *kuśa* grass whose tips point eastward, pure and facing the east, or if standing while gazing at the sun, one should perform the recitation (*japya*) with a concentrated mind. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.77)
A rosary should be made from crystal, indrākṣa, rudrākṣa, or produced from putrajīva; this is remembered as the most excellent among the superior types.
During the time of recitation, the wise man should not speak, nor should he look at other things;
he should not move his head or neck, nor should he expose his teeth. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.79)
Since Guhyakas, Rākṣasas, and Siddhas may carry one off by force,
one should therefore perform the recitation in a solitary and very auspicious place.
Having seen a Caṇḍāla, one who is impure, or an outcast, one should sip water and recite [the mantra] again;
having conversed with them, one should bathe and recite it yet again.
Having sipped water and being purified, one should always recite, upon seeing something impure,
solar mantras according to one's ability, and the Pāvamānī verses as desired.
If one is indeed wearing wet clothes, one should perform the recitation while standing in the midst of water;
otherwise, however, one should do so on clean ground upon *darbha* grass, being well-composed in mind.
Having circumambulated clockwise and paid homage,
and then having sipped water (ācamana) upon the ground according to the scriptures, one should perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) according to one's ability.
Then he should satiate the gods, the ṛṣis, and the hosts of ancestors; having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, he should say at the end: "I satiate you with reverence. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.85)
One should satisfy the gods and the Brahman-sages with water mixed with unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
and the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds (tila) with devotion, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra.
With his left hand held back and his right hand forward,
the wise man should satisfy the celestial seers and the ancestors with handfuls of water.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), one should offer libations to the gods; wearing it around the neck (nivītī) during the satiation of the ṛṣis; and wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) for the ancestors, with devotion through one's own [appropriate] part of the hand.
Having wrung out his bathing garment and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should, remaining silent,
worship the gods with his own mantras using flowers, leaves, or even water.
With devotion, free from anger and without haste, one should worship Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Sūrya, as well as Madhusūdana and other deities of one's choice.
Or else, one should offer flowers with the Puruṣasūkta;
by that, all the waters have been properly worshipped as deities.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind, preceded by the syllable *praṇava*, one should indeed offer flowers individually to the deities with a salutation.
There exists no Vedic rite more meritorious than the propitiation of Viṣṇu;
therefore, one should eternally worship Hari, who is without beginning, middle, or end.
With the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and with the Puruṣa Sūkta—
there is no mantra equal to these two, nor has any mantra equal to this Puruṣa Sūkta been declared even within the four Vedas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.94)
Then, with his mind fixed on Him and being tranquil, he should offer himself to Viṣṇu, whose splendor is stainless, by means of the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ."
Alternatively, one who is purified by inner disposition should worship the divine Lord Īśāna, the eternal Bhagavat Mahādeva, the Great Lord Maheśvara.
With the Rudrāgāyatrī mantra, or again with the Praṇava,
or with the Īśāna mantra, or with the Tryambaka Rudra mantra, one should remain composed.

Having addressed Maheśvara with flowers, leaves, or water, along with sandalwood and other offerings, one should offer them while reciting this mantra: "Obeisance to Śiva" (namaḥ śivāya). (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.98)
One should pay homage to Mahādeva, the Lord, with the words "Truth, Reality"; one should offer oneself to the Lord Brahmā with the words "The Lord. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.18.99)
The twice-born man should perform circumambulation while reciting the five Brahmans;
he should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna, the auspicious one situated in the midst of the sky.
Then, having looked at the sun with the verse "The swan dwelling in purity" (RV 4.40.5),
he should go home and, with a concentrated mind, perform the five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas).
The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits,
as well as the sacrifice to humans and the sacrifice to Brahman— these are declared to be the five sacrifices.
If the Brahmayajña has not been performed prior to the libation (tarpaṇa),
then after performing the Manuṣyayajña, one should indeed practice the Svādhyāya.
In the region to the west of the fire, or indeed at the conclusion of the *bhūtayajña*,
he should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, holding *kuśa* grass in his hands, with a concentrated mind.

Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite either in the domestic fire, or in the common (laukika) fire, or even in water or upon the ground; that indeed is remembered as the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña).
If food has been cooked in a worldly fire, it is offered there;
however, the food for the gods is offered in the domestic fire (śālāgni)—this is the eternal rule.
From the remnants of the food offered to the gods, one should offer the *bhūta-bali*.
That indeed should be known as the *bhūtayajña*, which bestows prosperity upon all embodied beings.
The best of the twice-born should offer the bali-oblation of food upon the ground for dogs, for those who cook dogs, for outcasts and others, and then for the birds.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali oblation without reciting mantras;
this is the perpetual sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), ordained for both evening and morning.
But one should feed even a single most excellent Brahmin with the ancestors in mind;
that is designated as the *nitya-śrāddha*, a sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*) that bestows a favorable rebirth.
Or, having set aside some food according to his ability, being composed in mind,
he should present it to a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
One should always honor the guest and bow down to the twice-born who has arrived at one's own home; thereafter, one should worship that peaceful person with thought, word, and deed.
A twice-born man should always give alms to a guest, either the first portion of his food (*hantakāra*) or as much as he is able; thus he should perceive the Supreme Lord.
They say that a mouthful (*grāsa*) is the measure of a single *bhikṣā*;
four times that is a *puṣkala*, and four times a *puṣkala* is called an *hantakāra*.
One should personally wait for a guest for as long as it takes to milk a cow;
one should honor those who have arrived according to one's ability, just as one would honor a guest.
One should indeed give alms according to the rule to a mendicant who observes the vow of celibacy;
free from greed, one should give food to those in need according to one's ability.
But if not even all of these are available, one should offer food to the cows;
then, remaining silent and without disparaging the food, one should eat it together with one's kinsmen.
O best of the twice-born, if a twice-born man eats without having performed the five great sacrifices,
that deluded soul goes to the womb of an animal.
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices,
forbearance, and likewise the worship of the gods, quickly destroy all sins.
He who, out of delusion or laziness, eats without having performed the worship of the deity,
goes to the hells and is reborn among pigs.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, having performed all rites with every effort, one should eat together with one's own kin; thus one goes to the supreme goal.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Upper Division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
One should eat one’s food facing the east or indeed facing the sun.
Seated upon a pure seat, having placed his two feet upon the ground, he should remain there.
One who eats facing east gains long life; facing south, one gains fame;
facing west, one enjoys prosperity; and facing north, one enjoys truth.
One should eat while the five [limbs] are still moist, having placed the vessel upon the ground;
Prajāpati Manu has declared that this is equal to fasting.
Having washed his feet and hands in a clean, smeared place,
and having sipped water with a moist face and free from anger, he should take his meal while five parts of him remain wet.
Having enveloped the food with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and with water, one should perform the ritual of *āpośāna* with the mantra: "Thou art the spreading of the nectar. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.19.5)
Then, one should offer the first oblation for the vital breath (prāṇa), joined with the syllable *svāhā* and the *praṇava*;
after that, having offered for the downward breath (apāna), one should immediately thereafter offer for the pervasive breath (vyāna).
Then he should perform the offering for *udāna*, and the fifth for *samāna*;
having understood the true nature of these, the twice-born man should offer them into his own self.
Having meditated in his mind upon the Lord, the Self, who is indeed Prajāpati, one should eat the remaining food as desired together with people.
With the mantra "Thou art the covering of immortality," he should drink water from above; having sipped water once, he should sip again with the mantra "This cow... (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.19.9).
Or, having recited the *drupadā* mantra three times, which destroys all sins,
he should then touch his heart with the mantra beginning, "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths."
Having sipped water, with the thumb of his right foot measuring [the height of the water], he should,
with hands raised and composed, pour the water from his hand down upon his right big toe.
One should perform the consecration of the oblation with the mantra beginning "śraddhāyām";
then, indeed, one should unite oneself with Brahman by means of the syllable Om. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.19.12)
Of all sacrifices, the sacrifice of the self is remembered as the supreme;
he who performs it according to this rule goes to the abode of Brahmā.
Wearing the sacred thread, adorned with garlands and fragrances, and being pure,
he should eat in the evening and the morning, and especially during the twilight hours.
One should not eat before a solar eclipse during the day, nor after a lunar eclipse in the evening;
one should not eat during the time of the eclipse itself, but may eat after bathing once both have been released.
One should eat when the moon has been released [from eclipse], provided it is not the dead of night;
if both have not yet been released or have already set, one should eat on the following day after seeing them.
A foolish person should not eat without first giving [a portion] to those who are looking on;
nor should one eat without the remnants of a sacrifice, nor while angry, nor with a distracted mind.
For one whose eating is for his own sake, whose sexual union is for pleasure, and whose study is for livelihood, his life is fruitless. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.19.18)
Whatever one eats with the head covered, whatever one eats facing north, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes—all that should be known as pertaining to the Asuras. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.19.19)
Not at midnight, nor at midday, nor when one has indigestion, nor while wearing wet clothes;
nor while seated on a broken seat, nor while lying down, nor even while standing.
One should not take clarified butter from a broken vessel, nor from the ground, nor from one's own hands; while impure from eating, one should neither take it nor even touch one's head.
One should not recite the Veda while speaking with others, nor when not concluding it, nor in the company of one's wife;
nor in darkness, nor in the open air, nor in temples and similar places.
One should not eat while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing on a vehicle or a bed; nor should one eat while wearing sandals, nor while laughing or even while lamenting.
Having eaten thus and established himself in comfort, he should digest that food;
he should augment the meaning of the Vedas by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Then the twice-born man should perform the twilight worship according to the previously mentioned rule;
sitting down, he should recite the goddess Gāyatrī toward the west.
But he who neither stands during the morning twilight nor sits during the evening twilight is equal to a Śūdra in this world, being devoid of all dharma.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules with mantras, and having eaten the remnants of the sacrifice,
he should sleep at night on a dry bed together with his servants and kinsmen.
One should not sleep facing north, nor facing west;
nor in the open air, nor naked, nor while impure, nor on a seat anywhere.
One should never sleep on a broken bedstead, nor indeed in an empty house; nor on a bed made of bamboo, nor on one made of *pālāśa* wood.
Thus, day after day, I have indeed explained in its entirety this collection of duties for Brahmins, which bestows the fruit of liberation.
The Brahmin who does not perform [this] out of atheism or laziness goes to terrible hells and is born into the womb of a crow.
There is no other path to liberation than one's own prescribed duty (*āśrama-vidhi*);
therefore, perform rituals for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the upper division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Now, the Śrāddha ceremony should be performed by the best of the twice-born when the new moon day (Amāvāsyā) arrives.
The Piṇḍānvāhāryaka rite, when performed with devotion, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The Śrāddha consisting of the Anvāhārya rice-ball is recommended when the moon has waned;
it should be performed in the afternoon for the twice-born, and with highly praised meat.
For in the dark fortnight, the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) are recommended in ascending order,
with the exception of the fourteenth day.
The new moon day, the three Aṣṭakās in the months beginning with Pauṣa,
the three Anvaṣṭakās, and likewise the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha, are meritorious.
The thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism, especially during the rainy season,
is declared to be the constant time for the Śrāddha ceremony upon the ripening of grain, to be observed day after day.
However, on the occasion of an eclipse of the moon or the sun, and upon the death of a kinsman, one must perform the rite; otherwise, one would become a denizen of hell.

One should also perform optional śrāddhas at the end of the harvest seasons, during eclipses and the like, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, and on the occasion of the vyatīpāta yoga; these yield infinite merit.
The Śrāddha performed on the days of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) is inexhaustible, as is that performed on birthdays;
it should be performed on all lunar mansions (nakṣatras), especially for those rites intended to fulfill specific desires (kāmya).
Having performed [the rite] under the asterism Kṛttikā, the best of the twice-born attains heaven;
under Rohiṇī, he obtains offspring; and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), he gains spiritual luster.
The accomplishment of fierce deeds and valor is attained in Ārdrā;
likewise, land and prosperity are gained in Punarvasu, and the same for Puṣya.
Likewise, one obtains all desires under the constellation Āśleṣā; under Maghā, good fortune;
under Ārdrā, one shall find wealth; and under Phālgunī, the destruction of sin.
Under Hasta one attains preeminence among kinsmen, and under Citrā many sons;
under Svātī there is success in trade, and under Viśākhā, gold.
In Maitra (Anurādhā), there are many friends; likewise in Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā), one gains a kingdom.
Under Mūla, one obtains success in agriculture; under Āpya (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), one attains success through watercraft from the sea.
One obtains all desires under the Vaiśvadeva constellation, preeminence under Śravaṇa,
likewise desires under Śraviṣṭhā, and supreme strength under Vāruṇa.
Under Ajaikapāda, there shall be base metals; under Ahirbudhnya, an auspicious house;
under Revatī, many cows; and likewise under Aśvinī, horses.
Furthermore, under Yama (Bharaṇī), that livelihood shall be attained if one offers the Śrāddha.
On Sunday there is health; on Monday, good fortune;
on Tuesday, victory everywhere; and on Wednesday, all desires are fulfilled.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), one obtains desired knowledge if Jupiter is there, wealth if Venus is there,
long life if Rāhu is there, and auspicious sons if the Moon is there.
On the second day one obtains a daughter; on the third, bards;
on the fourth, small livestock; and on the fifth, handsome sons.

On the sixth day, a man obtains success in gambling and agriculture; on the seventh, he gains [success in] agriculture; and on the eighth, the one who offers the śrāddha always obtains success in trade.
On the ninth day, there is a single-hoofed animal; on the tenth, many two-hoofed animals;
and on the eleventh, likewise silver, as well as sons endowed with Vedic splendor.
On the twelfth day, the giver of the śrāddha always obtains gold, silver, and base metals;
on the thirteenth, preeminence among kinsmen; on the fourteenth, however, offspring who are prone to anger;
and on the fifteenth, he attains all desires.
Therefore, the twice-born should not perform a śrāddha on the fourteenth day;
however, they may indeed arrange a śrāddha for those who were slain by a weapon on that day.
When the excellence of the material substance and the brāhmaṇa recipient is present, no restriction regarding time is prescribed;
therefore, the twice-born should perform the śrāddha for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
In all undertakings of ritual action, one should again perform that which leads to prosperity;
on occasions such as the birth of a son, the Śrāddha is prescribed, and on festival days (parvan), the Pārvaṇa rite is ordained.

The daily rite should be performed constantly day after day; furthermore, the optional and the occasional rites, as well as the *ekoddiṣṭa* and others, should be understood [as distinct], while the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is of the *pārvaṇa* type.
These five kinds of *śrāddha* have been proclaimed by Manu;
the sixth is declared to be for the sake of a journey, and one should observe it with great care.
The seventh Śrāddha was described by Brahmā for the sake of purification;
the eighth is the Daivika Śrāddha, by performing which one is released from fear.
One should not perform [the rite] during the two twilights or at night, except when there is a visible eclipse of Rāhu;
moreover, in certain specific regions, it shall yield infinite merit.
"The ancestors sing this verse and the wise proclaim it: 'The Śrāddha performed on the Gaṅgā, at Prayāga, and at Amarakaṇṭaka is inexhaustible. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.20.29)
One should desire many sons who are virtuous and endowed with good qualities;
for if even one among them, when they are gathered together, should go to Gayā.
If, upon reaching Gayā incidentally, one should perform a śrāddha ceremony,
his ancestors are thereby delivered, and he goes to the supreme goal.
And especially on Mount Varāha, and particularly at the Gaṅgā,
and especially at Vārāṇasī, where the god Hara himself resides.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prabhāsa, at Bilvaka, on Mount Nīla,
at Kurukṣetra, at Kubjāmra, at Bhṛgutuṅga, and at Mahālaya.
At Kedāra, at Phalgutīrtha, and indeed at Naimiṣāraṇya;
especially at the Sarasvatī, and most particularly at the Puṣkaras.
At Kuśāvarta on the Narmadā, at Śrīśaila and Bhadrakarṇaka,
and especially at the Vetravatī, the Vipāśā, and the Godāvarī.
In such and other sacred fords, on sandy banks,
and on the shores of rivers, the ancestors are always gratified.
With rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits;
with *śyāmāka* millet, *yava* barley, vegetables, wild rice, and *priyaṅgu*;
or with wheat, sesame, and mung beans—one gratifies the ancestors for a month. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.20.37)
At the time of the śrāddha, one should cause mangoes, sugarcane, grapes, pomegranates, vidārī, and bhaṇḍa to be offered.
One should offer parched grains mixed with honey, and groats together with sugar;
one should diligently offer water-chestnuts and lotus stalks at the śrāddha ceremony.
For two months one may subsist on fish-meat, for three months on the meat of the deer,
for four months on the meat of sheep, and for five months here on the meat of birds.

For six months one should offer goat meat, or indeed for seven months venison; for eight months with the meat of the Eṇa deer, and for nine months with the meat of the Ruru deer. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.20.41)
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boar and buffalo;
however, by the flesh of rabbit and tortoise, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
By means of cow's milk, by milk-rice (pāyasa),
and by the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa, satisfaction lasting for twelve years is attained for one year.
Black potherb, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red deer, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for sages lead indeed to infinity.

Whether having purchased it, obtained it, or even having brought it himself from those who have died, a twice-born man should diligently offer it at a śrāddha; that is said to be inexhaustible for him.
Long pepper, betel nut, and likewise lentils;
pumpkin, bottle gourd, eggplant, bhūstṛṇa, and likewise surasa.
One should indeed avoid safflower, piṇḍamūla, and tandulīyaka,
as well as kidney beans and buffalo milk.
At the time of a śrāddha, the best of the twice-born should avoid, with every effort, kodrava, kovidāra, pālakyā, and likewise black pepper.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the latter section of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Having bathed as prescribed and having offered libations to the ancestors during the waning of the moon, the twice-born man...
With a serene mind and being pure, he should perform the Śrāddha rite consisting of the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka.
One should first examine a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
he is considered a worthy recipient for the offering of sacrificial oblations to gods and ancestors, and is regarded as a guest.
Those who drink soma, who are free from passion, knowers of dharma, and tranquil in mind;
who observe vows, abide by their restraints, and approach their wives only during the proper season.
Even one who maintains the five fires, one who studies [the Vedas], one who knows the Yajurveda, a Bahvṛca (Rigvedin), or one who possesses the Trisauparṇa or the Trimadhu; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.4.
One who has mastered the Triṇāciketa, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman chants, a student of the Atharvaśiras, and especially one who recites the Rudrādhyāya; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.5.

The learned man devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, one who knows the rules of logic, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, and he who is a reciter of the Dharma; // KūrmP_2.21.6 //
One who observes the vows of a seer, one who is like a seer, as well as one who has performed the twelve-year penance,
one whose lineage is descended from those given by Brahmā, one pure in conception, and a giver of a thousand— [these are the ones to be honored].
One who observes the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, speaks the truth, knows the Purāṇas,
is devoted to the worship of the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, and is intent upon knowledge.
Liberated from everything, steadfast, having become Brahman, the best of the twice-born,
devoted to the worship of Mahādeva, a Vaiṣṇava— he is the purifier of the assembly.
Those who are constantly devoted to non-violence and likewise refrain from accepting gifts,
as well as those who perform sacrifices and are intent on giving— these should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
Young, learned in the Vedas, healthy, and devoted to the great sacrifices; Brahmins who are intent on the recitation of the Sāvitrī and who purify the assembly at meals.
Those who are of noble birth, learned in the scriptures, possessed of good character, and ascetic;
Brahmins who maintain the sacred fires and have completed their student vows—these are to be known as the sanctifiers of the assembly.
A twice-born man who is devoted to the welfare of his mother and father, who bathes at dawn,
who is a sage learned in the supreme self, and who is self-controlled, should be known as a purifier of the assembly.
Established in knowledge, a great yogi, and a contemplator of the meaning of the Vedānta;
full of faith, devoted to ancestral rites, such a Brāhmaṇa is a sanctifier of the assembly.
A Brāhmaṇa who delights in the knowledge of the Vedas, has performed his ritual ablutions, is ever devoted to celibacy,
belongs to the Atharvaveda, and seeks liberation, is a sanctifier of the assembly.
For a Brāhmaṇa who has not shared the same *pravara*, as well as one who does not belong to the same *gotra* and is not a relative, should be known as a purifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
One should first feed a yogin who is a renunciant devoted to the knowledge of reality;
in his absence, one should feed a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) who is self-controlled, or likewise a student (upakurvāṇaka).
If such a person is not available, one should feed a householder who seeks liberation and is free from attachments;
if no one at all is available, one may even feed a practicing householder.
For that ascetic who, knowing the true nature of the qualities of Prakṛti, partakes of the sacrificial oblation,
his reward exceeds that of a thousand knowers of the Vedas.

Therefore, with diligence, one should feed a lord of yogins who is intent upon the knowledge of the Lord during offerings to the gods and ancestors, rather than other twice-born men if they are unavailable.
This indeed is the primary rule regarding the offering of oblations to the gods and the ancestors;
however, this secondary rule should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the preceptor, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a kinsman, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; rather, one should win him over with wealth, for such a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs to the *piśācas* and yields no fruit in the hereafter.
At a *śrāddha*, one should honor a friend, but not an enemy, even if he is otherwise worthy; for an oblation consumed by an enemy becomes fruitless after death. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.24)
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.
Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit,
so too a donor who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain fruit.
As many morsels as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows during offerings to the gods and ancestors,
so many glowing, massive iron balls shall he swallow after death.

O twice-born ones, even if they are endowed with learning and noble lineage, those lowest of men who follow a degraded conduct— if such persons consume the sacrificial offering (havya), that becomes demonic (āsura).
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar have been severed for three generations is indeed a base Brāhmaṇa and is never worthy of being invited to Śrāddha and other rites.
A servant of a Śūdra, one hired by a king, a low-born man who officiates at village sacrifices,
and one who subsists on killing and binding— these six are mere Brahmins in name (brahmabandhus).
Manu declared that those who accept gifts for the sake of their livelihood have fallen;
indeed, these sellers of the Veda are censured at śrāddha ceremonies and other rites.
Those who sell the Vedas, those born of women previously married to others,
and those who officiate at sacrifices for persons of unequal status— these are proclaimed to be fallen.
Those who teach the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), those servants who cause others to teach it,
and likewise those who study the Vedas [in such a manner], are proclaimed to be fallen.
The Vṛddha-śrāvakas, the Nirgranthas, people who know the five nights (the Pāñcarātras),
the Kāpālikas, the Pāśupatas, and those heretics of similar kind.
If these evil-minded ones of a tamasic nature eat the sacrificial offerings,
that śrāddha will not yield fruit for him either in this world or after death.
O Brahmins, those twice-born men who belong to no stage of life, those who belong to a stage of life in vain,
and those who adopt a stage of life falsely— these should be known as defilers of the assembly.

One with diseased skin, one with deformed nails, one afflicted by leprosy, one with white spots, one with black teeth, one whose generative organ is pierced, a thief, a eunuch, and likewise an atheist; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.37.

A drinker of intoxicants, one attached to a low-caste woman, a slayer of a hero, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, an arsonist of houses, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, and twice-born men who sell *soma*—these are [excluded]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.38)

One who marries before his elder brother, a violent man, one whose younger brother marries first, one who has been expelled from his caste, the son of a remarried woman, a lazy man, and likewise one who subsists by astrology; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.39.
One who is devoted to singing and instrumental music, one who is diseased, one who is one-eyed,
one with missing limbs, one with redundant limbs, and likewise one who has broken his vow of celibacy (an avakīrṇin).

One who defiles a maiden, one born from a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka*, one accused of a grave crime, a temple-priest for hire, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, and one who is constantly subservient to his wife; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.21.41.
One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher; likewise one who abandons his wife;
one who has betrayed his lineage, one who has fallen from purity, and likewise one who touches a [missile] shaft while impure; KūrmP 2.21.42.
One who is childless, a false witness, a beggar, one who lives by the stage, a sea-faring merchant, a betrayer of trusts, and likewise a breaker of agreements.
Those who are intent on reviling the gods, those who delight in reviling the Vedas, and those who delight in reviling the twice-born— these are to be avoided at rites such as the śrāddha.
The ungrateful, the slanderer, the cruel, the atheist, the reviler of the Vedas,
the betrayer of friends, and the deceiver— these especially are defilers of the row [at a meal].
Furthermore, all those whose food is unfit to be eaten, who are unworthy of receiving gifts for religious rites,
and who have been cast out by the Brahmanas must be avoided with great effort.
A Brāhmaṇa whose limbs are nourished by the food of a Śūdra, who neglects the twilight prayers,
and who is devoid of the great sacrifices, is a defiler of the assembly.
One who causes the loss of what has been studied, one who is devoid of ritual bathing and burnt offerings,
and one who is of tamasic or rajasic nature— such a Brāhmaṇa is a defiler of the assembly.
What need is there for much speaking here? Those who do not perform what is enjoined and practice what is censured must be avoided with great effort.
Thus, in the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses, in the latter section, the twenty-first chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having purified the ground with cow-dung and water, being composed in mind, [one should proceed].
Having assembled all the twice-born, he should invite them together with virtuous men.

"My śrāddha will take place tomorrow; therefore, having honored [the guests] on the previous day—or, if that is not possible, on the day before—[one should invite those] endowed with the characteristics as previously described."
When they hear that the time for the śrāddha has arrived, those ancestors,
having reflected upon one another in their minds, descend with the speed of thought.
For the ancestors dwelling in the intermediate space eat together with those brahmins;
having become like the wind, they remain there, and after eating, they proceed to the supreme goal.
And when the time for the śrāddha has arrived, those invited brāhmaṇas should all remain self-restrained, devoted to celibacy.
Free from anger, not hasty, not intoxicated, truthful in speech, and composed,
one who performs the *śrāddha* rite should avoid recitation (*japa*) while carrying a burden, during sexual intercourse, or while traveling on a road.
Whether it be a Brahmin or anyone else who, having been invited, grants his permission to another [to eat],
he goes to a terrible hell and attains the state of a pig.
Having invited one [brahmin], he who out of delusion invites another brahmin instead becomes a sinner even more grave than that [first offender] and is reborn as a worm in excrement.
A Brahmin who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, engages in sexual intercourse,
incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and is born into the womb of an animal.
If an invited Brahmin, being of wicked mind, goes on a journey,
his ancestors shall subsist on dust for that entire month.
If a twice-born man, having been invited to a śrāddha, should engage in a quarrel,
his ancestors will consume excrement for that entire month.
Therefore, a twice-born man invited to a *śrāddha* should remain self-restrained;
he should be free from anger, devoted to purity, and a performer who has conquered his senses.
When the next day has dawned, having gone toward the southern direction with a concentrated mind,
he should fetch very pure darbha grass together with its roots, with the tips pointing southward.
One should smear with cow dung a pure and secluded place that slopes toward the south, is smooth, well-proportioned, and possesses auspicious characteristics.
The ancestors are always satisfied by what is given on the banks of rivers, at sacred fords (tīrthas), on their own lands, on mountain ridges, and in secluded places. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.22.15)
One should never offer oblations to the ancestors on land belonging to another;
whatever is performed by men out of delusion on such ground is obstructed by the owners.
Forests, mountains, sacred fords, and shrines—
all these are said to be without owners, for there is no private possession over them.
One should scatter sesame seeds there and tie goats on all sides;
everything defiled by Asuras is purified by sesame seeds or by a goat.
Then, one should prepare food according to one's ability— well-prepared with many condiments, not lacking in variety, and enriched with items to be sucked and drunk.
Then, when midday has passed, he should approach the twice-born whose hair and nails have been trimmed and provide them with a tooth-stick according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oil for anointing, bathing water, and various kinds of bath-powders using vessels made of udumbara wood, preceded by offerings to the Viśvedevas.
Then, having bathed and returned, he should rise to meet them with palms joined in reverence and offer water for the feet and water for sipping in due order.
And those Brahmins who have been previously invited here for the Viśvedevas should have their seats facing east, each provided with three blades of darbha grass.
The seats for the ancestors should be arranged facing south,
with single blades of darbha grass pointing toward the south, and they must be sprinkled with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Having touched the seats, he should cause those twice-born ones to sit upon them while addressing each one individually, saying, "Be seated. KūrmP 2.22.25.

In the rite for the gods, two [seats] should face east; likewise, in the rite for the ancestors, three should face north. Or there may be one each for those of the gods and the maternal grandfather as well.
Hospitality, proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmin—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.
Alternatively, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning, virtuous conduct, and other such qualities, and who is free from inauspicious marks.
Having again taken that food from all the prepared meal into a vessel,
he should offer it in a temple and then proceed with the rest.
One should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin);
therefore, one should feed even a single eminent learned twice-born man.
Whether it be a mendicant or a celibate student who has arrived for the sake of food, one should,
if desired, feed him as well once those invited to the *śrāddha* have been seated.
That śrāddha in which a guest does not eat is not praised;
therefore, guests should indeed be honored with great effort by the twice-born during śrāddhas.
Those twice-born who eat at a śrāddha that is devoid of hospitality go to the womb of a crow, as does the giver; of this there is no doubt.
One with missing limbs, one who has fallen from his caste, a leper, one with open sores,
a Pukkasa, an atheist, as well as cocks, pigs, and dogs— these should be avoided from afar at Śrāddha ceremonies.
One should avoid one who is loathsome, impure, naked, intoxicated, or deceitful; a woman in her menses; one dressed in blue or saffron robes; and those belonging to heretical sects.
Whatever rite pertaining to the ancestors is performed there with respect to the Brahmins,
all of that must be performed preceded by the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Once they have all been seated, the decorator should adorn them with garlands,
head-wraps, incense, garments, and unguents.
Then, with the permission of the Brahmins, he should invoke the gods facing north, according to the rule, with the verse beginning "viśve devāsaḥ."
Then, having taken two strainers and poured water into a washed vessel with the mantra "śaṃ no devī," he likewise adds barley grains with the mantra "yavo 'si."
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should pour the *argha* water into the hand;
one should also offer perfumes, garlands, incense, and so forth, according to one's ability.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and facing south for the ancestors,
the wise man should perform the invocation with the verse beginning "uśantas tvā."
Having invoked [the ancestors] and being permitted by them, he should then recite:
"May they come to us," "May the divine waters be auspicious to us," and likewise "Thou art sesame" over the water in the vessel and the sesame seeds.
Having offered the *argha* as before and having again placed [water] in their hands, he,
being composed, should then collect all the remnants (*saṃsrava*) into a vessel;
with this [mantra], he should cause the vessel to be placed face down as the seat for the ancestors.
Saying "I shall offer into the fire," he takes up food soaked in ghee and asks for permission;
being granted leave with the words "Do so," he, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, should perform the oblation.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin), holding kuśa grass in the hand;
the rite for the ancestors (pitrya) should be performed with the thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), while the rite for the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadeva) is like the fire-oblation.
A man attending upon the gods should cause his right knee to touch the ground;
likewise, in the service of the ancestors, he should cause the other [left knee] to touch it.
Saying, "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! Homage! one should then offer an oblation with the words, "To Agni, the bearer of the *kavyas*, Svadhā! (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.22.47).
In the absence of fire, however, one who is well-composed should place [the offering] directly into the hand of a Brahmin,
or in the presence of Mahādeva, or in a cow-pen.
Then, permitted by them, he went to the southern direction,
smeared his feet with cow-dung, and prepared a sandy spot as a sacred site.
The mandala should be square or sloping toward the south, which is auspicious;
one should indeed scratch its center three times with a single blade of darbha grass.
Then, having spread darbha grass with their tips pointing toward the south in that place,
he, being composed, should offer three pindas there from the remains of the sacrificial oblation.
Having offered the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he should wipe that hand on those *darbha* grasses for the sake of the "smear-partakers" (*lepabhāgin*).
Then, having sipped water (*ācamya*) and slowly restraining his breath three times, the knower of mantras should pay homage to that food and to the ancestors themselves. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.22.52)
One should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls;
then, being composed, one should smell those rice balls in the order they were placed.
Then, one should cause the twice-born to eat the food remaining from the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the prescribed rite;
one should give them meats, various cakes, and dishes of kṛsara and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Soup, vegetables, fruits, sugarcane, milk, curd, ghee, honey, and various kinds of food, snacks, and drinks, according to one's desire. ||| KūrmP_2.22.55 |||
Whatever is desired by the foremost of the twice-born, all that one should offer:
grains, sesame seeds of various kinds, and likewise various types of sugar.
One who desires the highest good should give warm food to the twice-born,
with the exception of fruits, roots, and likewise beverages.
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
That which is given in anger, that which is eaten again in haste,
and that which is offered while talking— these the Yātudhānas plunder.
One whose body is perspiring should not remain in the presence of the twice-born;
nor should one drive away birds such as hawks or crows from that place,
for it is the ancestors in those very forms who arrive there, desiring food.
One should not give salt directly with the hand,
nor from an iron vessel, nor indeed without faith.
That which is given in a vessel made of gold, or of silver or udumbara wood, attains imperishability; this is especially true when the gift is given in a vessel of rhinoceros horn.
He who indeed feeds the ancestors at a śrāddha in an earthen vessel goes to a terrible hell, as do the one who eats there and the officiating priest.
One should not give unequally in a row, nor should one beg, nor cause others to give;
the one who begs, the one who causes to give, and the giver all go to terrible hells.
The remaining [guests] should eat while restrained in speech and should not speak of ordinary qualities;
for the ancestors eat only so long as the qualities of the sacrificial food have not been mentioned.
A twice-born man should not eat first while seated on a seat of honor;
among many looking on, that ignorant man takes upon himself the sins of the entire row.
An excellent twice-born man who has been appointed to a śrāddha ceremony should avoid nothing;
he should not forbid meat, nor should he look with disapproval at the food of another.
That twice-born man who does not eat meat when appointed to a rite for the ancestors goes,
after death, to the state of a beast for twenty-one successive births.
He should cause them to hear their own sacred recitations (svādhyāya), as well as the treatises on Dharma,
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and the auspicious ritual manuals for Śrāddha ceremonies.
Then, after they have eaten, he should scatter some food on the ground in front of them;
having asked, "Are you satisfied?", he should then cause those who are satisfied to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
After they have sipped water, he should give permission, saying, "May you rest at your ease";
and immediately thereafter, the Brāhmaṇas should say to him, "Svadhā! (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.22.71).
Then, once they have finished eating, one should offer them the remainder of the food;
having been authorized by the twice-born, one should act exactly as they direct.
At a rite for the ancestors, the appropriate expression is "svaditam"; in the cow-pens, "sūnṛtam";
at a prosperity-rite, "saṃpannam"; and at a rite for the gods, "rocate."
Having dismissed those Brahmins according to the rites for the gods, he should remain silent and,
facing the southern direction, request these boons from the ancestors.
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
One should give the rice-balls to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else cast them into fire or water;
however, the wife who desires a son should eat the middlemost rice-ball from among them.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should satisfy his kinsmen with the remainder;
when the kinsmen have also been satisfied, he should then feed his own servants.
Afterwards, he himself, together with his wives, should partake of the remaining food.
One should not remove that leavings until the sun has set;
for that night, the couple should remain as celibates.
He who, having given a śrāddha and likewise having eaten, engages in sexual intercourse,
reaches the Mahāraurava hell and then enters the womb of an insect once more.
Pure, free from anger, tranquil, truthful, and composed, one should avoid reciting the Vedas while traveling on a road, as well as eating [in such circumstances]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.22.80)
Those twice-born who, having eaten at one *śrāddha*, eat at another *śrāddha*,
are equal to those who commit great sins and go to many hells.
This eternal ritual procedure for the śrāddha has been correctly prescribed for you;
one who knows the truth, remaining detached, should always subsist on raw food.
A twice-born man who is without a sacred fire, or one traveling on a journey, or likewise one afflicted by calamity,
may perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food) if he is knowledgeable in the rules and endowed with faith;
he should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite with that [raw food] and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) with that very same [food].
He who, with a restrained mind, performs the ancestral rite (śrāddha) according to this method,
being eternally free from defilement, abides in the station of the yogins.
Therefore, the best of the twice-born should perform the śrāddha with every effort;
by that, the eternal Lord is properly propitiated.
Even a poor twice-born man may perform [the rite] with roots or even fruits;
or, having bathed with a concentrated mind, he should satisfy the ancestors with water and sesame seeds.
One whose father is living should not offer [the śrāddha]; it is declared that [the rite] ends with the homa.
Or, some authorities declare that for those for whom the father himself would offer [it], the son may do so.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
to whichever among these one dies, [the offering] should be given to him by that person, and not to anyone else.
Or one may feed the living [deceased] according to one's desire with devotion;
for it is heard in the Śruti that one does not give by bypassing those who are still alive.
A son born of two fathers (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa) shall give an equal share to both the progenitor and the owner of the field;
however, if he was procreated through the practice of *niyoga*, he shall take half of the inheritance from the estate.
A son who is born here without being appointed, but through payment (śulka), shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the progenitor;
otherwise, he shall offer it to the owner of the field (the husband).
One should offer two funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to those two— the owner of the field and the sower of the seed—
and then one should mention the sower and the owner of the field in a single [cake].
On the anniversary of the day of death, the ekoddiṣṭa rite must be performed according to the prescribed rule;
once one's own period of impurity has completely ceased, the optional (kāmya) rite may again be performed at will.
A person seeking prosperity should perform the Śrāddha in the forenoon;
everything should be done like that for the gods, and the rites involving sesame seeds should be performed with barley.
The darbha grass should be made straight, and one should feed an even number of brahmins;
one should cause them to recite: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased."
The śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed by that for the paternal ancestors;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—thus, at a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi), three śrāddhas are prescribed.
One should indeed offer [the oblation] preceded by the *dava* rite; one should not perform it without circumambulation.
Facing the east, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), and being composed, one should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
First, however, the Mothers, together with Gaṇeśvara, should indeed be worshipped with devotion upon various sacrificial altars, in images, or in the presence of the twice-born.
Having worshipped the host of Mothers with flowers, incense, food offerings, perfumes, and ornaments, the wise man should perform the three śrāddhas.
If one serves the śrāddha meal without having performed the sacrifice to the Mothers (mātṛ-yāga),
the Mothers, possessed by wrath, will seek to cause him harm.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: The wise declare that the period of impurity for sapindas lasts ten days.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies] when Brahmins have died or been born.

One should not perform any prescribed rites, whether they are obligatory (nitya) or especially those performed for specific desires (kāmya), nor even mentally recite the Vedic study (svādhyāya). KūrmP 2.23.2.
One should honor pure, non-angry, and earth-dwelling twice-born men at the hall-fire;
likewise, one should offer oblations into the sacrificial fire with dry food or even with fruits.
Others should not touch these [remains], nor should one bring them from them;
contact is declared by the wise to occur on the fourth or fifth day.
During the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), however, physical contact with the sapinda relatives does not cause defilement for men,
provided that they avoid the woman who has given birth and the state of impurity itself.

The father who is a student of the Vedas, a performer of sacrifices, and a knower of the Vedas—all of these may be touched immediately; however, the mother [may be touched] after ten days from her ritual bath.
Impurity is declared to last ten days for one devoid of qualities, and twelve days for one who is utterly devoid of qualities;
for those endowed with one, two, or three qualities, one becomes pure after four, three, or two days respectively.
But after ten days, one may properly study and offer oblations;
on the fourth day, Prajāpati Manu has declared that one may touch him.
They say that for one who is devoid of ritual action, a fool, or even one who is gravely ill,
as well as for one who acts according to their own whims, impurity lasts until death.
The period of impurity for Brāhmaṇas lasts either three nights or ten nights;
it shall be three nights prior to the sacramental rites, and ten nights thereafter.
When a child less than two years old dies, that [impurity] is prescribed for the mother and father;
however, any other person becomes pure after three nights, provided they are utterly devoid of merit.
In the case of death before the eruption of teeth, a one-day period of impurity is prescribed for the parents;
if the teeth have erupted, it shall be three nights, provided they are devoid of virtuous qualities.
Until the eruption of teeth, impurity lasts for an immediate day;
until the tonsure ceremony, it lasts for one night; and until the initiation ceremony (upanayana), it is declared that for sapinda relatives, it lasts for three nights.
If the death of the father or the mother should occur for a newborn infant, that would constitute *sūtaka*;
yet the father would indeed be fit to be touched.
Immediate purification must be observed by the sapinda relatives and the uterine brother;
however, after ten days have passed, the uterine brother is purified in one day if he is devoid of merit.
Now, after the eruption of teeth, the period of impurity for sapinda relatives is one night for those devoid of qualities;
beyond the wearing of clothes [i.e., after the first year], it is three nights.
O best of beings, if death should occur before the eruption of teeth,
the sapindas shall observe impurity for one night, provided they are utterly devoid of merit.
Prior to the instruction for the vows, bathing is prescribed for all sapinda relatives;
however, for those possessing [Vedic] learning, it is again different after that time.
If there should be a miscarriage among women within six months,
then their period of impurity is prescribed by tradition to be equal in number of days to the number of months [of pregnancy].
But after that, in the case of a miscarriage, the purification for women lasts twelve nights;
however, for the sapinda relatives, there is immediate purification, or it may be according to the [duration of the] pregnancy.

In the case of a miscarriage, the impurity lasts for one day and night; for a sapinda who is utterly devoid of merit, it lasts three nights; and for a kinsman who behaves according to his own whims, this is the settled rule.

If a birth should occur during a period of birth-impurity, or death during a period of death-impurity, purification shall occur by means of the remainder alone; if there is a remainder of a day, it takes three nights.
In the case of a conjunction involving death or birth, purification is held to occur after the death;
however, if there is an increase in impurity (*aghavṛddhi*), one is purified by the subsequent [period].
But if it should occur after the fifth night has passed,
then that impurity, which involves an increase in sin, is purified by the preceding period.
Upon hearing of birth or death occurring in another country,
a mortal remains impure until the period of impurity has fully elapsed.
Regarding a birth-impurity (sūtaka) that occurred in the past, it has been declared that for sapindas there is a period of three nights;
likewise, in the case of a death, if it occurs after one year has passed, purification is attained through bathing alone.
For one who knows the Vedānta, who is studying it, who maintains the sacred fires, and who is emaciated by his religious observances,
there shall always be immediate purification in all circumstances and at all times.

But for women who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the impurity for sapinda relatives shall always be three nights prior to their marriage; however, once the rite is performed, it lasts only for the duration of the husband's impurity.
In the case of unmarried girls who have not been given away in marriage, impurity is prescribed upon their death;
however, in the case of the death of children less than two years old, immediate purification is declared.
For a uterine brother, impurity lasts until the teeth erupt; until the tonsure ceremony (caula), it lasts for one night;
until the giving of the bride (pradāna), it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, it lasts for ten nights.
Upon the death of maternal grandfathers, there shall be a period of impurity for three nights;
likewise, this same rule applies upon the death of those entitled to offer water (ekodaka) and in the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
In the case of a relationship through the womb (uterine kin), as well as among other kinsmen,
and likewise for a teacher or a fellow student of the Veda, one night is prescribed.
When the king has died, for one who resides within his realm, [the impurity lasts] as long as the light [of the sun or moon];
when daughters have died or been given away in marriage, it lasts for three days for the father.

In the case of wives who have had previous husbands, as well as adopted sons, one should observe a three-night period of impurity; likewise for a teacher and for one's own wives who have gone to another man.
For the son of a teacher and for his wife, it is declared that [impurity lasts] one day and night;
for a sub-teacher (upādhyāya) and for a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) within one's own village, it shall be one day.
If those who are not *asapiṇḍa* relatives die in one's own house, the impurity lasts for three nights;
if it is a person of lower caste, it lasts for one day; that is what is prescribed.
In the event of the death of a mother-in-law, it is likewise for three nights; indeed, the same applies to the death of a father-in-law.
Immediate purification (sadyaḥ-śauca) is prescribed when a member of one's own lineage (sagotra) has passed away.
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a king (Kṣatriya) in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra becomes pure in a month.
If there are kinsmen of a Brahmin who are heirs from the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes,
it is prescribed that the purification for the Brahmin occurs after ten days, even during their period of impurity.
Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas likewise, when born from wombs of lower castes, should undoubtedly perform their own specific purification for the sake of purity. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.23.40)

All those of the higher castes should respectfully perform the impurity rites for them according to the rules prescribed for their own caste; however, they should perform their own purification rites among those of their own birth.
For Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas, the period of impurity shall be six nights, three nights, or one night respectively; however, for Śūdras, it is simply [the same duration] as their own [caste].
O best of the twice-born, for Śūdras, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas, the period of impurity in the case of Vaiśyas is prescribed as half a month, six nights, and three nights, respectively.
O best of the twice-born, impurity for a Kṣatriya is declared to be six nights for Brāhmaṇas, ten days for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and [ten days] respectively for the others.
"But when a Brāhmaṇa has died, the purification for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas shall take ten nights; so said the Lotus-born One."
Having carried out a deceased twice-born person who is not a sapinda relative like a kinsman,
and having eaten with him and lived together, a Brahmin becomes pure after ten nights.
If one eats the food of those [outcastes], one becomes pure after three nights; however, if one does not eat their food, one becomes pure in a single day, provided one does not dwell in that house.
In the case of those who have access to water, this same rule applies when the mother's relatives are trustworthy;
however, upon touching a corpse, even a sapinda becomes pure only after ten days.
If one carries out the cremation of a deceased person while his mind is overcome by greed,
a twice-born man shall be purified in ten days, and a king in twelve days.
A Vaiśya is purified in half a month, while a Śūdra is purified in a full month;
alternatively, all may be purified in six nights, or again, in three nights.
Having carried out the funeral rites for a destitute Brāhmaṇa who is without wealth,
Brāhmaṇas and the other castes become pure by bathing and consuming clarified butter.
If a superior person touches an inferior caste, or an inferior person touches a superior caste,
out of affection while in a state of impurity, then he becomes pure through that very impurity.
If a Brahmin follows out of desire a twice-born man who has become a *preta*,
he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
Purification for a Kṣatriya occurs in one day, while for a Vaiśya it should be in two days;
for a Śūdra, three days are prescribed, followed by one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

If a Brāhmaṇa wails for his own kinsmen at a Śūdra’s cremation where the bones have not yet been gathered, there shall be impurity for three nights; otherwise, it is traditionally taught that the impurity lasts for one day.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, impurity lasts for one day prior to the collection of the bones;
otherwise, it lasts as long as the sun or stars remain visible, but for the Brāhmaṇa, there is only bathing.
O Brahmin, if a Brāhmaṇa should cry out while the collection of bones has not yet been gathered, then purification occurs simply by bathing with one's clothes on; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever shares meals with them, or even shares beds and so forth—
whether he be a relative or another person— is purified after ten days.
He who eats the food of these people even once out of desire becomes pure after their period of impurity has ended, provided he performs a ritual bath.
For as many days as a man afflicted by famine continues to eat that food, for that long there shall be impurity; thereafter, he should perform an expiation.
The impurity resulting from cremation and other rites must be observed by twice-born Agnihotrins upon the death of their sapindas, as well as in the case of others [such as teachers].
Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a Samānodaka persists as long as the birth and the name are not forgotten.

The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—these three are the partakers of the lepa (the smearings); the self [is included], and the sapinda relationship extends to seven generations.
The divine Grandfather (Brahmā) has declared that for unmarried women, the sapinda relationship extends to seven generations; for those who are married, it is a sapinda relationship with the husband.
And those who are born of a single [ancestral] lineage, though they may have different origins and different castes,
their sapinda relationship shall extend through three generations.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as female and male servants, donors, those who observe vows, the knower of Brahman, and the celibate student; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.23.66.
Those who perform sacrificial sessions (satrin) and those observing vows are declared to be immediately pure;
so too are kings who have been consecrated and those whose sacrificial session consists of their very life-breaths.
Immediate purification is declared for a sacrifice, at the time of a wedding, likewise at a rite to the gods, as well as during a famine or a calamity.
Immediate purification is declared for those killed in a riot, by lightning, or by kings and twice-born men, as well as in the case of death by snakes and similar causes.

Immediate purification is ordained for those who have cast themselves into fire, leaped from a mountain precipice, perished on a heroic journey, or died by fasting unto death for the sake of a Brahmin.
For lifelong celibates, forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students,
no period of impurity is declared by the virtuous, even when one has fallen from his status or has died.
For those who have fallen [from their caste], there shall be no cremation, no funeral rites, and no collection of bones;
nor should the shedding of tears, the offering of rice balls, or any śrāddha ceremony ever be performed for them.
Likewise, for one who would kill himself by means of fire, poison, or other such means, no period of impurity is prescribed;
nor is there to be fire, water, or any other funeral rites.
Now, if someone dies through negligence by means of fire, poison, or the like,
for him the period of impurity must be observed and the water-libation and other rites must be performed.
When a son is born, on that very day one may freely accept gifts of gold,
grain, cows, clothing, sesame seeds, food, molasses, and clarified butter.
Fruits, flowers, vegetables, salt, wood,
water, curd, clarified butter, oil, medicine, milk,
and likewise dry food— these may always be accepted from the house of those who are in a state of ritual impurity. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.23.76)
One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to rule with the three fires;
one who has not maintained them with the domestic fire; and any other person with the common worldly fire.
In the absence of a body, having fashioned a substitute image out of Palāśa leaves,
the cremation should be performed according to the rules by the sapindas endowed with faith.
Restraining their speech, they all, wearing wet clothes, shall pour out water once with the [deceased's] name and lineage, together with their kinsmen for ten days.
They should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) every day, morning and evening, according to the prescribed rule;
and on the fourth day, they should feed the twice-born at the door of the house for the sake of the deceased.
On the second day, the shaving of the hair should be performed by the relatives;
on the fourth day, the collection of the bones should take place with all the relatives.
Prior to that, however, one should devoutly feed an even number of pure Brahmins.
On the fifth, the ninth, and likewise on the eleventh day, one should feed an odd number of Brahmins; they know that to be the *navaśrāddha*.
On the eleventh day, one should perform [the rite] with devotion for the sake of the deceased,
or it should be performed on the twelfth day, or indeed on any blameless day;
there shall be a single purifier (*pavitra*), a single water-offering (*argha*), and likewise a single vessel for the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*).
In this manner, the rite should be performed on the anniversary of the day of death every month for a year;
furthermore, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is prescribed once again when the full year has elapsed.
O best of the twice-born, one should prepare four vessels for the pretas and others;
then, for the sake of the preta, one should pour the vessel [of food] into the vessels of the ancestors.
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," one should likewise offer the rice-balls;
thus the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha is prescribed, preceded by the rites for the gods.
There, one should invoke the ancestors and specifically designate the deceased;
for those deceased who have been made part of the sapinda rite, there should be no separate performance [of offerings]. He who makes a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa) becomes a slayer of his ancestors.
When the father has died, the son should indeed perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for a year;
he should give food along with a water-pot every day according to the rites for the deceased.
The annual rite is prescribed according to the Pārvaṇa procedure;
it should be performed every year—this is the eternal rule.
Whatever rites, such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), are to be performed for parents by their sons, these should be performed by the wife in the absence of sons;
in the absence of a wife, by a uterine brother.
By this very procedure, one may perform the *śrāddha* while living;
having performed all [acts] such as giving, one should do so endowed with faith and with a concentrated mind.
This rule for the ritual duties of householders has been correctly declared to you;
however, for women, service to their husbands is the dharma, and no other is recognized here.
Constantly devoted to his own duty and with his mind surrendered to the Lord,
he attains that supreme state which has been described by the exponents of the Vedas.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
One should always offer the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and the end of both day and night.
Indeed, by the Darśa at the end of the fortnight and by the Paurṇamāsa as well.
At the end of the harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the ritual sacrifices;
at the end of the solstice, he should offer an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and desires to live a long life should not consume new grain or meat without first having performed the sacrifice for the new harvest or an animal sacrifice.
Having failed to offer sacrifices with new grain and animal oblations,
those who are greedy for new food and meat merely desire to devour their own vital breaths.
One should constantly perform the Sāvitra and Śānti oblations on the Parvan days;
and one should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭaka and Anvaṣṭaka days.
This is the eternal, supreme dharma; any other is called adharma for the three castes dwelling here in the householder stage of life.
He who, out of atheism or laziness, does not desire to establish the sacred fires,
or does not perform sacrifice with a ritual, goes to many hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
Kumbhīpāka, Vaitaraṇī, and likewise Asipatravana.
O Brahmins, having reached other terrible hells at the end, that person of evil intellect is born into the family of outcastes or from a Śūdra womb.
Therefore, with every effort, especially a Brahmin who has established the sacred fires and whose self is purified, should worship the Supreme Lord.
No duty higher than the Agnihotra exists for the twice-born in this world;
therefore, one should constantly worship the Eternal through the Agnihotra.
And he who, having established the sacred fire, does not wish to sacrifice to the gods due to laziness—that fool is not even to be spoken to; how much less so the person who is an atheist?
He who possesses three years' worth of food sufficient for the maintenance of his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
This Soma is indeed the first among all sacrifices to be undertaken;
one should propitiate the Lord with Soma, the Great Lord of the world of Soma.
There is no sacrifice superior to the Soma-sacrifice for the propitiation of Maheśa, nor is there one equal to it; therefore, one should worship the Supreme with Soma.

In the beginning, the Grandfather proclaimed to the Brahmins this auspicious dharma for the sake of liberation; it is directly revealed as both Śrauta and Smārta, and is further divided into two kinds.
The Smārta rite was previously described by me because of its connection with the three Śrauta fires;
however, the Śrauta rite is most conducive to supreme welfare, therefore one should perform the Śrauta rite.
Both of these two dharmas have issued forth from the Veda alone;
the third would be the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), in the absence of revelation (śruti) and tradition (smṛti).
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired in accordance with the Dharma,
are declared to be cultured Brahmins, who are eternally endowed with personal virtues.
"That which is always held in their hearts alone is declared by the virtuous to be Dharma; this is the firm conviction regarding others. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.24.20)
The Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras are the supplements of the Vedas;
from one [source] comes the knowledge of Brahman, and likewise from the other, the knowledge of Dharma.
For those desiring to know the Dharma, that is remembered as the most authoritative means of knowledge;
the Purāṇa is the scripture of Dharma, and it is the supreme authority for the knowledge of Brahman.
Dharma and Vedic knowledge of Brahman do not arise from any other source;
therefore, the twice-born should have faith in the ancient Dharma.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
This entire [duty] for those dwelling in the stage of the householder has been declared to you.
Learn now the supreme duty of the twice-born and their various modes of livelihood.
A householder should be known to be of two kinds: the successful practitioner and the unsuccessful practitioner.
For the former, they prescribe teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts;
for the latter, he may practice money-lending, agriculture, and trade, provided they are not performed by himself.
In the absence of agriculture, trade [should be practiced]; in its absence, money-lending.
This should be known as a provision for times of distress; that which was mentioned previously is intended as the primary [means of livelihood].
One may either perform cultivation oneself or engage in trade or moneylending;
however, moneylending is a miserable and most sinful livelihood, so one should avoid it.
They declare that agriculture is not the supreme occupation for the twice-born;
therefore, a twice-born man may, in times of distress, subsist by the livelihood of a kṣatriya.
If he cannot subsist by that, a Brāhmaṇa may resort to agriculture, which is the livelihood of a Vaiśya;
however, under no circumstances should a Brāhmaṇa perform the work of a farmer.
One who has obtained a gain should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins;
when they are satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify that fault for him. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.25.7)
One who practices agriculture does not incur sin if he gives a twentieth part as a share to the gods and the ancestors, and a thirtieth part to the Brahmins.
A merchant may pay double, while a moneylender pays threefold;
however, a farmer is not subject to this fault—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, a householder who is a seeker of spiritual perfection may subsist by gathering gleanings;
however, there are many other means of livelihood, such as learning, crafts, and so forth.
But for that householder who is declared to be unsuccessful [in his duties], two modes of livelihood— gleaning and picking— have been prescribed by the supreme seers.
Whether one lives by nectar or even by death,
that which is unasked for is nectar, whereas alms obtained by begging are indeed death.
He may be one who possesses grain in a granary, or one who possesses grain in a jar;
he may be one who has enough for three days, or even one who does not store for the morrow.
Among these four types of twice-born householders,
each subsequent one should be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the "Brahma-sacrifice."
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
he should always perform only the *iṣṭis* prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
One should never, for the sake of livelihood, adopt the ways of the world;
rather, one should live the pure life of a Brahmin, free from crookedness and guile.
Or, having requested food from the virtuous, one should satisfy the ancestors and the gods;
or one may request it from a pure and self-controlled person, but one should not fail to satisfy oneself with it.
But he who, having acquired wealth, does not satisfy the gods and the ancestors according to the prescribed rule while remaining a householder, goes to the womb of a dog.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa constitute the fourfold goal of human welfare.
For Brahmins, however, kāma should be that which is not in conflict with dharma, and nothing else.
That wealth which is for the sake of Dharma and not for one's own sake is true wealth; otherwise, it is a misfortune.
