Therefore, having acquired wealth, one should indeed give it away, offer oblations, and perform sacrifices.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the unsurpassed dharma of giving (dāna).
This was previously declared by Brahmā to the sages who discourse upon Brahman.
The faithful bestowal of wealth upon a worthy recipient when it has arisen is designated as "giving" (dāna), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That which one gives to distinguished persons, endowed with supreme faith—that indeed I consider to be true wealth; the rest merely protects someone else's property.
Giving is said to be of three kinds: constant, occasional, and for the sake of a desired object;
the fourth is declared to be the stainless, which is the most excellent among all gifts.
Whatever is given day after day to one who does not return the favor,
without aiming for any fruit— that is the perpetual duty toward a Brāhmaṇa.
That which is given into the hands of the learned for the sake of pacifying sin is designated as occasional (naimittika) giving; this is the practice performed by the virtuous.
That gift which is bestowed for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty,
or heaven is declared by the sages who contemplate dharma to be "kāmya" (desire-based).
If a gift is bestowed upon those who know Brahman for the sake of pleasing Īśvara,
with a mind joined to righteousness, that gift is stainless and auspicious.
One should practice the duty of giving whenever a worthy recipient is encountered, according to one's ability;
for such a recipient will surely arise who delivers one from all [suffering].
That which remains after providing for one's family and their food and clothing should be given as a gift;
for that which is given otherwise does not yield fruit.
It should be given with devotion to one who is learned in the Vedas, of noble birth, humble, ascetic, established in virtuous conduct, and poor.
But he who would give land with devotion to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires goes to the supreme abode, having gone to which he does not grieve.
He who gives land covered with sugarcane and abounding in barley, wheat,
and rice to one learned in the Vedas is not born again.
Or whoever bestows even a piece of land the size of a cow's hide upon a poor Brāhmaṇa is liberated from all sins.
There is no gift whatsoever in this world superior to the gift of land;
the gift of food is equal to it, and the gift of knowledge is greater than that.
He who bestows knowledge according to the prescribed rite upon a Brahmin who is peaceful, pure, and devoted to the Dharma, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One should daily give food with faith to a student of sacred knowledge;
being liberated from all sins, he shall attain the abode of Brahman.
By giving food to a householder, a person obtains fruit;
raw grain itself should be given to him, for by giving it, one attains the supreme goal.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having fasted according to the prescribed rite, being peaceful, pure, and self-controlled, one should [honour] seven or five Brāhmaṇas.
Having worshipped with black sesame seeds and especially with honey,
and having honored [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, one should cause [a Brahmin] to recite or speak it oneself.
"May Dharmarāja be pleased"— whatever such thought dwells in one's mind,
even the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a brahmin overcomes all evil deeds.
By offering prepared food and a water-pot, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
and dedicating it to Dharmarāja and the Brahmins, one is liberated from fear.
By satisfying seven or five Brahmins with water-pots containing gold and sesame seeds, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the month of Māgha, a brāhmaṇa who has fasted on the twelfth lunar day,
wearing white garments, should offer oblations of black sesame seeds into the fire.
A twice-born man who, with a concentrated mind, gives sesame seeds to Brahmins indeed crosses over all the evil committed since his birth.
Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should give whatever [is available] to an ascetic Brahmin, dedicating it to Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods.
May the Lord Soma, the eternal Mahādeva, be pleased;
the sin committed during seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
But he who, having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, worships the god who wields the Pināka bow through the mouth of a twice-born brahmin, for him there is no rebirth.
Especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having bathed and worshipped according to the rules by washing the feet and other rites, one should [honour] a righteous twice-born man.
"May Mahādeva be pleased with me; may He grant His own wealth.
Freed from all sins, one attains the supreme goal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.26.31)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
and on the new moon day, the Three-eyed Lord should be worshipped with devotion by the twice-born.
Fasting on the eleventh day, one should worship Puruṣottama on the twelfth day through the mouth of a brāhmaṇa; he shall go to the supreme state.
This lunar day, the twelfth (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight, belongs to Viṣṇu;
on that day, one should worship the Lord Janārdana with great effort.
Whatever is given to a pure Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the divine Lord Īśāna,
or even for Viṣṇu, that yields infinite fruit.
For whatever deity a man may wish to propitiate,
he should diligently honor Brahmins and thereby satisfy that deity.
The deities always abide by assuming the bodies of the twice-born;
in the absence of Brāhmaṇas, they are sometimes worshipped even in images and the like.
Therefore, by every effort, one who desires various fruits should always worship the deities especially among the twice-born.
One who desires prosperity should constantly worship Purandara;
one who desires spiritual luster should worship Brahmā; and one who desires sacred knowledge should worship [Brahmā].
One desiring health should worship the Sun; one desiring wealth, the Fire-god;
but one desiring the successful accomplishment of their undertakings should indeed worship Vināyaka.
One who desires enjoyments should worship the Moon; one who desires strength, Vāyu;
but one who seeks liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence should worship Hari with diligent effort.
But he who seeks yoga, as well as liberation and divine knowledge,
should indeed worship Virūpākṣa, the Lord of lords, with diligent effort.
Those who desire great yogas and the knowledges of Maheśvara worship Bhūteśa, while those who seek enjoyments worship Keśava as well.
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.26.44)
The giver of land obtains everything; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of Vradhna.
The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains identity with Brahman.
One should also bestow grains upon Brahmins according to one's ability—
specifically those who are distinguished as knowers of the Vedas— and thereby enjoys heaven after death.
By providing fodder for cows, one is liberated from all sins;
by providing fuel, a man becomes possessed of a blazing fire.
One should always joyfully offer fruits, roots, vegetables, and various kinds of foods to the Brāhmaṇas.
One who gives medicine, oil, and food to a sick person for the sake of curing their illness becomes free from disease, happy, and long-lived. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.26.51)
The man who gives an umbrella and sandals crosses the path of the Sword-Leaf Forest, which is lined with razor edges and intense heat.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is beloved in the home—
that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtue by one who desires the eye of merit.
What is given during one's own equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses, and at times such as the transits of the sun, becomes inexhaustible.
By giving gifts at holy fords such as Prayāga, in sacred shrines,
by rivers, and in forests, one obtains inexhaustible merit.
No dharma superior to the dharma of giving exists for living beings here in this world;
therefore, the twice-born should give to a brahmin who is learned in the Vedas.
One who desires a long life and prosperity, as well as one seeking the pacification of evil,
and likewise one desiring liberation, should give [gifts] to the Brahmins every day.
But that evil-souled person who, out of delusion, prevents cows, Brahmins, fire, or deities from receiving what is being given,
shall go to the womb of an animal.
But he who, having acquired wealth, does not honor the Brahmins and the gods,
the king shall confiscate all his property and banish him from the realm.
But that Brāhmaṇa who does not provide food and sustenance during a time of famine,
while other Brāhmaṇas are dying, is indeed censurable.
Therefore, people should neither accept gifts from him nor enter his service;
having branded him, the king should banish him from his own kingdom.
But that man who gives his own wealth, the means for practicing dharma, to the unworthy in this world,
is a sinner even more grave than the former and is cooked in hell.
One should give to those best of the twice-born who are Brahmins devoted to sacred study, possessed of learning, masters of their senses, and endowed with truthfulness and self-restraint.
One should feed even a learned and righteous twice-born man who has already eaten well,
rather than a fool who is not established in good conduct, even if he has fasted for ten nights.
He who, bypassing one who is nearby, bestows [a gift] upon a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya),
becomes a sinner by that act and burns his lineage down to the seventh generation.
If there should be a Brahmin who is himself superior in terms of conduct, learning, and other such qualities,
one should give to him with effort, even bypassing what is nearby.
He who accepts a gift with honor and he who gives it with honor—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell.
A knower of dharma should not bestow even water upon an atheist, nor upon a rationalist, nor upon any heretics, nor upon one who does not know the Veda.
An ignorant person who accepts a cake, gold, a cow, a horse, land, or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood.
The best of the twice-born should seek wealth from praiseworthy members of the twice-born,
or even from those who are merely by birth twice-born, but never under any circumstances from a Śūdra.
One should seek the contraction of one's livelihood and not strive for the expansion of wealth;
for one who is attached to the greed for wealth falls away from his very status as a Brahmin.
Even after studying all the Vedas and performing all sacrifices in every way,
one does not attain that state which one might attain through [the practice of] saṅkoca.
One should not have a desire for receiving gifts; one may collect them only for the sake of sustenance. A Brāhmaṇa who accepts more than what is necessary for his livelihood goes to a low state.
But he who is a constant beggar is not a vessel for heaven;
he causes living beings distress just like a thief.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests,
he may accept gifts from all sources, but he himself should not find satisfaction therein.
Thus, a householder who is disciplined in soul, honoring the deities and guests,
and who lives with a self-restrained mind, goes to that supreme state.
Or, having entrusted everything to his son, the knower of reality should go to the forest and wander there always alone, indifferent and composed.
O best of the twice-born, this dharma of householders has been declared to you;
having understood it, one should practice it with constancy and likewise cause the twice-born to practice it.
Thus, one should constantly worship the one Lord, the beginningless God, by means of the duties of a householder;
having transcended Him, the source of all beings—
It returns to its original nature and does not undergo further birth.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus remained in the householder stage of life for the second portion of one's lifespan, [one should proceed].
He should go to the forest-dweller stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama) together with his wife and his sacred fires.
Having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may go to the forest;
or else, having seen the offspring of his offspring, his body worn out by old age.
In the forenoon of the bright fortnight, during the auspicious northern course of the sun,
one who is self-restrained and composed should go to the forest and perform austerities.
One should always take pure fruits and roots as food;
with whatever food one may have, with that one should worship the ancestors and the deities.
Having always honored the guest and bathed, one should worship the gods;
then, having brought food from the house, one should eat eight morsels with a concentrated mind.
He should always wear matted locks and never discard his nails or hair;
he should constantly engage in the private recitation of sacred texts and restrain his speech from other matters.
One should offer the Agnihotra oblation and perform the five great sacrifices with various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits.
He should always wear garments of bark, bathe three times a day with purity,
be compassionate toward all living beings, and avoid accepting gifts.
A twice-born man should constantly perform the New Moon (Darśa) and Full Moon (Paurṇamāsa) sacrifices;
he should also perform the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice during the constellations [of the rainy season] and offer the Cāturmāsya sacrifices,
as well as the Uttarāyaṇa and Dakṣiṇāyana rites in their proper sequence.
With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately offer sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and cooked oblations (caru) according to the prescribed rules.
Having offered that most pure forest oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plowshare, even if it has been discarded by someone; nor should one eat flowers or fruits grown in a village, even when afflicted by hunger.
One should always attend upon the fire according to the very rite prescribed for Śrāvaṇa;
one should not bear malice toward any living beings, and one should become free from the pairs of opposites and fearless.
One should not eat anything at night; one should be devoted to meditation during the night. Having conquered the senses and subdued anger, one should contemplate the knowledge of reality.
One should always be a celibate student (brahmacārī) and should not even resort to a wife.
But he who, having gone to the forest with his wife, should engage in sexual intercourse out of desire,
his vow would be lost, and that twice-born man must perform penance.
The child born therein is not to be touched by the twice-born;
for he has no entitlement to the Veda, and it is exactly the same regarding his lineage as well.
He should always sleep on the ground, remain intent upon the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra,
be a refuge for all beings, and always be devoted to sharing his possessions.
One should avoid slander, false speech, sleep, and laziness;
one should maintain the sacred fire alone, remain homeless, and take refuge on ground that has been consecrated by sprinkling.
He should dwell together with deer and live in their company;
he should sleep on a stone or on gravel, remaining perfectly composed in mind.
He may be one who washes away [impurities] immediately, or one who stores for a month;
he may be one who accumulates for six months, or even one who accumulates for a year.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard what has been fully prepared and previously accumulated,
as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
He may either use his teeth as a mortar, adopt the lifestyle of a pigeon,
grind with a stone, or eat only what has ripened naturally in its own time.
One should eat food at night after having gathered it by day according to one's ability;
or one may eat only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime.
Or he may conduct himself according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance during both the bright and dark fortnights,
eating boiled barley-gruel only once every fortnight.
Abiding by the Vaikhānasa doctrine, one should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits— either naturally occurring or those that have fallen of their own accord.
He should either roll upon the ground or stand on his tiptoes for the duration of the day; he should pass his time alternating between standing and sitting, never relinquishing his fortitude.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.
Having performed ablutions three times a day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
he should then stand on one foot or drink the rays of the sun.
He may practice the five-fire austerity, subsist on smoke, or subsist on heat; he may also drink soma.
He should drink milk during the bright fortnight and cow dung during the dark fortnight;
or he may subsist on withered leaves, or constantly maintain himself through various *kṛcchra* penances.
He should be devoted to the practice of yoga and should always recite the Rudrādhyāya;
he should be a student of the Atharvaśiras and intent upon the study of Vedānta.
One should constantly practice the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas) without laziness;
wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment and possessing a white sacred thread.
Then, having internalized the sacred fires within himself and being intent on meditation,
the sage should become fireless and homeless, devoted solely to liberation.
He should obtain alms for his sustenance only from brahmins who are ascetics,
and from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Or, dwelling in the forest, he may eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from a village,
having received them either in a leaf-cup, in his hand, or in a potsherd.
For the sake of perfecting the self, one should mutter various Upaniṣads,
as well as specific vidyās, the Sāvitrī, and likewise the Rudrādhyāya.
And he should undertake the great final journey, or fasting,
or entering the fire, or some other [method], remaining established in the rite of offering to Brahman.
But that ascetic who properly takes refuge in this auspicious stage of life, which destroys the mass of inauspiciousness,
shall attain the supreme state of the Lord.
Wherever the stability of this world proceeds.
Thus, in the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses, in the latter division, the twenty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus remained in the forest hermitage for the third part of one's life, [one should proceed].
One should gradually spend the fourth quarter of one's life in renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Having established the sacred fires within himself, the twice-born man should become a wandering mendicant,
devoted to the practice of yoga, tranquil, and dedicated to the knowledge of Brahman.
When a lack of craving for all things has arisen in the mind, then one should desire renunciation; otherwise, one would be fallen.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, or alternatively the Āgneyī,
being self-controlled and with his passions matured, he should enter the stage of life of a Brahman (the Brahmāśrama).
Some are renunciants of knowledge, others are renunciants of the Vedas, and still others are renunciants of action; thus they are proclaimed to be of three kinds.
He who is liberated from all attachments, free from the pairs of opposites, and fearless,
is called a renunciant of knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsī), established solely within his own self.
One who constantly studies the Veda alone, free from desire and without possessions,
is called a renunciant of the Veda— one seeking liberation whose senses are conquered.
But that twice-born one who, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, is intent on offering everything to Brahman,
should be known as a renunciant of action, devoted to the great sacrifices.
And among these three, the man of knowledge is considered superior;
for that wise one, there is no duty to be performed, nor any outward mark.
Free from possessiveness, fearless, peaceful, and beyond dualities, he should subsist on leaves,
wear a worn-out loincloth, or remain naked, being solely intent upon meditation.
A celibate student, moderate in diet, should collect food from the village;
with his mind fixed on the inner self, he should remain indifferent and free from worldly desires.
One should wander here for the sake of happiness with oneself alone as one's companion;
one should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life.
One should simply await the [proper] time, just as a servant awaits an order;
one must never study, speak, or listen [to worldly matters].
Knowing this, the supreme yogi becomes fit for absorption into Brahman.
Whether wearing a single garment or merely a loincloth for cover, the wise man may be shaven-headed or wear a topknot; he should carry three staffs and remain free from possessions,
always clad in ochre robes and devoted to the yoga of meditation.
He should dwell at the edge of a village, at the foot of a tree, or even in a temple;
he should be impartial toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
he should always subsist on alms and never eat the food of a single person.
But for that ascetic who, out of delusion or laziness, becomes an eater of food from a single house,
no atonement whatsoever is declared for him in the treatises on dharma.
With a self liberated from passion and hatred, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
abstaining from harming living beings, one should be a silent sage, free from all longing.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified.
A mendicant should not dwell in a single place except during the rainy season;
he should always be devoted to bathing and purification, pure, and carrying a water-pot in his hand.
Constantly devoted to the celibate life (brahmacarya), he should be intent on dwelling in the forest;
devoted to the treatises on liberation, wearing the sacred thread, he should have his senses conquered.
Freed from hypocrisy and egoism, avoiding censure and calumny,
and endowed with the quality of self-knowledge, the ascetic shall attain liberation.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, being pure in temples and other sacred places, one should constantly practice the eternal Veda known as the Praṇava.
Wearing the sacred thread, with a tranquil mind, holding kusha grass in his hand, and composed in meditation,
he was clad in washed saffron robes, his body covered in ashes.
One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and that which is declared in the Vedānta.
Whether living among his sons or dwelling as a celibate student, an ascetic, or a sage,
he who constantly practices the Veda alone attains the supreme goal.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, supreme austerity,
forbearance, compassion, and contentment are his specific vows above all.
Or one who is established in the knowledge of Vedānta, being composed, should perform the five sacrifices day after day after bathing, subsisting solely on food obtained through alms.
One should daily recite the *homamantras* at the proper times with a concentrated mind;
one should perform one's private Vedic study every day and recite the *Sāvitrī* during the two twilights.
One should constantly meditate upon the Supreme Lord, the God, in solitude;
one should always avoid eating food from a single source, as well as desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Clad in one garment or two, wearing a topknot and the sacrificial thread,
holding a water-pot in his hand, the wise man who carries the triple staff goes to that supreme state.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
"In this manner, for ascetics who are firmly established in their own stage of life (āśrama) and whose minds are self-restrained..."
Subsistence by means of alms is prescribed, or else by means of fruits and roots.
One should go for alms only once a day and should not be attached to abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached to sense-objects as well.
One should wander for alms at seven houses; if nothing is obtained, one should wander again. Having washed the bowl, one should eat, and one should wash it with water.
Alternatively, he should always eat from a vessel using another [leaf] as a base;
having eaten, he who is free from greed should discard that vessel, taking only what is necessary for his journey.
When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms.
A monk should remain with his face turned downwards for as long as it takes to milk a cow;
having said "Bhikṣā" once, he should eat in silence, restrained in speech, and pure.
Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
he should show the food to the sun and eat while facing either the east or the north.
Having offered the five oblations of breath and eight morsels with a concentrated mind,
and having sipped water for purification, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, the divine Brahmā.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and then one of bamboo—
Manu Prajāpati has declared these to be the four vessels for ascetics.
In the first watch of the night, in the last watch, and likewise in the middle watch,
as well as during the twilights and especially by day, one should constantly contemplate the Lord.
Having established within the abode of the heart-lotus the Self— known as the universe, the source of the universe, and situated beyond the darkness of all beings— KūrmP_2,29.11.
It is the support of all things, O Ānanda, the imperishable light,
transcending both Pradhāna and Puruṣa— the space, the fire, the auspicious one.
Within that, one should meditate upon the Lord, whose form is Brahman, who is the essence of all beings,
beginningless, non-dual, and the abode of qualities such as bliss.
The great, supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, the true and immutable,
whose form is both white and other than red (dark), the Great Lord who possesses the universal form.
Then, having established oneself within the Supreme Self at the conclusion of the syllable Oṃ,
one should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna as being situated in the midst of space, within the sky.
By meditating upon Śambhu—the ancient Puruṣa, the cause of all beings, and the sole refuge of bliss—one shall be liberated from bondage. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.29.16)
Or else, having meditated upon the supreme ether—the sole cause of all beings—within the cave of primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the abode that deludes the world; Kūrma Purāṇa 2.29.17.
It is the life-force of all beings, wherein the world dissolves;
it is the subtle bliss of Brahman which those seeking liberation behold.
In the midst of that, one should remain self-restrained, meditating upon Brahman alone— characterized by pure knowledge, infinite, true, and sovereign.
This knowledge, the most secret of secrets, has been declared for ascetics;
he who practices it according to Maheśa attains the sovereign yoga.

Therefore, always delighting in meditation and devoted to the knowledge of the Self, one should thoroughly practice that Brahman-knowledge by which one is released from bondage. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.29.21)
Having realized one's own self as distinct from everything else and as absolute,
one should further meditate upon that supreme, undecaying bliss which is pure knowledge.
Since from him all beings arise, and having gone to whom one is not born again in this world,
he is therefore the Lord, the God, who presides over that which is beyond.
That which is within that space is the eternal, auspicious, and imperishable;
that part which transcends it is the God Maheśvara.
Regarding those vows that belong to the monks, as well as the secondary vows (upavrata),
a penance is prescribed for the transgression of each one of them.
Having approached a woman out of lust,
one who is composed and pure should perform the Sāṃtapana penance accompanied by breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, with a restrained mind, he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance according to the rules;
having returned again to his hermitage, he should practice [his duties] with devotion and without sloth.
The wise maintain that an untruth joined with righteousness does no harm;
nevertheless, it should not be committed, for such a practice leads to terrible consequences.
Having spoken a falsehood, an ascetic who desires to attain dharma must perform a fast for one night and likewise a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one must not commit theft from another;
for it is recorded in the Smṛti that there is no unrighteousness greater than theft.
Furthermore, this is declared to be another form of violence, which destroys the knowledge of the Self.
That which is called "wealth" is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa) existing externally;
he who takes away another's wealth takes away that person's very life-breaths.
Having acted thus, that evil-minded man, whose conduct has become corrupted and who has fallen from his vow,
shall again fall into despondency and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"According to the scripture, he should do so for a year by the prescribed rite;
having attained even greater detachment, the mendicant should wander about without sloth. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.29.33)
If a monk should commit an act of violence even unintentionally,
he should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance or else the Cāndrāyaṇa.
If an ascetic, upon seeing a woman, should experience an emission due to the weakness of his senses,
he must indeed perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
If the emission occurs during the day, there shall be three nights of penance as well as one hundred breath-restraints.
For eating food alone, for honey and meat, for the same regarding a *navashrāddha* (a funeral rite on the day of death),
and for the direct consumption of salt, the *prājāpatya* penance is declared as the means of purification.
All sin is constantly destroyed for one who is steadfast in meditation;
therefore, having known Maheśvara, one should be devoted to his meditation. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.29.37)
That which is Brahman, the supreme light, the foundation, the imperishable, and non-dual—
he who is within it as the Supreme Brahman is to be known as Maheśvara.
This god is Mahādeva, the absolute, supreme Śiva;
he is that very syllable, the non-dual, and that which is the supreme within the sun.
Because the God is magnified in his own abode, which is designated as knowledge and called the reality of self-yoga, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva.
One perceives nothing other than Mahādeva as distinct from the gods;
he who follows that very Self goes to the supreme state.
Those who consider their own self to be distinct from the Supreme Lord do not behold that God; their exertion is in vain.
The one supreme Brahman alone is the imperishable reality to be known;
that deity is Mahādeva, and by knowing this, one is not bound.
Therefore, a self-controlled ascetic, with a restrained mind, devoted to the yoga of knowledge, peaceful, and dedicated to Mahādeva, should strive with constancy.
This auspicious hermitage of ascetics has been described to you as a brahmin;
it was previously proclaimed by the powerful Grandfather to the sages.

One should not give this unsurpassed knowledge—proclaimed by the Self-born, auspicious, and based on the duties of ascetics—to those who are neither sons nor disciples nor yogis. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.29.46)
Thus has been declared this rule for the observances of ascetics, which serves as the sole cause for the gratification of Paśupati; moreover,
there is neither arising nor destruction of these observances.
Those whose minds are set upon the vow practice [this] constantly.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the auspicious procedure for expiation (prāyaścitta).
For the welfare of all Brahmins and for the removal of their defects.
By failing to perform prescribed duties and by performing those that are censured, a person incurs fault;
expiation is the means of purification.
A Brāhmaṇa should never remain anywhere without having performed expiation;
he should practice whatever the peaceful and learned Brāhmaṇas may prescribe.
A twice-born man who is the best knower of the meaning of the Vedas, who is tranquil, who desires dharma, and who maintains the sacred fires—
he alone is the supreme dharma whom even a single person may resolve to follow.
Those Brahmins who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet have mastered the meaning of the three Vedas and desire righteousness—
whatever they say should be known as the means for accomplishing dharma.
These seven are proclaimed to be those who know many treatises on dharma, who are skilled in reasoning and refutation, and who are perfected in the study of the Vedas.
The twice-born ones, who know the true principles of Mīmāṃsā knowledge and are skilled in Vedānta—
numbering twenty-one in all— declare the expiation.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these are the great sinners (mahāpātakin), as is he who dwells together with them.
But he who knowingly maintains constant association with outcasts for a year— whether by means of vehicles, beds, or seats— he indeed becomes an outcast.

Having officiated at a sacrifice for someone unworthy, having formed a matrimonial alliance with such a person, likewise having taught them, or having even eaten together with them, a twice-born man falls immediately through his own knowledge [of what he has done]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.30.10)
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, should perform teaching without having understood [the texts] himself,
he falls from his status within a year, as does the student who studies with him.
Having constructed a hut, one should dwell in the forest for twelve years subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, bearing the skull of a corpse as a banner.
He should avoid all dwellings of Brahmins and temples,
while censuring himself and keeping that Brahmin in mind.
One should enter seven houses that have been prepared without prior intention, always silently when the smoke has ceased, the embers have been extinguished, and the people have already eaten.
He should go for alms only once a day, making known his faults to men;
or, sustained by fortitude, he should subsist on wild roots and fruits.
Carrying a skull in his hand and a khaṭvāṅga staff, devoted to the practice of celibacy,
he removes the sin of killing a Brahmin once twelve years are complete.
When a sin has been committed unintentionally, this auspicious expiation is prescribed;
for a sin committed intentionally, purification is to be known as occurring through death, and not by any other means.
One might practice fasting, or even throw oneself from a precipice;
one might enter blazing fire, or enter the water oneself. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.30.18)
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should properly sacrifice one's life;
or else, for the purpose of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin, one should do so even if already dead in the interim.
By restoring a Brahmin afflicted with a chronic disease to health and giving him food during a famine, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
A twice-born man becomes pure by bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice,
or by giving away his entire property to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas.
At the world-renowned confluence of the Sarasvatī with the Aruṇā,
a twice-born man who has fasted for three nights shall become purified by bathing at the three daily sessions.
Having gone to the meritorious Rāmeśvara and bathed in the great ocean,
one who is endowed with celibacy and other virtues is liberated upon beholding Rudra.
There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) of the trident-bearing God named Kapālamocana;
by bathing there and worshipping the ancestors with devotion, one casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Where, in former times, the skull of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was placed by the god of gods, Bhārava, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Having worshipped Mahādeva there in his form as Bhairava,
and having offered libations to the ancestors and bathed, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Upper Division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"How was it that by the god Rudra, Śaṅkara, of immeasurable splendor..."
In former times, the skull born from the body of Brahmā was placed upon the earth.
Sūta said: Listen, O sages, to this meritorious narrative that destroys all sins—
the majesty of Mahādeva, the wise God of gods.
In ancient times, on the peak of Mount Meru, the great seers bowed down to the god Pitāmaha, the origin of the worlds, and asked: "What is the one imperishable reality? (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.31.3)
Deluded by the illusion of Maheśa, that source of the world,
failing to recognize the supreme state, spoke of himself as a conqueror.
"I am the Sustainer, the source of the universe, the Self-existent, the sole Lord.
By worshipping me—the beginningless, supreme Brahman—one is liberated. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.31.5)
For I am the one who sets all the gods in motion and the one who withdraws them;
there is no one whatsoever in the worlds who is superior to me.
As he was thinking thus, one born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa appeared;
with eyes copper-red with rage, he spoke these words while smiling.
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of this behavior of yours at present?
Being joined with the yoga of ignorance, this is not fitting for you."
For I am the sustainer of the worlds, the sacrifice, and the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
without me, there is never anywhere any means of life for this universe.
I alone am the supreme light; I alone am the ultimate goal.
By you, impelled by me, the entire circle of worlds was created.
While the two gods were thus disputing out of delusion, each desiring victory over the other, the four Vedas themselves arrived at that place where they were.
Having reflected upon the god Brahmā, who was established as the very soul of the sacrifice, they,
with agitated hearts, spoke of the true nature of the Supreme Lord.
The Ṛgveda said: He within whom all beings reside, from whom everything proceeds,
and whom they call the supreme reality— that god must be Maheśvara.
The Yajurveda said: He who is worshipped by all sacrifices and by yoga as the Lord,
whom they call the Sovereign God— that God must be the wielder of the Pināka bow.
The Sāmaveda said: He by whom this wheel is made to revolve, who is the auspicious space within the sky,
whose reality is known by yogins— he is Mahādeva, that Śaṅkara.
The Atharvaveda said: That Lord who is the Great Ruler, the Supreme Person, Rudra— the very God Bhava— whom striving ascetics behold as the supreme Lord of Yoga.
Having thus heard this auspicious proclamation of the Vedas, even that Blessed One Brahmā,
the soul of the universe, was himself bewildered and spoke these words with a smile.
How does that Supreme Brahman, who is free from all attachments,
take delight with his wife and with his exceedingly proud attendants?
Then, having ceased [speaking], the eternal Lord, whose self is the *praṇava*, becoming embodied though formless, spoke these words to the Grandfather: KūrmP_2.31.19.
Praṇava said:
Indeed, this Lord Rudra never takes delight with a wife who is distinct from his own self; for such is Maheśvara.
This is that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, the self-luminous and eternal;
the Goddess Śivā is said to be his own blissful nature, not something adventitious.
Even when this had been said at that time,
the ignorance of the unborn Yajñamūrti did not go to destruction, due to the very *māyā* of the Lord.
In that interval, Viriñca, the creator of the universe, beheld a great, divine, and wondrous light that filled the expanse of the sky.
O best of the twice-born, situated in the midst of that, a pure, divine mandala, blazing with splendor, appeared in the center of the sky.
Having seen that divine face upon his head,
the Grandfather of the World beheld with him that terrible and faultless maṇḍala.
The fifth head of Brahmā blazed up with extreme anger;
in an instant, a great person, blue and red in hue, became visible.
The Lord Brahmā spoke to that Śaṅkara Nīlalohita, the god who was tawny with a trident and wore a serpent as his sacred thread.
"O Śaṅkara, O Maheśāna, I know that your previous manifestation was from my very forehead; therefore, come to me alone for refuge. (KūrmP 2.31.28)
Then, having heard those arrogant words of the Lotus-born One,
the Lord dispatched the personified Time, Bhairava, the burner of the worlds.
Having waged a truly great battle with Brahmā, Kālabhairava then severed the fifth face of Viriñca.
The god Brahmā had his face cut off by the god Śambhu;
yet, through the power of the Lord (Īśa), the creator of the universe died and regained his life.
Then he beheld Giriśa,
the eternal Mahādeva, seated with the Great Goddess within the circle.
Adorned with bracelets of serpent-kings and ornaments made of portions of the moon,
he resembles ten million suns and is resplendent with a mass of matted hair.
Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with divine garlands,
holding a trident in his hand, difficult to behold, the yogin is decorated with sacred ashes.
He beheld that primordial god, Brahmā, the Great Lord, whom those established in yoga perceive within the heart as the Lord.
He whose supreme goddess Śakti is established in the ether—
he is indeed seen as Maheśa, whose nature is the union with infinite sovereignty.
He by whose mere single prostration the delusion that is the seed of the entire world goes to its dissolution— he indeed is seen as Rudra.
Furthermore, it is said that the Leader of the worlds is seen as one who liberates only those devoted to him, even if they are not intent on right conduct. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.31.38)
He whose stainless form is known by those who know the Vedas— those who are tranquil, free from the pairs of opposites, and celibate— it is said that Śambhu is truly seen.
He whose linga Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the seers who discourse on Brahman, always worship— he is indeed seen as the Lord of the Universe.
He by whose mere single prostration the delusion that is the seed of the entire world goes to its dissolution— he indeed is seen as Rudra.
Accompanied by Vidyā, that Blessed One resides within another maṇḍala;
he is indeed seen as Īśvara, the son of Hiraṇyagarbha.
He was seen— Śaṅkara, whose side is never forsaken by the Sovereign Goddess, whose body is consciousness, and who is the source of the entire world.
Whether it be a flower, a leaf, or even water offered at his pair of feet, one crosses the cycle of existence; indeed, such a person is seen as Rudra himself.
In his presence, the eternal Time brings everything under control;
indeed, he is the soul of yoga, for he is seen as the death of time itself.
He is the life of all worlds and the ornament of the three realms;
that god Soma is seen whose very ornament is Soma.
He whose union with the Goddess is eternally manifest by his very nature is indeed proclaimed to have attained supreme liberation; such a yogi is truly seen.
Yogins who know the reality of yoga, constantly intent on union, meditate upon that yoga of the Goddess; indeed, such a one is seen as a true yogin.
Having beheld Mahādeva, the eternal one,
seated upon an excellent throne together with Mahādevī, he attained supreme mindfulness.
Having regained his divine recollection of Maheśvara,
the unborn Lord gratified Soma, the granter of boons, who is adorned by the moon.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to the Great God; salutations again and again to the Great Goddess. Salutations to Śiva, the Peaceful One; salutations to Śivā, the Peaceful One.
Oṃ, salutations to you, O Brahman; salutations again and again to you, the Vidyā.
Salutations to the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti); salutations again and again to Maheśa. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.31.52)
Homage to you whose body is consciousness; salutations again and again to you, O Thought! Homage to you, the Death of Death; salutations again and again to you, the Sovereign Lady!
Homage, homage be to Rudra; homage, homage to you, O Rudrāṇī!
Homage, homage to you, O Kāma; and homage, homage to Māyā!
Salutations again and again to the controller of all actions, the agitator;
salutations be to you, the primordial nature (prakṛti), and salutations to Nārāyaṇa as well.
Salutations to you, the source of yoga; salutations to the teacher of yogins.
Salutations to the destroyer of saṃsāra; salutations to the origin of saṃsāra.
Salutations to the eternal bliss, the all-pervading Lord; salutations to Him whose form is bliss. Salutations to Him who is devoid of effects; salutations to the primordial nature of the universe.
Salutations to you, whose form is the syllable Oṃ, and who are established within it;
salutations to you who abide in the ether, and repeated salutations to the power of the ether.
Thus, with these eight verses concerning Soma, the Grandfather (Brahmā) prostrated before the Lord;
he fell upon the ground like a staff, chanting the Śatarudriya.
Then the god Mahādeva, Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him, raised [him] with both hands and said: "I am pleased with you now."
Having bestowed that supreme yoga and great, incomparable sovereignty,
he spoke to the god Nīlalohita, the Lord, who stood before him.
This Brahmā is the first-born son of this world, worthy of worship;
he is your elder father and your teacher, who must be protected by you.
"O sinless one, this Ancient Puruṣa must not be slain by you;
through the majesty of his own yogic sovereignty, he has come to me alone for refuge."
And this Lord Sacrifice, O sinless one, who has become arrogant, must be subdued by you;
furthermore, the head of Viriñca must be borne by you.
To demonstrate to the world the vow for the expiation of the murder of a Brahmin,
constantly subsist on alms and establish the gods and the twice-born.
Having spoken these words, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign,
departed for his own natural, divine abode, that supreme station.
Then that Blessed Lord Īśa, Nīlalohita,
caused the face of Brahmā at Kaparda to become Kālabhairava.
Perform this vow, which brings benefit to the world, for the sake of destroying your sins;
let the Blessed One, with a skull in his hand, accept alms from everywhere.
Having spoken thus, he dispatched the maiden known as Brahman-slaughter (Brahmahatyā),
whose mouth was terrifying with fangs and who was adorned with garlands of flames.
Until he reaches the divine city of Vārāṇasī,
you, O Bhīṣaṇā, must follow the three-eyed Lord for that duration.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Maheśvara said to Kālāgni:
"Wander through the entire world for the sake of alms, by my command."
When you behold Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, who is free from all ailment,
then he will clearly explain the means for the purification of sins.
Having heard the words of the god of gods, the blessed Hara,
the soul of the universe, wandered through the three worlds with a skull in his hand.
Having assumed a transformed appearance, blazing with his own splendor,
he was glorious, pure, incomparable, and adorned with a mass of matted hair.
Surrounded by the exceedingly proud Pramathas, who resemble ten million suns,
Mahādeva, whose eyes are like the fire of time, shines resplendent.
Having drunk the divine nectar of the bliss of the Supreme Lord,
the Sovereign, abounding in playful charms, comes to the worlds.
Seeing that Śaṅkara as Kālabhairava with a dark countenance,
yet endowed with beauty and charm, the multitude of women followed after him.
They sang various songs and danced before the Lord;
looking at his smiling face, they even knit their brows.
Having visited the regions of the gods, dānavas, and others, the wielder of the trident went to the abode of Viṣṇu, where Madhusūdana resides.
Having gazed upon the divine abode, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
prepared to enter it together with the foremost of the bhūtas.
Not recognizing that supreme, divine,
and transcendent state of the Great Lord marked by the trident, the mighty gatekeeper barred the way.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments, and possessing mighty arms,
he was known as Viṣvaksena, born from a portion of Viṣṇu.
Then, at the command of Bhairava, a terrifying attendant of Śaṅkara known as Kālavega fought against him who was born from Viṣṇu.
Having conquered that Kālavega, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
he hurled the Sudarśana, fierce as Rudra, toward Rudra.
Then the god Mahādeva, the enemy of Tripura, the wielder of the trident and conqueror of foes, looked with disdain upon him as he was rushing forward.
In that interval, a great being, resembling the fire at the end of an eon,
pierced him in the chest with a trident and cast him down to the earth.
Struck excessively by the spear and having lost his supreme strength,
he gave up his life upon seeing death, like those struck down by disease.
Having slain Viṣṇu’s person along with the foremost of the Pramathas,
he entered the inner chamber, taking the body with him.
Having observed that the Lord Hari was the cause of the world,
he split his own head from his forehead and let fall a stream of blood.
"O Lord of immeasurable splendor, accept my alms;
O Destroyer of Tripura, nothing remains that has not already been offered to you."
That skull of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was not completely full;
indeed, that stream flowed for a thousand divine years.
Then the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, having praised Kālarudra with Vedic mantras and with great respect, spoke to him.
"For what purpose was this face of Brahmā assumed by you?
To this, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara related the entire account.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, the infallible Lord of gods, summoned Brahmahatyā and entreated the wielder of the trident, saying, "Release him."
Even though she was addressed by Murāri, she did not leave his side;
after reflecting for a long time, the omniscient Śaṅkara, the source of the universe, spoke.
"O Blessed One, go to the divine and auspicious city of Vārāṇasī,
where the Lord of Horses swiftly destroys the defects of the entire world."
Then, desiring the welfare of the worlds, the Lord went with ease to all the secret sacred fords and sanctuaries.
Being praised here and there by the Pramathas and great yogis,
the great yogi danced with his body resting upon his hand.
The Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa himself rushed toward him,
having assumed another form out of a desire to witness the dance.
Gazing upon Nārāyaṇa, whose command is marked by the bull-emblem,
he who is the soul of infinite yoga danced again and again with a smile.
Then Rudra, together with his attendants and accompanied by Hari, whose vehicle is dharma,
proceeded to the city of Mahādeva known as Vārāṇasī.
As soon as the Lord of Gods had entered, the Brahman-slaughter [personified] cried out "Alas!
Alas! with a loud noise and, being distressed, fled to the netherworld, O Kapardin.
Having entered the supreme abode, the god Hara, Śaṅkara, placed the skull of Brahmā at the forefront of his attendants.
Having set it aside, Mahādeva, that Lord and ocean of compassion, spoke to Viṣṇu: "Let this body be restored to life. KūrmP_2.31.104.
Those who constantly remember my supreme Kāpāla attire—
their transgressions perish quickly, both in this world and in the next.
Having arrived at this most excellent sacred ford and performed a ritual bath according to the prescribed rules,
and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"Knowing the world to be impermanent, those who indeed dwell in this place—
upon the end of the body, I grant them that supreme knowledge, the highest state."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One embraced Janārdana and,
together with the lords of the Pramathas, vanished in an instant.
Having obtained Viṣvaksena from the wielder of the trident, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa quickly returned to his own place, assuming his supreme form.
This meritorious account has been told to you, which destroys great sins—
the auspicious Kapālamocana Tīrtha, which brings pleasure to Sthāṇu.
Whoever recites this chapter in the presence of Brāhmaṇas is liberated from sins committed through speech, mind, and body.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the Upper Division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said:
"But the drinker of spirituous liquor shall himself drink hot liquor, glowing like fire."
When his body has been consumed by that [fire], O best of the twice-born, he is liberated.
Whether it be cow’s urine the color of fire, or the liquid from cow dung,
or milk, ghee, or water— one is liberated from sin by that.
Clad in wet garments and purified, having meditated upon Hari Nārāyaṇa,
he should then perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin for the sake of pacifying that sin.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should declare his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me."
Taking up a club, the king himself should strike him once;
by such execution, the thief is purified, or in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he is purified through austerity alone.
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood,
or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron mace.
He must go to the king with disheveled hair, running and proclaiming that evil deed: "I am a doer of such an act; punish me! (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.32.7).
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his theft;
however, by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
But a twice-born man who desires to remove the impurity born of stealing gold should wear rags and perform in the forest the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin.
Or else, having bathed at the final purificatory ablution (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice, the twice-born man shall become purified;
or he may give to the Brahmins gold equal in weight to his own body.
A Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold, however, should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year, devoted to celibacy, in order to remove that sin.
A Brahmin, deluded by lust, having ascended upon the wife of his guru,
shall embrace a woman made of heated, glowing black iron.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in a vessel,
he should walk toward the southern direction without looking back until he collapses.
One who has killed his teacher’s property is purified by dying for its sake, or the slayer of a Brahmin must perform the vow; likewise,
one who has violated the teacher’s bed is released from sin if he embraces a thorny branch for a year, remaining self-controlled and sleeping on the ground.
Or a Brahmin, composed in mind and clothed in bark garments, should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for a year;
or, by bathing at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice, a man is purified.

Eating only at the proper time or at the eighth meal-time, remaining a celibate student always observing his vows, passing his time by alternating between standing and sitting postures, and approaching water for ablutions three times a day; KūrmP_2,32.16.
Sleeping on the ground for three years, he removes that sin;
or alternatively, he should perform five or four *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
Now I shall declare the expiation for those who have associated with outcasts.
Whatever twice-born man enters into association with an outcast by means of any [act],
he should perform that very same vow for the sake of removing that sin.
Or else, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year without sloth;
however, in the case of association for six months, he deserves half of that expiation.
By these vows, those who have committed great sins cast off their impurity; or else, on this earth, expiation is achieved by visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.

Having intentionally committed the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, or sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru, or having formed an association with those who have committed such acts, a Brāhmaṇa [is purified by the following].
A Brahmin, being composed, may practice fasting at a sacred ford,
or he may enter a blazing fire after meditating upon the god with matted hair.
For no other atonement has been seen by the sages who proclaim the Dharma;
therefore, one should burn one's own body at meritorious sacred fords.
Having gone [to the forest], the Brahmin should intentionally enter a blazing fire—whether it be his daughter, his sister, or even his daughter-in-law; such is the established rule.
Having had sexual intercourse with a maternal aunt, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt,
or a sister’s daughter, one should perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the pacification of that sin,
while meditating upon the Supreme Lord, the source of the universe, who is without beginning or end.
Having had sexual intercourse with his brother's wife,
he should, being well-composed, perform four or five *cāndrāyaṇa* penances in order to pacify that sin.
Having approached the daughter of his father's sister, or the daughter of his mother's sister,
or even the daughter of his maternal uncle, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having approached the wife of a friend and likewise the wife of a brother-in-law,
one should remain fasting for a day and night and perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
A Brahmin is purified by a three-night fast for approaching a woman in her courses;
for approaching a Caṇḍāla woman, they prescribe three *taptakṛcchra* penances along with a *sāntapana*; it is declared that there is no other atonement for this.
Having approached a woman of the same maternal lineage (mātṛgotra) or likewise of the same ancestral lineages (samānapravara),
one who is self-restrained and composed shall be purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Brāhmaṇī woman shall perform one Gṛcchra penance;
but having defiled a maiden, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having emitted semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper womb, or into water, a man shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
A Brahmin is purified by a three-night fast for approaching a harlot;
having indulged in sexual intercourse with a cow, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with a goat or a sheep, a twice-born man should perform a Prājāpatya penance;
and having approached a fallen woman, he becomes purified by three Kṛcchra penances.
Upon approaching a Pulkasī woman, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances; likewise,
having approached a Naṭī, a Śailūṣakī, a Rajakī, a Veṇujīvinī, or a Carmopajīvinī,
one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa.
If a celibate student should somehow approach a woman, deluded by lust,
he must wear the skin of a donkey and beg for alms at seven houses.
Performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day while proclaiming one's own sin,
one is liberated from that sin after the course of a single year.
Or else, the self-controlled man should perform the vow for the murder of a Brahmin for six months;
for by remaining with the permission of the Brahmins, he who has violated his vow of chastity is indeed liberated.
If one fails to perform the practice of begging for alms and the worship of the sacred fire for seven nights,
or if there is an emission of semen, one should perform an expiation.
But by always eating at night for one year while subsisting on alms, remaining pure and reciting the Great Utterances preceded by the syllable Oṃ; KūrmP_2,32.41.
And one should constantly recite the Sāvitrī mantra, free from anger;
by doing so at riverbanks or sacred fords (tīrthas), one is liberated from that sin.
Having unintentionally killed a Kṣatriya, a Brahmin should perform the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; indeed, for six months, he should give five hundred cows.
For one year, the forest-dweller, self-restrained and composed,
should perform either the Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, or the Taptakṛcchra penance himself.
Having unintentionally killed a Vaiśya, one should perform the vow for a Brahmin-slayer for two years and give a thousand cows plus a quarter;
or else, one should perform the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having killed a Śūdra through negligence, one should observe a vow for one year and give half of a thousand cows (five hundred) as a quarter-portion for the pacification of that sin.
One who has killed a Brāhmaṇa should perform the vow for eight years, six years, or three years;
having killed a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, one should do so respectively in that same order.
Having killed a Brāhmaṇī woman, a Brahmin shall observe a vow for eight years;
for killing a Rājanyā woman, six years; and for a Vaiśyā woman, three years.
Having killed a Śūdrā woman, the best of the twice-born becomes purified after one year. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.32.48)
Having killed a Vaiśya through negligence, one should give something to a twice-born man;
and for the killing of those born of the lowest castes (antyajas), one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow,
or purification may be achieved by means of a Parāka penance— so said the Lord, the Unborn One.
Having killed a frog, a mongoose, a crow, a venomous snake, or a rat,
as well as a dog, a twice-born man should then perform a vow consisting of one-sixteenth part [of the standard penance].

Having killed a dog, a cat, or a mongoose, one who is well-restrained should drink milk for three nights; or else, he should travel a distance of one yojana along the road. For killing a horse, a twice-born man should perform the twelve-night kṛcchra penance.
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give a hoe made of black iron, a load of straw, a eunuch, and one māṣa of lead. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.32.52)
Having killed a boar carrying a jar, a partridge with a drona-measure of sesame seeds, a parrot, a two-year-old calf, or a three-year-old crane, one must perform penance. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.32.53)
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock, as well as a monkey,
a hawk, and a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, one should give a kṛṣṇala of gold.
If one kills any creature possessing bones, one should give something to a Brahmin;
for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred ṛcs should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
And for all other trees and succulent plants that produce fruit and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the means of purification.
For the killing of elephants, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is seen as the means of purification;
likewise for killing a cow through negligence, one may perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* or *parāka*. However, for the intentional killing of such a cow, no atonement is prescribed.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the Upper Division of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: Having committed the abduction of men, women, and houses—
And the water from ponds and wells is purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having stolen articles of little value from another's house,
one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance and restore the goods for the sake of self-purification.
But having intentionally stolen grain, food, or wealth from the house of one belonging to his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by half a *kṛcchra* penance.
For the theft of food, whether chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, seats,
flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver,
iron, bell-metal, or stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed animals, single-hoofed animals,
birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk for three days.
Having eaten human flesh, one should then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, having eaten a crow, a dog, an elephant,
a boar, or a cock, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
If one consumes the flesh of carnivorous animals, as well as excrement or urine, or the meat of cows, jackals, and monkeys, one should observe that same vow;
having fasted for twelve days, one should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.33.9)
Having eaten a mongoose, an owl, or a cat, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance;
having eaten a wild beast, a camel, or a donkey, one becomes pure through the *taptakṛcchra*.
Furthermore, the ritual consecration should be performed according to the previous rule, as if for a religious vow.
Having eaten a crane, a heron, a swan, a kāraṇḍava duck,
a ruddy goose, or a water-fowl, one must fast for twelve days.
Having eaten a pigeon, a ṭiṭṭibha bird, a parrot, a crane, an owl, or a web-footed bird, one should likewise observe this vow.
Having eaten a porpoise, a blue jay, or likewise the flesh of fish,
as well as food from a frying pan, one should perform this very same vow.
By subsisting on cow urine and barley gruel for one month, one is purified even after [eating] a cuckoo, fish, a frog, or likewise a serpent. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.33.14)
Having eaten aquatic animals, water-born creatures, peckers, claw-scratchers,
and those with red feet, one should perform this [penance] for seven days.
Having eaten dog meat, dried meat, or meat prepared for one's own sake,
one should perform this month-long penance for the removal of that sin.
Having eaten eggplant, bhustṛṇa, śigru, khukhuṇḍa, karaka,
as well as śaṅkha and kumbhīka, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Having eaten onions or garlic, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having eaten nālikā or taṇḍulīya, one becomes pure through the Prājāpatya penance.
Likewise, one is purified from eating *aśmāntaka* and *pota* by means of the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
purification occurs through the *prājāpatya* penance for consuming *kakkubhāṇḍa*.
Having eaten an alābu gourd and a kiṃśuka flower, one should perform this vow;
and having eaten an udumbara fruit out of desire, one is purified by the taptakṛcchra penance.
Having eaten such food as this— kṛsara, saṃyāva, and an abundance of milk-rice and cakes— one becomes purified after three nights.
Having drunk milk that should not be drunk, a celibate student who is composed,
subsisting on cow urine and barley gruel, becomes purified in one month.

One who drinks cow's milk, buffalo milk, or goat's milk within ten days of calving, as well as the milk of a cow that is both lactating and pregnant, or the milk of one whose calf has died, must perform this penance.
And having consumed the products of these [forbidden animals] out of delusion,
a person is purified after seven nights by subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel.
Having eaten at a *navaśrāddha*, or likewise during a period of impurity due to death or birth,
a composed Brāhmaṇa shall attain purification through the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
If a twice-born man constantly offers oblations into the fire for whom no portion is first given,
he should properly perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the time of that person's first consumption of food.
But having eaten the prepared food of any of those whose food should not be eaten,
or that of outcastes (antāvasāyin), one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.

Having eaten the food of a Cāṇḍāla, a twice-born man should properly perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; but if he did so intentionally, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance for a year and undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again.
By drinking the intoxicant *asurā*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow;
and by eating food that should not be eaten, one becomes pure through the *prājāpatya* penance. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.33.29)
Having consumed feces, urine, or semen, one should perform this same penance;
and for those [impurities] not specifically prescribed, one should fast for one day, in all cases according to the actual nature of the offense.
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again.
If the best of the twice-born should, out of delusion, consume the urine or excrement of carnivorous animals or birds, he should perform the Mahāsāṃtapana penance; likewise, for eating a vulture,
a frog, a heron, or any bird that scratches for food, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
One becomes purified by the Prājāpatya penance for eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa;
for the leavings of a Kṣatriya, there should be the Taptakṛcchra; and for a Vaiśya, the Atikṛcchra.
Having eaten the leavings of a Śūdra, a twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.33.34)
Having drunk water from the interior of a liquor jar, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
a twice-born man who has eaten the leavings of a dog becomes pure after three nights;
and one who is passionate, having consumed what remains after being drunk, shall subsist on cow-urine and barley-gruel.
When one consumes water that has been defiled by urine, feces, or other such impurities,
then the Sāṃtapana vow is prescribed as the means for purifying that sin.
If a Brāhmaṇa knowingly drinks water from the wells or vessels of Cāṇḍālas, he shall perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the purification of his sin.
But if the best of the twice-born drinks water touched by a Cāṇḍāla,
he shall become pure after three nights and by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

If a twice-born man, being deluded in mind, intentionally eats after coming into contact with one who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin) and has not bathed, he should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Having touched a person who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), a Caṇḍāla, or a woman in her courses,
or having eaten food through negligence, one becomes pure after three nights.

If one should eat when it is time for bathing, one becomes pure after a day and night; however, if it is done intentionally, the Lord who was born from the lotus declared that purification is achieved through the *kṛcchra* penance.
Having eaten food that is dried, stale, and so forth, or that has been defiled by cows and other such things,
one should observe a fast or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.

At the end of the year, a Brahmin should perform the *kṛcchra* penance again and again for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; for that which was known, however, the penance is especially severe.
Having performed a sacrifice for Vratyas, the funeral rites for others,
malevolent magic (abhicāra), or the Ahīna sacrifice, one is purified by three Kṛcchra penances.
But for those killed by Brāhmaṇas and others, having performed the cremation and other rites,
one becomes pure through the Prājāpatya penance while subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
If one who has been anointed with oil should void urine or feces, he becomes pure after a day and night; the same applies to shaving and sexual intercourse.
Having avoided the marriage fire for one day, the best of the twice-born becomes purified after three nights;
furthermore, after six days, he is purified from a period of three nights.
If one neglects [the observance] for ten or twelve days through negligence,
one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances for the removal of that sin.
"Having taken property from one who has fallen [from his caste], he is purified by its renunciation; he should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance—so said the Blessed Lord. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.33.49)
But those who have desisted from fasting and likewise those who have completed their period of wandering as renunciants,
should perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances.

Furthermore, the twice-born, having been refined by the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), shall become pure; they should properly observe those vows, increasing their righteousness.
But one who has not performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) should remain there for that day as a laborer;
if he has not fasted, he should dwell with a restrained mind during the night, and indeed for the night alone.
Without having performed the offering of fuel sticks, one who is pure, having bathed and composed the mind,
should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī eight thousand times for the sake of purification.
If even a householder, through negligence, fails to perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
he is immediately purified by bathing, provided he is exhausted by the practice of self-restraint.
Having omitted the obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
and having violated the vows of a *snātaka*, one should fast for a day.
The best of the twice-born who has extinguished his sacred fires shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year;
one who is a *vrātya* shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*, and is purified by the gift of a cow.
If a twice-born man should practice atheism, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
for treachery against the gods or treachery against his guru, he is purified by the Taptakṛcchra.
Having intentionally mounted a camel-vehicle or a donkey-vehicle,
one shall become pure after three nights, or else one may enter the water naked.
Eating only at every sixth mealtime, the constant recitation of the Saṃhitā,
and Śākala oblations are the perpetual means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals.
Indeed, having worn blue or red garments,
a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Caṇḍāla recites the Vedas, the Dharmaśāstras, or the Purāṇas, purification shall be achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; indeed, there is no other atonement for him.
If a Brahmin should ever touch one who has been killed by hanging or other such means,
his purification shall be achieved through either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Prājāpatya penance.
If a twice-born man, while still impure from food remnants and having not yet sipped water, should touch a Caṇḍāla or others through negligence,
he must bathe and recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times.
Even after consuming a hundred drupada formulas, a self-controlled celibate who has fasted for three nights is completely purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a twice-born man, out of desire, should touch a Caṇḍāla, one who has fallen from his caste, or others of that sort while he is impure from eating,
he must perform the Prājāpatya penance for purification.
Having touched a Cāṇḍāla, one who has recently given birth, a corpse, or a woman in her menses,
as well as one who has touched such a person, one should bathe for the sake of purification.
If one should touch, through negligence, anything touched by a Cāṇḍāla, a birth-impurity, or a corpse, then,
having sipped water (ācamana), one should perform recitation (japa) with a concentrated mind.

Having intentionally touched one who has touched that [impurity], the best of the twice-born should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the sake of purification; so said the Lord Grandfather.
If, while eating, the anus of a Brahmin should ever leak,
he should perform purification, then bathe, fast, and offer oblations of clarified butter.
Having touched a Cāṇḍāla, an outcaste, or a corpse, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for purification;
but having touched an untouchable while already smeared with oil, one becomes pure after a day and a night.
Having touched liquor, a twice-born man should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) to become pure;
likewise, having consumed onion or garlic, he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter (ghṛta).
A Brahmin bitten by a dog should drink milk for three days at evening;
however, for one bitten above the navel, that same penance shall be doubled.
It may be thus: if the best of the twice-born is bitten by dogs, he should recite the Sāvitrī mantra three times over his arms and four times over his head after bathing.
But that best of the twice-born who,
being free from illness and possessing wealth, eats without having first performed the great sacrifices, is purified by half a *kṛcchra* penance.
He who maintains the sacred fires but fails to perform the ritual attendance on them during the festival days,
or he who does not approach his wife during her season, shall likewise perform half a *kṛcchra* penance.
Even when distressed by a lack of water,
one who has deposited his body within the waters becomes purified by immersing himself in water along with his clothes and touching a cow.
But if it occurs intentionally, the twice-born man, having entered the water, should mutter the Gāyatrī eight thousand times; furthermore, the observer of the vow should fast for three days.
