If a twice-born man follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse out of desire,
he must recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times while standing in rivers.
But a Brahmin who has taken an oath involving the killing of another Brahmin shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow while subsisting on false barley-gruel.
Having made an unequal distribution of gifts within a row, one is purified with difficulty;
having stepped upon the shadow of a dog-cooker (śvapāka), one should bathe and consume clarified butter.
One who is impure shall gaze at the sun, or at fire, or at the moon;
having touched a human bone, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having performed false study, one should practice begging for alms for one year;
a thankless person shall observe the vow in the house of a Brāhmaṇa for five years.
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" or an elder with "tvaṃ," one should bathe and spend the remainder of the day without eating, and then propitiate them by prostrating.
Even after striking him with a blade of grass, or binding his neck with a cloth,
or even after defeating him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by bowing down.
Having merely threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; for striking him down, the *atikṛcchra*;
and for causing blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*.
Having uttered abuse or falsehood against one's guru,
one should perform purification for one night or three nights in order to remove that sin.
If one spits or abuses a celestial sage (devarṣi) in his presence,
one's tongue should be burned with a firebrand and a fine of gold must be paid.
If a twice-born man should ever void urine or excrement in a divine grove,
he should cut off his penis for the sake of purification, or else perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If the best of the twice-born, out of delusion, voids urine in a temple of the gods,
he should undergo the excision of his penis and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having committed an act of reviling deities, sages, or even the gods,
the best of the twice-born should duly perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Having conversed with them and bathed, one should worship the gods;
having seen [them], one should gaze at the sun, and having remembered Viśveśvara, one should meditate upon him.
For one who reviles the Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of the Universe,
no atonement can be made even in hundreds of years.
One should first perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, as well as the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
by taking refuge in the God, one is liberated from that sin.
The gift of one's entire possessions according to the prescribed rule purifies all sins;
likewise do the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Kṛcchra, and the Atikṛcchra penances when performed according to the rules.
Visiting fields of merit destroys all sins;
for human beings, the worship of deities destroys every trace of evil.
Having reached the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), whoever propitiates Śiva after having fed the Brāhmaṇas is liberated from all sins.
By worshipping Mahādeva on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and likewise on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa, one is liberated from all sins.
Likewise, by beholding the three-eyed Lord with offerings on the night of the thirteenth day during the first watch, one is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with a concentrated mind,
[one should offer oblations] to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and Antaka.

Having bathed in a river during the forenoon, one should offer seven handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds individually to Vaivasvata Kāla and to the Destroyer of all beings; thus one is liberated from all sins.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, observe fasting, and worship the twice-born;
while engaged in these vows, one should remain peaceful with a restrained mind.
On the new moon day, having honored three Brahmins while dedicating the rite to Brahmā, the Grandfather, one is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the sixth day of the bright fortnight with a concentrated mind,
one who worships the Sun-god on the seventh day is liberated from all sins.
On the day of Bharaṇī, on the fourth lunar day, and on a Saturday, a man should worship Yama;
he is liberated from the sins arising from seven lifetimes.
Having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped Janārdana,
one is liberated from great sins by fasting again on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Austerity, recitation of mantras, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and Brahmins at times such as eclipses serve to purify one from great sins.
Even a man burdened with every sin, if he should give up his life at sacred fords according to the prescribed rule, shall be liberated from all his transgressions.
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or defiled by a great sin,
a woman shall deliver him by entering the fire along with him.
The wise know this alone to be the supreme expiation for women arising from all sins; there should be no hesitation in this matter. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.33.109)
But for that woman who is devoted to her husband and is eager to serve him,
no sin exists either in this world or in the next.
Devoted to her husband and delighting in dharma, she is undoubtedly like Rudrāṇī herself;
no person anywhere in this world is able to bring about her defeat.
Just as Rāma’s auspicious Sītā, the goddess renowned throughout the three worlds and wife of the son of Daśaratha, conquered the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Driven by time, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, lusted after Sītā, the pure and large-eyed wife of Rāma.
Having assumed a deceptive guise, she was wandering in a lonely forest;
it is said that the ascetic then set his mind upon abducting that amorous woman.
Having understood his state of mind and remembering her husband, the son of Daśaratha,
she of the pure smile sought refuge with the domestic fire.
With palms joined in reverence, the wife of Rāma approached that great yoga which destroys all defects, as if approaching her own infallible husband in person.
I pay homage to the Great Yoga, the ultimate end, the profound and supreme,
the burner of all beings, the Lord in the form of Time.
I pay homage to the purifying god, the witness whose face is turned in every direction,
the self of radiant form who dwells in the hearts of all beings.
I seek refuge in Agni, the friend of Brahman, whose form is Brahman;
the Lord of beings, clad in animal skins, the worthy refuge, the supreme state.
Oṃ, I take refuge in the one whose form is the world, the source of all splendors,
the great Lord of Yoga, the Fire, the Sun, and the Supreme Being.
I take refuge in Rudra, the great devourer, the wielder of the trident,
the fire of time, the lord of yogins, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I take refuge in you, O Virūpākṣa, whose nature is the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar;
you who are hidden in a golden abode, the Great One of immeasurable splendor.
I take refuge in Vaiśvānara, who dwells within all beings;
I take refuge in the divine Fire, the Lord, the carrier of oblations to the gods and the ancestors.
I take refuge in that supreme reality, the most excellent *bharga* of Savitṛ himself, the fire-like light beyond all fires; O Havyavāhana, protect me!
Having thus recited the eight verses addressed to Agni,
the illustrious wife of Rāma remained with her eyes wide open, meditating upon Rāma in her mind.
Then, from the domestic fire, the Lord Maheśvara, the bearer of oblations,
appeared with his self brilliantly radiant, as if burning with splendor.
Having fashioned an illusory Sītā with his magic power, Agni, desiring the destruction of Rāvaṇa,
took that most virtuous Sītā and vanished.
Having seen Sītā in such a state, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
took her and went to Laṅkā, situated within the ocean.
Then, having accomplished the slaying of Rāvaṇa, Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa,
approached Sītā with a mind agitated by doubt.
For the sake of providing proof to living beings, Sītā again underwent a display of illusion;
she entered the blazing fire, and the fire consumed her as well.
Having burned the illusory Sītā, the Lord of fierce radiance, Agni,
who is dear to the gods, revealed the true Sītā to Rāma.
Grasping her husband’s feet with both hands,
that slender-waisted daughter of Janaka prostrated herself upon the ground before Rāma.
Having seen this, Rāma, his mind filled with joy and his eyes clouded with wonder, bowed his head to the fire; thus did the descendant of Raghu propitiate him.
The Blessed One said to Vahni: "Why has this woman of excellent complexion, who was previously seen by you and burnt by the Blessed One, now come into my presence?"
The god who is the burner of the worlds and the carrier of oblations spoke thus to the son of Daśaratha, recounting everything as it had happened in the presence of all living beings.
This very [daughter] was obtained by the Lord of Mithilā through ascetic penance after he had propitiated Pārvatī, the beloved of Rudra; she is exceedingly dear to the Goddess.
Endowed with service to her husband and possessed of excellent character,
this devoted wife was brought to the side of Bhavānī by me, having been desired by Rāvaṇa.
That Sītā who was carried off by the lord of the Rākṣasas and recovered by the Blessed One—
that one was created by me as an illusory being for the sake of Rāvaṇa’s destruction.
For that purpose, the wicked Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas and the destroyer of the world, was withdrawn by me and slain.
"Accept this Jānakī, Vimalā, at my word;
behold the god Nārāyaṇa, your own self, the source and the imperishable."
Having spoken thus, the fierce Lord Agni, whose flames are manifold and whose faces are turned in every direction, being honored by Rāghava, vanished along with the elemental beings.
Thus has the greatness of devoted wives been recounted by me;
this is remembered as the expiation that pacifies all the sins of women.
Even a man burdened with every kind of sin, if he is well-restrained,
shall be liberated from his transgressions by casting off his own body at sacred fords (puṇyatīrtha).
Having bathed in all the holy fords on earth, or in any meritorious waters, a twice-born man—
or indeed any person— is liberated from all sins, even when they are accumulated together.
Vyāsa said:
Thus has this dharma of Manu been recounted to you by me,
as well as the eternal yoga of knowledge, for the purpose of propitiating Maheśa.
He who practices the yoga of knowledge according to this method beholds Mahādeva; no other does so even in hundreds of kalpas.
He who establishes the supreme Dharma—that knowledge which belongs to the Supreme Lord—is considered the highest yogi in the world; there is none superior to him.
That person who, though capable of establishing [the self], does not do so because he is deluded—
even if that sage is engaged in yoga— he is not exceedingly dear to the Blessed One.
Therefore, one should always give, especially to Brahmins who are endowed with righteousness, who are peaceful, and who are possessed of faith.
Whoever should constantly recite this dialogue between you and me shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme goal.
One should always recite this with a cheerful mind during ancestral rites (śrāddha), in rites for the gods (daivika), or in the presence of Brāhmaṇas; it should also be heard by the twice-born.
Having reflected upon its meaning, one whose mind is disciplined should cause pure Brahmins to hear it;
having cast off the cloak of faults, he goes to the god Maheśvara.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī,
comforted the sages and Sūta, and departed as he had come.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the upper section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The sages said:
"Those holy fords (*tīrthas*) which are renowned and great in this world—"
Tell us those things now, O Romaharṣaṇa.
Romaharṣaṇa said:
Listen, for I shall describe to you various sacred fords (tīrthas) as they have been recounted in the Purāṇas by the sages who discourse upon Brahman.
O best of sages, whatever bathing, recitation, fire-offering, ancestral rite, or gift is performed there— even individually— purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
The famous sacred site of Prayāga belongs to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin and extends five yojanas in width; its greatness has been proclaimed.
Furthermore, there is another preeminent sacred site of the Kurus, honored by the gods,
frequented by the hermitages of sages, and the purifier of all sins.
Having bathed there, one whose soul is purified and who is free from hypocrisy and envy purifies both lineages by giving even the slightest gift.
Gayātīrtha is supremely secret and exceedingly dear to the ancestors;
by performing the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, a man is not born again.
Whoever, having visited Gayā even once, offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa),
by him his ancestors are delivered and shall go to the supreme goal.
There, for the sake of the welfare of the world, Rudra, the Supreme Self, placed his foot upon the surface of the stone; there one should propitiate the ancestors.
If one who is capable of performing the pilgrimage to Gayā does not go there, his ancestors indeed grieve for him; his exertion is in vain.
The ancestors sing verses and the great seers proclaim:
"Whoever shall go to Gayā, he will deliver us."
"If there should be a descendant in our lineage who, even if he is possessed of sin and devoid of delight in his own duty,
goes to Gayā, he shall deliver us."
One should desire many sons who are virtuous and endowed with good qualities;
for if even one among those gathered together should go to Gayā, [the ancestors are liberated].
Therefore, with every effort— and especially so for a Brāhmaṇa—
one should go to Gayā and, being composed, offer the funeral cakes according to the prescribed rules.
Blessed indeed are those mortals who offer the funeral cakes at Gayā;
having rescued seven generations of their lineage on both sides, they shall attain the Supreme.
Furthermore, there is another preeminent sacred site (tīrtha) proclaimed as the abode of the Siddhas,
renowned as Prabhāsa, where the Blessed Lord Bhava resides.
Having performed bathing, austerity, ancestral rites (śrāddha), and the worship of Brāhmaṇas there,
one attains the supreme, imperishable world of Brahmā.
There is a sacred ford named Traiyambaka, which is saluted by all the gods;
having worshipped Rudra there, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having worshipped Mahādeva, the golden-eyed one with matted hair,
and having honored the Brāhmaṇas, one will certainly attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
Someśvara is the best of holy places belonging to Rudra, the Supreme Lord;
it is meritorious, removes all diseases, and is the cause for attaining the same world as Rudra.
The supreme among holy places is the beautiful one named Vijaya;
there stands the famous Liṅga of Maheśa known as Vijaya.
O best of Brahmins, having dwelt there for six months with restricted diet, practicing celibacy, and remaining concentrated, they shall go to the supreme state.
Moreover, there is another most excellent sacred site in the eastern region,
the very beautiful Ekāmra, which bestows the fruit of lordship over the Gaṇas upon the God of gods.
Having given even a small portion of auspicious land here to devotees of Śiva, one becomes a sovereign king; if one desires liberation, one shall attain liberation.
The water of a great river is meritorious and destroys all sins;
by performing ablutions during an eclipse, one is liberated from all transgressions.
And there is another river, O Brahmins, renowned throughout the three worlds, named Virajā;
having bathed in it, a man is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
There is another sacred site of Nārāyaṇa known by the name Puruṣottama;
there dwells the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
Having worshipped the supreme Viṣṇu and bathed there, O best of the twice-born,
and having honored the Brāhmaṇas, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Gokarṇa by name is renowned as the supreme sacred site among all sacred sites;
it removes all sins and is the abode of Śambhu, the Supreme Lord.
Having beheld the supreme Liṅga of the God, Gokarṇeśvara,
one obtains all desired objects and becomes beloved of Rudra.
And by worshipping the northern Gokarṇa Liṅga of the trident-bearing Mahādeva, one shall attain union with Śiva.
There dwells the god Mahādeva, renowned as Sthāṇu;
by seeing him, a person is instantly liberated from all sins.
There is another incomparable place, Kubjāmra, belonging to the high-souled Viṣṇu;
by worshipping the Person Viṣṇu there, one is glorified in Śvetadvīpa.
There, the god Nārāyaṇa, having performed the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, was dismissed by Rudra, the enemy of Tripura.
A league in every direction, the field is honored by hosts of perfected sages;
there stands the holy abode of Viṣṇu, where Puruṣottama resides.
There is another sacred site of Viṣṇu, the performer of wondrous deeds, called Kokāmukha;
one who dies here, liberated from all sins, shall attain the same form as Viṣṇu.
Śālagrāma is a great sacred site that increases the delight of Viṣṇu;
by casting off his life-breaths there, a man beholds Hṛṣīkeśa.
Known as Aśvatīrtha, it is a most purifying abode of the Siddhas;
there Nārāyaṇa himself, in the form of Hayaśiras, dwells eternally.
Puṣkara, the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds, belongs to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin; it destroys all sins and grants the world of Brahmā to those who have died there.
That best of the twice-born who even mentally recollects Puṣkara is purified of all sins and rejoices together with Śakra.
There, the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
as well as hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), attend upon Brahmā, who is born from the lotus.
Having bathed there, one becomes pure; having worshipped Brahmā Parameṣṭhin and the best of the twice-born, one beholds Brahmā himself.
Having approached the blameless Lord of the Gods, Puruhūta, there,
a mortal is born with a beautiful form and shall obtain all his desires.
The supreme Saptasārasvata Tīrtha is frequented by Brahmā and the other gods;
having worshipped Rudra there, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
There Maṅkaṇaka, having sought refuge in Rudra, the Supreme Lord,
worshipped Hara while being devoted to the five-syllable mantra.
Chanting the supreme five-syllabled mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya," the sage propitiated Śiva, whose banner is the bull, through his ascetic penance.
Then the sage Maṅkaṇaka blazed with ascetic power;
knowing that Rudra had arrived, he danced with a surge of joy.
The Blessed Lord Rudra said to him: "For what purpose did you dance?
Even after seeing the Lord Īśāna, you danced again and again."
Having observed this, the Blessed Lord Īśa, for the sake of quelling his pride,
tore open his own body and showed him a heap of ashes.
Behold this heap of ashes arising from my body, O best of the twice-born;
such is the majesty of asceticism, and another like you also possesses it.
O bull among sages, that which was danced by you with pride is not fitting for an ascetic; for I am indeed superior even to you in this matter.
Having thus addressed the best of sages, that Rudra, the all-seeing Hara,
assuming a supreme state, indeed danced for the sake of the world.
Having become thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, and thousand-footed,
with a mouth formidable with fangs and garlanded with flames, he was terrifying.
He beheld, at the side of that trident-bearing Lord,
a certain goddess with wide eyes, charmingly playful,
possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns, gracious-faced, and auspicious.
Beholding the Lord of the Universe standing there with a smile and of immeasurable splendor,
the lordly sage, his heart filled with trepidation and trembling,
bowed his head to Rudra while the self-controlled one recited the *Rudrādhyāya*.
The blessed Lord Īśvara, the three-eyed one, who is affectionate toward his devotees, became pleased;
he resumed his former appearance, and the Goddess vanished.
Embracing his devoted devotee who was prostrate before him, Śiva himself, the God of gods, said:
"Do not be afraid, my child; what shall I give to you?"
Having bowed his head to Giriśa Hara, the destroyer of Tripura,
the sage, joyful and desiring to ask a question, then made his request.
Homage be to you, O Mahādeva; homage be to you, O Maheśvara!
What is this most terrible form of yours, O Blessed One, which faces in every direction?
And who is she that stands resplendent by the side of the Blessed One, appearing as if suddenly vanished? I wish to know all of this.
When this had been said, Hara,
the Great Lord Maheśa, who is like the fire that consumes Tripura, spoke thus to Maṅkaṇaka regarding his own yoga and the Goddess.
I am the thousand-eyed one, the self of all, facing every direction;
I am the burner of all sins, Time, the maker of time, and Hara.
By me alone is the entire universe, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, impelled;
I am that Inner Controller, I am that Puruṣa, indeed, I am the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
That supreme illusion of his, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), is called by the sages his power (śakti), the eternal source of the world, and primordial nature (prakṛti).
This very Nārāyaṇa, the knower of all, deludes the universe by means of his illusory power (māyā); he is the supreme, unmanifest one whose form is māyā—so says the Śruti.
In this very way, I always sustain this entire world;
I unite the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, with Prakṛti.
Thus indeed, the Lord— immutable, all-pervading, and stainless—
united with his own form, the unborn Prakṛti, creates this entire universe.
That divine Lord Brahmā, the universal-formed Grandfather,
has correctly explained to you this supreme nature of the Self as the Creator.
"I alone am the Lord, Time itself, without beginning and the end-maker, the all-pervading one;
having established myself in the supreme state, I am called Rudra by the wise."
Indeed, that other power of mine is the goddess renowned as Vidyā;
for you have surely seen her, and therefore I am the one whose body is Vidyā.
Thus, these principles are Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara;
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the Lord Rudra, and Kāla—so says the Śruti.
This triad, which is without beginning or end, is established in Brahman alone;
it is of the nature of that, unmanifest, and imperishable—so says the Śruti.
The supreme reality is the bliss of the Self, pure consciousness, the highest state;
it is the space-like, partless Brahman, and nothing else exists apart from it.
Having understood this, you should worship and honor me by taking refuge in the yoga of devotion; therefore, behold that eternal one.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Hara vanished from sight;
there, the sage continued to worship Rudra through the yoga of devotion.
This incomparable, holy place of pilgrimage, frequented by Brahmanical sages,
liberates a learned Brāhmaṇa from all sins upon its full utilization.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the upper section of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
There is another vast and holy place of pilgrimage (*tīrtha*), renowned throughout the three worlds.
It is known as Rudrakoṭi, belonging to Rudra Parameṣṭhin.
In former times, during a most meritorious age, ten million self-controlled brahmin-sages, intent on beholding the gods, went to that supreme region.
"I shall see Giriśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, even before you;
for indeed, an obstacle arises between those who are mutually devoted. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.35.3)
Then, seeing their devotion, Giriśa, the teacher of yogins, became ten million forms; thus Rudra is remembered as "Koṭirudra."
Beholding Mahādeva Hara, the lord of Pārvatī, dwelling in the mountain cave, they all became joyful and their minds were filled with satisfaction.
"I have seen the Lord, the Great God, who is without beginning or end, even from the very beginning"— with these words, they fixed their minds upon Rudra through devotion.
Then, in the intermediate space, they all beheld a vast and stainless light; there, longing for the supreme state, they remained.
This most meritorious and auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha) is inhabited by him along with his attendants;
having seen Rudra and worshipped him there, one shall attain proximity to Rudra.
Furthermore, there is another preeminent sacred site known by the name Madhuvana;
having gone there with self-restraint, one shall obtain half of Indra’s throne.
Now, there is another most meritorious and auspicious region called Puṣpanagarī;
having gone there and worshipped the ancestors, one shall deliver a hundred of one's lineages.
Kālañjara is a great sacred ford; there in the world is Rudra Maheśvara, the god Hara, who is fond of devotion, by whom Time was worn away.
In ancient times, there was a preeminent royal sage named Śveta, a devotee of Śiva;
with his blessings and his salutations, he worshipped the wielder of the trident.
Having installed the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the yoga of devotion,
he chanted the *Rudra-mantra* incessantly there, with his mind fully surrendered.
Then that Kāla, blazing in nature, took up a terrifying trident and arrived at the place where the king was staying, in order to lead him away.
Seeing him approaching with a trident in hand— Kāla, the bringer of death, terrible, fearsome, and of fierce radiance— the king was overcome with fear.
Then, having touched the Lord’s linga with both hands,
he bowed his head to Rudra and recited the Śatarudriya.
As the king was muttering prayers and bowing repeatedly to Bhava, Kṛtānta stood before him as if laughing and said, "Come, come! (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.35.17).
Overcome by fear, the king, who was devoted to Rudra, said to him:
"Slay another, leaving aside this one who is solely intent on the worship of the Lord."
To him who had spoken thus with a fearful mind, the Blessed One said:
"Who that is devoted to the worship of Rudra does not abide under my control?"
Having spoken thus to the king, Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds, bound him with nooses; the king, for his part, recited the Śatarudriya.
Then, in the intermediate space, [he beheld] the ancient mass of splendor of the Sustainer of Beings, stainless and blazing,
enveloped in garlands of flames, pervading the entire universe.
He beheld it as it had appeared and remained established.
In the midst of that, he, greatly rejoiced, beheld the God, a person of golden hue, together with the Goddess, his limbs radiant as the crescent moon, and whose form was composed of splendor.
And he thought, "Our protector is coming."
Then, seeing from no great distance the Lord Maheśa, the God of gods, approaching with Kālī, Kāla—
free from fear— beheld the sole Lord of all.
The royal sage came forward to lead him away.
Beholding him, that Blessed One— the god Rudra of fierce deeds, the sustainer of beings, the ancient one—
[beheld] that single devotee who was intent on me and remembering me.
"Give this to me," he said at that time. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.35.24)
Having heard the speech of the Lord of the Cows, he of fierce nature, being the very soul of Time, considering it his own inherent disposition,
again bound the devotee with nooses.
Enraged, he rushed impetuously toward Rudra.
Then the Lord,
the knower of the methods of universal illusion, seeing Mṛtyu approaching, looked at him from behind and, with contempt, struck him with his left foot.
While Śveta was looking on, he struck him down.
Struck by the foot of Maheśa, that most terrifying one died;
the Lord of the Devas, the wielder of the Pināka bow, shone resplendent together with Umā.
Then that bull among kings, with a joyful mind, beheld the Lord Hara, the imperishable one accompanied by Ambā, and bowed down before him.
Homage to Bhava, the cause, to Hara, the source of the universe;
homage to Śiva, the wise one, homage to the bestower of liberation.
Homage, homage, homage be to you, O possessor of great majesty;
homage to you whose form is indivisible, homage to you, the Lord of Men.
Homage be to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, destroyer of the suffering of those who have sought refuge,
the eternal being from beginningless time, who bears the tusk of the Boar!
Homage to you who have the bull as your banner; homage to you who wear a garland of skulls.
Homage to you, the great dancer; homage to you who have the bull as your banner.
Then Śaṅkara, having shown favor to the king who was intent on prostration,
granted him his own imperishable status as a Gaṇapati as well as the gift of a form identical to his own.
Accompanied by Umā and his attendants, Hara,
that preeminent king who is worshipped by the lords of sages and the perfected ones, vanished in an instant.
When Kāla was struck down by Maheśa, the Grandfather, the Lord of the World,
requested a boon from Rudra, saying, "Let this one become possessed of life."
O Lord whose banner is the bull, there is not even a trace of fault in you;
it was simply by the decree of Fate that you were appointed to carry out that task.
At the word of the God of gods, Hara, the Lord of the gods of gods,
the Soul of the Universe, said, "So be it," and he likewise became such as that.
This is the supreme sacred ford known as Kālañjara;
having gone there and worshipped Mahādeva, one attains the status of a Gaṇapati.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the Upper Division of the glorious *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
This supreme station, greater than the greatest secret, is now being described.
It is heard that this is the Mahālaya of the god Mahādeva.
There, Rudra, the god of gods and enemy of Tripura,
set his foot upon the surface of a stone as a demonstration for the atheists.
There, the peaceful followers of Paśupati, their bodies smeared with ashes and devoted to the study of the Vedas, worship Mahādeva.
Having bathed there and beheld the footprint of Śarva with devotion,
and having then prostrated with one's head, one shall attain proximity to Rudra.
Moreover, there is another abode of the great-souled Śambhu, the god of gods,
renowned as Kedāra, the auspicious dwelling place of the Siddhas.
Having bathed there, worshipped Mahādeva whose banner is the bull,
and having drunk the pure water, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
Having performed ancestral rites, charity, and other such acts, one indeed obtains the fruit that is cherished by the most eminent of the twice-born and by yogis of restrained mind.
The sacred ford of Plakṣāvataraṇa destroys all sins;
by worshipping Śrīnivāsa there, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, having gone there to another sacred ford of the King of Magadha that grants access to heaven, one obtains imperishable heaven.
The holy site of Kanakhala is meritorious and the destroyer of great sins;
it is there that the sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed by the god Rudra.
Having touched the waters of the Gaṅgā there, pure and endowed with right intention,
one is liberated from all sins and, upon death, attains the world of Brahmā.
It is renowned as the great sacred ford (mahātīrtha), meritorious and dear to Nārāyaṇa;
having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa there, one goes to Śvetadvīpa.

This alone is the supreme knowledge; this is proclaimed here as liberation.
This is described as stainless isolation (kaivalya) and the state of Brahman.
Relying upon this supreme [state], established in it and devoted to it as their ultimate goal,
the great-souled ascetics behold me, the Lord, as the universe.
This is that supreme knowledge, absolute and stainless;
for I am the Lord to be known, and this auspicious form is mine.
"Many means for spiritual accomplishment have indeed been taught here for the sake of success;
yet, O best of the twice-born, my knowledge is superior to them all."
Those who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge, who are peaceful, and have come to me alone for refuge—
they who, being intent upon the ash, constantly meditate upon me within their hearts.
For those ascetics who are constantly devoted to me as their supreme goal and whose impurities have been destroyed,
I quickly cause them to cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Tranquil, with a restrained mind, his body smeared with ashes,
devoted to celibacy and naked, he should observe the Pāśupata vow.
For in the past, I manifested the supreme Pāśupata vow—
more secret than the secret, subtle, the essence of the Vedas— for the sake of liberation.
Or, wearing only a loincloth or even a single garment, the wise sage,
devoted to the study of the Vedas, should meditate upon Śiva, the Lord of Creatures.
This Pāśupata yoga is to be practiced by those seeking liberation;
for it is well known that it must be constantly observed by those covered in ashes and free from desire.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me,
many have been purified by this yoga and have attained my own state.
Furthermore, other treatises in this world that are delusive and contrary to the teachings of the Vedas have been proclaimed by me alone.
The Vāma, Pāśupata, Soma, Lākula, and Bhairava [systems]—
these are declared to be unfit for service, as they are outside the Vedas and otherwise heterodox.
O brahmins, I am the embodiment of the Veda; my true nature is not known by those who know the meaning of other scriptures, except through the eternal Veda.
Establish this path and worship Maheśvara;
before long, divine knowledge will arise—of this there is no doubt.
"O best of beings, may you possess abundant devotion toward me;
for as soon as I am meditated upon, O most excellent sages, I shall grant my presence."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Soma vanished right there;
those two as well worshipped Śaṅkara in that Dāruvana forest,
devoted to celibacy, peaceful, and dedicated to the yoga of knowledge.
Having assembled, those great-souled sages, exponents of the Veda,
engaged in many discourses based upon the knowledge of the supreme self.
What is the root of this world? It is indeed the Self alone for us;
yet there may also be some Lord who is the cause of all existents.
While those who relied upon the path of meditation were thinking thus,
the Great Goddess, the goddess who is the daughter of the mountain king, appeared before them.
Resembling ten million suns and enveloped in garlands of flames,
she filled the expanse of the sky with her own stainless radiances.
They beheld that immeasurable Daughter of the Mountain seated amidst thousands of flames;
they bowed down before her alone, the consort of the Lord of all.
They know that to be the seed of the Supreme.
This peerless consort of the Supreme Lord is the goal and likewise the Self, designated as the Sky;
then, she beholds both herself and this entire universe.
And then, O sages and brahmins, these [others] were also born in her.
Beheld by the consort of the Supreme Lord,
they then see Śambhu— the God who is the cause of all, the Seer, and the Ruler.
The great Rudra, the ancient Puruṣa.
Then, having beheld the Goddess and the Lord, the Master,
they bowed down and attained supreme bliss; through the grace of the Blessed One, they received that divine knowledge.
He manifested as the cause of birth and destruction.
For this is that unique source of the world, the soul of all, and the regulator of all—
the power of Maheśvara, established from beginningless time.
Named Vyoma, it shines as if in the sky.
Beyond this [universe], the Great Parameṣṭhin,
Maheśvara, the one Śiva, or Rudra,
brought forth the universe which rests upon his supreme power (paraśakti).
Then, having mounted his illusory power, that God of gods—
The one God hidden within all beings is the illusory Rudra, both with parts and without parts;
he alone is the Goddess, and not distinct from her.
For having known this, they indeed go to immortality.
Then the Blessed Lord Īśvara, the God of gods, vanished together with the Goddess Bhargī;
they continued to worship that very same deity.
Those forest-dwellers then once again [sought refuge with] Rudra.
All this has been told to you— the deeds of the God of gods,
which were formerly heard by me in the Purāṇa concerning the Devadāru forest.
Whoever should constantly read or hear this is liberated from all sins;
or he who causes peaceful twice-born men to hear it attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Upper Division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
"This most meritorious goddess is served by gods and Gandharvas."
The Narmadā is world-renowned, the most excellent river among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Listen to her auspicious majesty as described by Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira, which destroys all sins. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.38.2)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, by your grace I have heard various duties,
as well as the majesty of Prayāga and its diverse sacred fords."
"O most excellent one, it has been declared that the Narmadā is indeed the foremost of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
you should now tell us of her majesty."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Narmadā, the best of rivers, has issued forth from the body of Rudra;
she shall deliver all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
I shall now proclaim that auspicious majesty of the Narmadā which I have heard in the Purāṇa; listen with a one-pointed mind. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.38.6)
The Gaṅgā is meritorious at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra;
yet the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere, whether in a village or in a forest.
The water of the Sarasvatī purifies in three days, that of the Yamunā in seven days,
that of the Gaṅgā immediately, and that of the Narmadā by the mere sight of it.
In the western half of the Kaliṅga country, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
there is a sacred place, beautiful and delightful, renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Indra among kings, the gods, asuras, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism,
having performed penance, attained supreme perfection.
Having bathed there, O King, a man who is observant of his vows and has conquered his senses,
by fasting for a single night, shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
O King of kings, that best of rivers is said to be more than a hundred yojanas in length,
while its width is two yojanas.
Sixty thousand and sixty million sacred fords (tīrtha) stand all around the mountain at Amarakaṇṭaka.
Having become pure as a celibate student, with anger conquered and senses subdued,
one should refrain from all violence and delight in the welfare of all beings.
O King, listen attentively, O monarch, to the fruit of the merit of one who, having practiced all such conduct, should renounce his life. KūrmP_2,38.15.
O Pāṇḍava, he rejoices in heaven for a hundred thousand years,
surrounded by hosts of Apsarases and attended by celestial women.
Anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine flowers,
he sports in the world of the gods and rejoices together with the deities.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes a righteous king;
indeed, he obtains a home endowed with various kinds of jewels.
With divine pillars made of jewels, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,
featuring bright painted vehicles, and provided with male and female servants.
The illustrious Lord of the Kings of Kings, beloved by all women,
shall live for more than a hundred years, endowed with enjoyments there.
Whether he enters the fire, or [dies] in water, or practices fasting unto death,
his destination is from which there is no return, just like that of the wind in the sky.
On the western mountain slope is the lake named Jaleśvara, which destroys all sins and is renowned throughout the three worlds.
There, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and by the performance of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), the ancestors shall be gratified for ten years; of this there is no doubt.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, not far away, stands the great river named Kapilā,
covered with *sarala* and *arjuna* trees.
That meritorious and highly fortunate place is renowned throughout the three worlds;
there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, are more than a hundred koṭis of sacred fords (tīrthas).
But those trees that have fallen at that tīrtha over the course of time,
being touched by the waters of the Narmadā, attain the supreme goal.
The second, however, is the highly fortunate and auspicious Viśalyakaraṇī;
having bathed at that tīrtha, a man becomes free from pain (viśalya) in an instant.
O best of kings, it is heard that Kapilā and Viśalyā were formerly proclaimed by the Lord out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.38.28)
O lord of men, he who practices fasting unto death at that sacred site goes to the world of Rudra, his soul purified of all sins.
O King, having bathed there, a person obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
those who dwell on the northern bank dwell in the world of Rudra.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Śaṅkara has told me that bathing and giving gifts are equal at the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, and the Narmadā.
He who gives up his life on the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred crores of years.
The sacred water of the Narmadā, adorned with foam and waves, is pure;
by saluting it with one's head, one is liberated from all sins.
The Narmadā is meritorious in every respect and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by fasting for a day and night, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Jāleśvara is the best of sacred fords, the destroyer of all sins;
having gone there and observing the prescribed restraints, a man shall obtain all his desires.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, a person who goes to Amarakaṇṭaka obtains merit ten times greater than that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
This excellent mountain is meritorious, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
filled with various trees and creepers, and adorned with diverse flowers.
There, O King, Maheśvara was present together with the Goddess,
as were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, along with hosts of Vidyādharas.
