There is a vast river named Kāverī, which destroys all sins;
having bathed there, one should worship Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull.
By bathing at the confluence of the Narmadā, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the upper division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The Narmadā is the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins."
It was previously declared by the sages, and by the self-existent Lord himself.
For this Narmadā, the most excellent river, praised by the sages,
has issued forth from the body of Rudra out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
She is the eternal remover of all sins, saluted by all the gods,
and likewise praised by the gods, gandharvas, and even the apsarases.
And on the northern bank of that very river is a sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds, named Bhadreśvara; it is meritorious, auspicious, and the remover of all sins.
Having bathed there, O King, a man rejoices together with the deities.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the sacred site of Āmrātakeśvara;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of [giving] a thousand cows.
Then, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Aṅgāreśvara;
with his soul purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the merit-bestowing place named Kedāra;
having bathed there and performed the water-libations, one shall obtain all desires.
From there, one should go to Pippaleśa, which destroys all sins;
having bathed there, O great king, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Vimaleśvara;
by abandoning one's life there, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
Thence one should go to Puṣkariṇī and perform a bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man shall obtain half of Indra’s throne.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the place known as Śūlabheda;
having bathed there and worshipped the deity, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Balitīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall become a lord of the lion-throne.
Then one should go to Śakratīrtha on the southern bank;
having fasted for one night and performed the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules, one should proceed.
One who propitiates the god Nārāyaṇa Hari through Mahāyoga attains the fruit of giving a thousand cows and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, having gone to the Ṛṣitīrtha, which removes all sins of men,
a man who merely bathes there is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Right there is the most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha) of Nārada;
merely by bathing there, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
There, in former times, Nārada, the celestial sage, performed austerities;
and Maheśvara, the God of gods, being pleased with him, bestowed upon him the yoga.
The linga fashioned by Brahmā is known as Brahmeśvara;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
From there, one should go to Ṛṇatīrtha; he will certainly be released from his debts.
Then one should go to Maheśvara; that is sufficient for the fruit of one's birth.
From there, one should go to Bhīmeśvara, which destroys all diseases;
merely by bathing there, a man is liberated from all sufferings.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Piṅgaleśvara;
by fasting for a day and a night, one obtains the fruit of a three-night fast.

O Indra among kings, he who bestows a Kapila cow at that sacred ford is honored in the world of Rudra for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on her body and on the bodies of those born in her lineage.
But he who should give up his life there, O lord of men,
rejoices for an inexhaustible time as long as the moon and sun endure.
Those men who dwell taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā go to heaven after death, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
From there, one should go to Dīpteśvara, Vyāsatīrtha, and Tapovana.
In ancient times, the Mahānadī river, terrified of Vyāsa, turned back there; but being rebuked by Vyāsa with the sound "huṃ," she then flowed toward the south.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who performs a circumambulation at that sacred site shall find Vyāsa pleased with him, and he obtains his desired fruit.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Ikṣunadī;
it is meritorious and renowned throughout the three worlds, for Śiva is ever-present there. Having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
From there, one should go to Skanda-tīrtha, which destroys all sins;
having bathed there, one casts off even the intense sin committed since birth.
There, the gods together with the gandharvas worship the unsurpassed son of Bhava,
the high-souled Lord Skanda, who wields the spear.
Thence one should go to Āṅgirasasnāna and perform an ablution there;
having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Where Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā, having propitiated the Lord of Gods, the bull-bannered Lord of the Universe,
through austerity, obtained supreme yoga.
From there, one should go to Kuśatīrtha, which destroys all sins;
by performing an ablution there, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
From there, one should go to Koṭitīrtha, which destroys all sins;
having bathed there, a man obtains a kingdom—of this there is no doubt.
Thence one should go to the Candrabhāgā and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Soma.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, there is the excellent Saṅgameśvara;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful holy site,
a delightful temple of Āditya, which was proclaimed by Īśvara.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, and having given gifts according to one's ability,
one obtains inexhaustible fruit through the power of that sacred ford.
Those who are poor, those who are diseased,
and those who have committed evil deeds are all liberated from every sin and go to the world of the Sun.
From there, one should go to Mārgeśvara and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man shall attain the world of heaven.
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should go westward to the supreme abode of Marut; having bathed there and become pure through diligent effort, one should remain so.
A twice-born man should give gold according to the extent of his wealth;
by means of a Puṣpaka celestial chariot, he goes to the world of Vāyu.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Ahalyātīrtha;
by merely bathing there, one rejoices with the Apsarases for an imperishable time.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight—
that day of Kāmadeva— he who worships Ahalyā [shall obtain great merit].
Wherever such a superior man is born, he shall be beloved there;
endowed with fortune, he will be dear to women, like a second God of Love.
Having reached Ayodhyā, the famous sacred site of Śakra,
a man who merely bathes there obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
One should then go to Somatīrtha and perform a bath there;
as soon as a man has bathed there, he is liberated from all sins.
O Indra among kings, during a lunar eclipse, it brings about the destruction of sins;
O King, the Soma-tīrtha is renowned throughout the three worlds and yields great fruit.
But he who, being composed, performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at that sacred ford,
his soul purified of all sins, goes to the world of Soma.
O lord of men, that mortal who enters the fire at Somatīrtha,
or likewise observes a fast in the water, is not born again.
From there, one should go to Stambhatīrtha and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Soma.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha,
which is celebrated as Yodhanīpura, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
There, millions of Asuras were fought by Vāsudeva;
a sacred ford (tīrtha) arose there, and one who bathes here becomes endowed with the glory of Viṣṇu.
By fasting for a day and night, one expiates even the murder of a Brahmin.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha) known as Kāmatīrtha, where Kāma worshipped Bhava.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and being devoted to fasting,
a man is glorified in the world in the form of Rudra, the wielder of the flower-bow.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Brahmatīrtha, known as Umāhaka;
there, one should satiate the ancestors with libations.
On the full moon and the new moon days, one should perform the ritual according to the prescribed rule;
there, a stone in the form of an elephant is situated in the midst of the water.
One should cause funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be offered there, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha;
having bathed with a concentrated mind, free from hypocrisy and envy, his ancestors remain satisfied as long as the earth endures. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.39.57)
From there, one should go to Siddheśvara and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man shall attain the station of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
From there, O king of kings, one should go to where Janārdana exists as a Liṅga;
having bathed there, O king of kings, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Where the divine Nārāyaṇa revealed his own self to the sages of purified souls— that is the supreme state, that is the Liṅga.
One should then go to Aṅkola, which destroys all sins;
bathing, giving gifts, feeding Brāhmaṇas,
and offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) performed right there yield infinite fruit after death.

Whoever cooks the sacrificial porridge (caru) with Traiyambaka water and offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at the root of an Aṅkola tree according to the prescribed rite, by that act his ancestors are delivered and remain satisfied as long as the moon and stars endure. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.39.62)
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Tāpaseśvara;
having bathed there, O king of kings, one shall obtain the fruit of asceticism.
From there, one should go to Śuklatīrtha, which destroys all sins;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is no tīrtha on the Narmadā equal to it.
From seeing it, from touching it, and from bathing, giving gifts, performing austerities, chanting,
offering oblations, and fasting at Śuklatīrtha, there is great fruit.
That sacred field is remembered as being one yojana in extent, frequented by gods and gandharvas;
it is renowned as Śuklatīrtha, the destroyer of all sins.
By beholding the tip of his foot, one is cleansed of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
there Śaṅkara, as Bharga, always dwells together with the Goddess.
O observer of noble vows, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha,
Hara, having emerged from Kailāsa, is present there.
O bull among men, gods, dānavas, gandharvas, as well as siddhas, vidyādharas,
hosts of apsarases, and nāgas, all dwell there.
Just as a washerman makes a garment white with water,
so too does one cast off the evil committed since birth at Śuklatīrtha;
bathing, giving, austerity, and ancestral rites performed there are seen to yield infinite merit.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford superior to Śuklatīrtha.
Having committed sinful deeds in the earlier stage of life,
a human being wipes them away by fasting for a day and night at Śuklatīrtha.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one should fast and bathe the Supreme Lord with clarified butter;
endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall not fall from the station of Īśvara.
Neither by austerity, nor by celibacy, nor again by sacrifice or charity,
does one attain that goal which one may obtain at Śuklatīrtha.
Śuklatīrtha is a great sacred ford frequented by ṛṣis and siddhas;
having bathed there, O King, a man does not undergo rebirth.
On the solstice, on the fourteenth day, at the sun's passage into a new sign, or likewise at the equinox,
having bathed and being fasting, self-controlled, and composed in mind—
One should give gifts according to one's ability so that Hari and Śaṅkara may be pleased;
by the power of this sacred ford, all of this becomes inexhaustible.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who causes a Brahmin— whether he be destitute and in distress, or otherwise well-supported— to recite the Veda at a sacred ford.
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on that [image], one is honored in the world of Rudra within the families of those who produced it.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Yamatīrtha,
O Yudhiṣṭhira; having performed an ablution on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha and subsisting on food eaten only at night, one shall not behold the distress of rebirth.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Eraṇḍī-tīrtha;
at the confluence, a man devoted to fasting should bathe and feed a single Brāhmaṇa, whereby ten million have been fed.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī with a spirit of devotion and being well-pleased,
one who places earth from that site upon his head and immerses himself in those waters mixed with the waters of the Narmadā is liberated from all sins.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the holy site of Kārṇāṭikeśvara;
on that auspicious day, the Gaṅgā descends there, of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed there, drunk [the water], and given according to the prescribed rule,
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thence one should go to Nanditīrtha and perform a ritual bath there;
Nandīśa is pleased with him, and he is glorified in the world of Soma.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the auspicious tīrtha called Anaraka;
having bathed there, O King, a man never beholds hell.
O king of kings, by casting one's own bones into that sacred ford,
one is born in this world endowed with beauty, wealth, and enjoyments.
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the most excellent Kapilātīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, especially on the fourteenth day,
a man, having fasted there with devotion, should offer a lamp with ghee.
One should bathe Rudra with clarified butter and burn bilva fruits together with clarified butter;
one should indeed cause a tawny cow, adorned with bells and ornaments, to be given as a gift.
Adorned with all ornaments and saluted by all the gods,
having attained strength equal to Śiva, he sports for a long time like Śiva himself.
When the day of Mars arrives, especially on the fourth lunar day,
one should bathe Śiva and provide food to the Brahmins.
Endowed with all enjoyments and celestial palaces that fulfill every desire,
he goes to the abode of Śakra and rejoices together with Śakra.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he shall become wealthy and possessed of enjoyments; moreover,
by diligently bathing there on the ninth lunar day of Aṅgāraka (Mars) as well as on the new moon day, one shall become handsome and fortunate.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Gaṇeśvara when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived.
Merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra;
having performed the libation for his ancestors, he is liberated from the three debts.
Near Gaṅgeśvara is the excellent Gaṅgāvadana;
whether free from desire or possessed of desire, a human being who bathes there is liberated from the sins committed since birth— of this there is no doubt.
To the west of that place, nearby and not very far away,
is the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having observed a fast for one night on the new moon day of the auspicious month of Bhādrapada, a man, having bathed, should worship the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).
Having traveled in a golden celestial chariot adorned with garlands of tinkling bells,
he rejoices together with Rudra in the beautiful city of Rudra.
One should perform a ritual bath there on every day of the year;
by performing the libation for the ancestors (tarpaṇa), one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the most excellent Bhṛgutīrtha.
In that regard, in former times, the divine Bhṛgu propitiated Rudra.
By the sight of that deity, one is immediately liberated from sin;
this field is exceedingly vast and destroys all evil.
Having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
Likewise, a pair of sandals should be given, as well as food with gold;
and a meal according to one's ability is said to become inexhaustible for them.
All gifts, sacrificial offerings, and acts of austerity and ritual performance eventually perish;
however, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that austerity which is practiced at Bhṛgutīrtha is inexhaustible.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Lord of Tripura, being pleased by that very same fierce austerity,
declared his presence there at Bhṛgutīrtha.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Gautameśvara,
where Gautama attained perfection after propitiating the one marked with the trident.
Having bathed there, O King, a man devoted to fasting is honored in the world of Brahmā by means of a golden celestial chariot.
Then one should go to Vṛṣotsarga; there one shall attain the eternal state.
Fools do not know this, being deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu.

From there, O King, one should go to Dhautapāpa, where [the sin] was washed away by the Bull; it is situated on the Narmadā and destroys all transgressions. Having bathed at that sacred ford, a man casts off even the murder of a Brahmin.
O Indra among kings, he who gives up his life at that sacred ford shall become four-armed, three-eyed, and equal in strength to Hara.
He shall dwell for more than ten thousand kalpas with prowess equal to Śiva;
after a long time, having been born, he shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Haṃsatīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to where Janārdana attained perfection;
it is celebrated as Varāhatīrtha, which grants access to the world of Viṣṇu.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Candratīrtha;
especially on the full moon day, one should perform a bath there.
Merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of the Moon.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Kanyātīrtha;
on the third day of the bright fortnight, one should perform a ritual bath there.
Merely by bathing there, a man shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
From there, one should go to Devatīrtha, which was established by all the gods;
having bathed there, O king of kings, one rejoices together with the deities.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Śikhitīrtha;
whatever gift is given there becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the auspicious tīrtha of the Grandfather (Brahmā);
whatever śrāddha is performed there, all of that becomes inexhaustible.
Whoever reaches the Sāvitrītīrtha and gives up their life there,
having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Right there is the most beautiful sacred site, Manohara;
having bathed there, O King, a man rejoices together with the gods.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme sacred site of Mānasa;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra.
From there, one should go to Svargabindu, a sacred ford honored by the gods;
having bathed there, O King, a man never goes to an evil state.
From there, one should go to Apsareśa and perform a ritual bath;
for, residing in the world of the gods, he sports and rejoices with the apsarases.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Bhārabhūti.
Having fasted, one should worship Īśa; one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
O King, dying at this tīrtha, one attains the status of a Gaṇapati.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship the Lord of Gods, the husband of Pārvatī;
the wise declare that this yields ten times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
He who would give a bull there, radiant like the jasmine flower or the moon,
goes to the world of Rudra by means of a vehicle yoked with bulls.
Whoever reaches this sacred ford and gives up their life there,
being purified of all sins, goes to the world of Rudra.
O lord of men, he who enters the water at that sacred ford goes to the heavenly world by means of a vehicle yoked with swans.
The confluence of the Eraṇḍī and the Narmadā is world-renowned;
there is a most meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) that destroys all sins.
O King of kings, by becoming devoted to fasting and constantly intent on vows,
one who bathes there is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean,
where Janārdana is known as the perfected one (Siddha) Jamadagni.
Having bathed there at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean, O King,
a man obtains three times the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Piṅgaleśvara;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whoever, having observed a fast there, beholds Vimaleśvara,
shall abandon the sins committed in seven lifetimes and go to the abode of Śiva.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Ālikātīrtha;
having fasted for one night, being self-controlled and restricted in diet, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin through the majesty of this sacred ford. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.40.35)
These have been described to you in brief according to their importance;
it is not possible, O Pāṇḍava, to state the number of sacred fords (tīrthas) in detail.
This river Narmadā, the most excellent of streams and beloved of Mahādeva, is pure, stainless, and renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who even mentally recollects the Narmadā obtains the full merit of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts; of this there is no doubt.
"Men who lack faith and have resorted to terrible atheism fall into a horrific hell," so said the Supreme Lord.
The Lord Maheśvara himself constantly frequents the Narmadā;
therefore, this river should be known as meritorious and the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
This supreme sacred site of Naimiṣa is renowned throughout the three worlds.
It brings delight to Mahādeva and destroys great sins.
O best of the twice-born, that place was created by Brahmā for the supreme ṛṣis who desire to behold Mahādeva and to perform austerities.
The Marīcis, the three Vipras, the Vasiṣṭhas, as well as the Kratus,
the Bhṛgus, and the ancient Aṅgirases [worshipped] Brahmā, who was born from the lotus.
Having approached the infallible Viśvakarman, who is the bestower of all boons, possesses four forms, and has four faces, they prostrated before him and questioned him.
The members of the six families said:
"O Blessed One, by what means may we behold the Lord, the God Īśāna, the singular Bharga with matted hair, who is saluted by the gods? Please tell us."
Brahmā said:
"Perform a sacrificial session (*satra*) for a thousand years, free from defects of speech and mind;
and I shall tell you the place in which you shall carry it out."
Having spoken thus and having created a mind-made wheel, he said to them:
"This wheel has been hurled by me; follow it without delay.
O bulls among men, that place where its rim shatters shall be [the site]."
Then he released that discus, and they followed it;
as it moved swiftly along, the place where its rim shattered became known by the name Naimiṣa— a sacred site honored everywhere.
This supreme Naimiṣa, the abode of the Blessed Lord Śambhu, is crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas and frequented by Yakṣas and Gandharvas.
In this place, in ancient times, the gods— along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas—
having performed austerities, obtained excellent boons.
Having taken refuge in this region, the practitioners of the six families, being composed in meditation,
worshipped the Lord of Gods with a sacrificial session and beheld Maheśvara.
O twice-born ones, whatever gift is given here, whatever austerity is practiced, and whatever bathing, recitation, and so forth are performed—
each one purifies the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes.
In this regard, formerly, while the seers were engaged in a sacrificial session,
the Blessed Vāyu proclaimed to them the ancient Purāṇa spoken by Brahmā.
Here, it is said, the Lord Mahādeva, the creator of the universe, even now delights with Rudrāṇī, surrounded by his attendants, the Pramathas.
Having renounced their lives here according to the prescribed rule, the twice-born shall go to the world of Brahmā, where having gone, one is not born again.
Moreover, there is another preeminent sacred site known as Jāpyeśvara,
where the great attendant Nandin incessantly recited the Rudra-mantra.
Delighted by him, Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, together with the Goddess,
granted him equality with himself as well as the very means of evading death.
There was a righteous sage named Śilāda, a knower of dharma,
who propitiated Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, for the sake of obtaining a son.
At the end of a thousand years of his performing austerities, Śarva, the creator of the universe, accompanied by his host and the giver of boons, spoke to him: "I am here."
He chose a boon from Īśāna, the most excellent lord and husband of Girijā:
"Grant me a son, not born of a womb, free from death, and equal to you."
"So be it," said the Blessed Maheśvara together with the Goddess;
as that brahmin-sage looked on, Hara vanished from sight.
Then Śilāda, the best among those who know the Dharma, desiring to perform a sacrifice, ploughed his own land;
as he tore up the earth with a plough, a beautiful being appeared.
Resembling the fire of universal destruction, the youth appeared as if laughing,
endowed with beauty and grace, illuminating the quarters with his splendor.
Equal to a prince and peerless, Nandin spoke again and again to Śilāda, "Father! Father! with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Seeing that Nandana had been born, Śilāda embraced him and showed him to the sages who were then residing in his hermitage.
He performed for him all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony;
and having initiated his son according to the scriptures, he taught him the Veda.
Having mastered the Vedas, the venerable Nandi, possessing supreme intelligence,
resolved to see the Lord Maheśvara, thinking, "I shall conquer Death, the Master."
Having gone to a sacred river, endowed with one-pointed faith and his mind fixed on Maheśa, he recited the Rudra mantra incessantly.
When that [period] was completed, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
arrived with Ambā and his attendants, and said, "I am here as a giver of boons."
He chose yet another boon, saying: "O Lord, O Mahādeva, grant me this favor: that my lifespan may last for ten million years. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.41.30)
Having said, "So be it," the Lord also vanished;
with his mind fixed entirely upon that, the Blessed One further recited ten million [mantras].
And when the second period was fully completed, the bull-bannered Lord Śiva,
surrounded by hosts of spirits, arrived and said, "I am here as a granter of boons."
"O Śaṅkara, I wish to recite the third [mantra] ten million times once again. "So be it," said the God, the Soul of the Universe, and he vanished. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.41.33)
Then, when the three crores were fully completed, the God, surrounded by hosts of spirits, arrived with a deeply pleased mind and said, "I am here as the bestower of boons."
"By your power alone, I shall indeed chant another ten million [times]," he said;
to which the Blessed One replied, "You must not chant again."
"Immortal and abandoned by old age, always remaining by my side,
O Maheśvara, become the son of the Goddess as Mahāgaṇapati."
The lord of yogins, the leader of yoga, the lord of the lords of the hosts,
the sovereign of all worlds, the illustrious, omniscient one endowed with my power.
That divine knowledge of mine shall be as clear to you as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of your hand;
then, remaining steadfast until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*), you shall go to my state.
Having said this, Mahādeva Śaṅkara summoned his attendants and invested Nandīśvara with a fitting consecration.
And the wielder of the Pināka himself married him [to] the auspicious daughter of the Maruts, renowned by the name Suyaśas.
This is the place of the Lord of Recitation, belonging to the trident-bearing God of gods;
wherever a mortal dies here, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the upper section of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said: Furthermore, there is another preeminent holy place (tīrtha) in the vicinity of Japyeśvara.
By name it is Pañcanada, meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
Having fasted there for three nights and worshipped Maheśvara,
one whose self is purified of all sins is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Furthermore, there is another preeminent sacred site of Śaṅkara, who possesses immeasurable splendor;
it is called Mahābhairava, and it is said to destroy even the greatest sins.
And among all sacred fords, the Vitastā is the supreme ford;
it is the most excellent river, meritorious and the remover of all sins, being herself the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
There is a sacred ford named Pañcatapas belonging to Śambhu of immeasurable splendor,
where Bhava was worshipped for the sake of the discus by the God of gods.
There, offerings such as the piṇḍa-oblation yield infinite fruit after death;
even one who dies there is certainly honored in the world of Brahmā.
The auspicious great temple of Mahādeva named Kāyāvarohaṇa is there,
where the Māheśvara doctrines were fully established by the sages.
For one who gives up their life-breaths while performing ancestral rites, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, or fasting, these acts become inexhaustible; such a person goes to the world of Rudra.
Furthermore, there is another preeminent sacred ford known as Kanyātīrtha;
having gone there, one who gives up their life attains eternal worlds.
But by bathing there at that excellent tīrtha of the auspicious Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, whose deeds are effortless, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having gone to the sacred ford known as Mahākāla, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
and having cast off one's life there, one shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
The most secret of secrets is the supreme holy site of Nakulīśvara;
there the glorious Lord Nakulīśvara is ever present.
On the delightful peak of the Himavat, at the most beautiful Gaṅgādvāra,
Mahādeva dwells eternally together with the Goddess, surrounded by his disciples.
Having bathed there and worshipped Mahādeva, whose emblem is the bull, one is liberated from all sins; upon death, one shall attain that knowledge.
Furthermore, there is another most meritorious and auspicious abode of the God of gods, renowned as Bhīmeśvara; by going there, one is released from sin.
Likewise, there is another confluence of the Caṇḍavegā river that destroys sin;
by bathing and drinking [the water] there, one is liberated from the murder of a Brahmin.
And among all these sacred fords, the divine city named Vārāṇasī is the supreme, surpassing ten million times ten million times ten thousand.
Her greatness has been described by me here before you;
liberation is not obtained elsewhere even by a yogi in a single birth.
These regions, which remove the sins of men, have been declared according to their primary importance;
having gone there, one may wash away the sin committed during hundreds of previous births.
Indeed, for one who abandons his own duties and resorts to sacred pilgrimage sites,
those sites bear no fruit for him, neither in this world nor in the next.
One who has performed penance, one whose wife is absent, a householder who has committed sins,
and others who are like them, should resort to sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
Or, accompanied by his wife and his sacred fire, he should diligently visit the sacred fords;
thus liberated from all sins, he shall attain the destination as described.
Having discharged the three debts, or having provided for his sons' livelihood and entrusted his wife to them, he may resort to sacred pilgrimage sites.
In the context of expiatory rites, the greatness of sacred fords has been proclaimed;
whoever reads or even hears this is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the upper division of the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa, in the Saṃhitā of sixty thousand verses.
Sūta said:
Having heard this wisdom uttered from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, [the sages were filled with wonder].
The sages questioned the Lord, the deity who had assumed the form of a tortoise.
The sages said:
"The duties have been described by you, as well as the knowledge of liberation in detail,
along with the expansion of the creation of the worlds, the genealogies, and the periods of the Manvantaras."
O Mādhava,
Lord of the past and future of all beings, you should now tell us about each successive dissolution (pratisarga), just as it was previously described by you.
Sūta said:
Having then heard their words, the Blessed One, the great yogi who had assumed the form of a tortoise, spoke regarding the dissolution of all beings.
The Tortoise said:
"In this Purāṇa, this dissolution (pratisaṃcara) is declared to be fourfold: the constant (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), as well as the elemental (prākṛta), and the absolute (ātyantika)."
This perpetual destruction of beings that is constantly observed here in the world is eternally designated by the name *pratisaṃcara* by the sages.
That which will occur at the end of the kalpa is called the Brahma-dissolution;
it is described by the wise as the re-absorption of these three worlds.
When everything from the Great Principle (Mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa) goes to its dissolution,
this is called the elemental re-absorption (prākṛta-pratisarga) by those who contemplate time.
Through knowledge, an absolute dissolution into the Supreme Self is proclaimed for the yogi;
this is the re-creation [of the world] as considered by the twice-born who are intent on the contemplation of time.
The ultimate dissolution has been described here along with its means;
now I shall briefly explain to you the occasional dissolution.
When the end of the four thousand yugas had arrived and the period of dissolution (pratisaṃcara) was reached,
Prajāpati resolved to establish the subjects within his own self.
Then there occurs a severe drought lasting for a hundred years;
it is terrible, causing the destruction of living beings, and bringing about the ruin of all creatures.
Then those beings on the surface of the earth who possess little essence dissolve first, and they return to the state of the earth itself.
Having become the chariot with seven rays, the Sun rises up;
drinking up the waters with his beams, he becomes one whose rays are unbearable.
Those seven rays of his drink the water in the great ocean;
by that nourishment, they become seven blazing suns.
Then those seven rays, having become suns,
likewise burn this entire fourfold world in the four directions with their flames.
And those brahmins, pervading both above and below with their rays,
shine like seven suns, possessing the scorching heat of the fire at the end of an eon.
Those suns, blazing with water and possessing many thousands of rays,
stand pervading the sky, utterly consuming the earth.
Then, scorched by their prowess, the earth—
with its mountains, rivers, oceans, and islands— became devoid of moisture.
It is completely enveloped on all sides— below, above, and across— by blazing and continuous rays that are firmly joined together.
When they are cleansed by the fire of the sun, mutually blended,
and have attained oneness, they indeed become a single flame.
And that fire, becoming the one with beautiful earrings (Sukuṇḍalin), brings about the destruction of the entire world and consumes this whole fourfold world with its own splendor.
Then, when all that is moving as well as stationary has dissolved, the earth,
devoid of trees and grass, appears like the back of a tortoise.
The entire world appears like a frying pan, completely filled;
indeed, everything is ablaze again, filled with those very flames.
Those beings who are in the netherworld (pātāla) and those who have gone into the great ocean—
thereupon they dissolve and attain the state of earth.
Having reduced all those continents, mountains, regions, and great oceans to ashes, the Lord Fire, consisting of seven forms, [remained].
Drinking up water from all sides— from the oceans, the rivers, and the netherworlds— the kindled fire blazes, resting upon the earth.
Then Saṃvartaka, having transcended the great mountains as well,
burns the worlds with his blazing self, manifested by the power of Rudra.
Having burnt the earth, the god dried up the subterranean realm;
having burnt the earth from below, he will burn the heavens above.
The flames of that Saṃvartaka fire rise up here for hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of yojanas.
Then, impelled by Kālarudra, that blazing fire consumes the Gandharvas, Piśācas, along with the Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
The Fire of Time himself, whose body is the universe, shall burn the entire Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and likewise Maharloka without exception.
When these worlds have been pervaded by fire— horizontally and upwards—
that heat reaches this entire world,
and then all of it gradually shines forth as one, resembling a glowing iron ball.
Then, resounding with the trumpeting of herds of elephants and adorned with flashes of lightning,
the terrible Saṃvartaka clouds arise in the sky.
Some were dark like blue lotuses, some resembled white water-lilies;
some were smoke-colored, and some were yellow clouds.
Some have the color of a donkey, others resemble lac juice;
some are like conch shells or jasmine, while others resemble natural collyrium.
Others have the hue of realgar, while others resemble pigeons;
some are like indragopa insects, and likewise some are like yellow orpiment;
some clouds resembling the bow of Indra arise in the sky. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.43.37)
Some resemble mountains, some are like herds of elephants;
others are like heaps of glowing coals, and some belong to the species of fish.
They possess many forms and terrible appearances, and they roar with dreadful sounds.
Then all the clouds fill the expanse of the sky;
thereafter, those formidable, roaring clouds, the sons of the Sun,
having divided themselves into seven forms, extinguish that fire.
Then those clouds release a rain here like a great flood;
it is utterly terrible and inauspicious, and it extinguishes the entire fire.
And when it rains excessively at that time, the world is filled with water;
because fire is overwhelmed by the waters, the fire then enters into the waters.
When the fire has been extinguished, after hundreds of years,
clouds born of destruction flood the world with great torrents of water.
Being impelled by the Self-Existent One, they fill this world with streams,
like the great ocean with its boundless floods of water reaching the shore.
Then the earth, together with its mountains and islands, is gradually submerged by the waters.
The water, drawn up by the rays of the sun, remains in the clouds;
it falls again upon the earth, and by that, the oceans are filled.
Then all the oceans completely transgress their shores,
the mountains dissolve away, and the earth sinks into the waters.
When that terrible single ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
the Lord Prajāpati, having entered into the yoga-sleep, lies down.
The great seers declare that a kalpa consists of a thousand cycles of four yugas;
the Vārāha kalpa is currently underway, the full extent of which has been described.
"Innumerable eons consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śiva have indeed been described in the Purāṇas by sages who contemplate time."
Furthermore, among the *sāttvika* kalpas, the majesty of Hari is predominant;
in the *tāmasa* kalpas, that of Hara is declared; and in the *rājasa* kalpas, that of Prajāpati.
This eon which proceeds is considered the Vārāha, characterized by goodness (sāttvika);
other eons are also characterized by goodness, and my domain extends over them all.
Having attained meditative absorption, austerity, and likewise knowledge, yogins,
having propitiated both Giriśa and me within those very [principles], go to that supreme state.
Therefore, having assumed the form of a being, I myself, as a master of illusion,
enter into yogic sleep within this world consisting of illusion, which is now a single ocean.
The great-souled maharṣis, dwelling in Janaloka, behold me— the Time who is asleep—
by means of their asceticism and the eye of yoga.
I am the Ancient Person, the source of the earth and the atmosphere, the all-pervading Lord;
I am the glorious one with a thousand feet, a thousand rays, and a thousand eyes.
I am the mantra, the fire, the Brahmins, and the cows; I am the kusha grass and the sacrificial fuel, as well as the sprinkling water and the ladle; and I am Soma and the clarified butter.
The one who brings about the dissolution of the world, the Great Self, the supreme purifier, glory itself;
he is the Veda, that which is to be known, the Lord, the protector, the master of the senses, and the mouth of Brahman.
The infinite savior, the yogin, the goal of those who possess a goal, the best among the excellent;
the swan, the vital breath, Kapila, the one whose form is the universe, the eternal.
The knower of the field (kṣetrajña), primordial nature (prakṛti), time (kāla), the seed of the world, and even immortality—Mahādeva is the mother and the father; indeed, nothing exists apart from me.
Nārāyaṇa, the Person whose form is Yoga, the protector of the world and resplendent as the sun—
him the ascetics established in yoga behold.
Having known the Self, they go to immortality.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the upper division of the glorious Kūrma Purāṇa, in the compendium of sixty thousand verses.
The Tortoise said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed account of the secondary creation (pratisarga).
Listen, therefore, as I speak in brief about Prākṛta.
When two parārdhas have passed, Time, the destroyer of the world,
sets his mind upon reducing everything to ashes with the fire of time.
Having entered his own self within himself and become the god Maheśvara,
he would burn the entire cosmic egg, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Entering him, the Lord Mahādeva, the blue-and-red one (Nīlalohita),
assuming a terrifying form, effects the destruction of the world.
Having entered the solar mandala and divided himself manifold once more, he,
assuming the form of the seven-horsed sun, consumes the entire world.
Having burnt every being with the great Brahmaśiras weapon,
which consumes everything, he hurls it into the bodies of the gods.
When all the gods had been consumed by fire, the goddess, daughter of the mountain,
remained as the sole witness of Śambhu, like the Vedic revelation itself.
Adorned with a supreme garland made from the skull-bones of the gods,
he filled the circle of the sky with the hosts of the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies.
The god with a thousand eyes, the Lord of a thousand forms,
with a thousand hands and feet, a thousand rays, and mighty arms.
With a face made terrible by fangs and eyes like blazing fire,
bearing a trident and clad in an animal skin, he had resorted to the sovereign yoga.
Having himself drunk that abundant nectar of supreme bliss,
the Supreme Lord performs the tāṇḍava dance while gazing upon the Goddess.
Having drunk the nectar of her husband’s dance,
the most auspicious goddess enters the body of the trident-bearing god by means of yoga.
Having abandoned the passion for the Tandava dance by his own will, the Lord who wields the Pinaka bow,
having burnt the circle of the cosmic egg, returned to his nature as pure light.
Then, when the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the wielder of the Pināka (Śiva)—
have ceased their activity, the earth, through all its qualities, undergoes dissolution into the waters.
The fire, the carrier of oblations, swallows the essence of water along with its qualities;
then that fire, conjoined with its qualities, goes to dissolution within the wind.
The wind, which possesses qualities and sustains the universe, undergoes dissolution into space;
and likewise, space, together with its qualities, dissolves into the principle of the elements (bhūtādi).
All the sense organs go to dissolution within the Taijasa [ego],
and the hosts of gods, O best of beings, go to their dissolution within the Vaikārika [ego].
O virtuous ones, this threefold ego— consisting of the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi— dissolves into the Mahat.
Together with these, he shall withdraw the great Brahmā, who is possessed of exceeding splendor,
the unmanifest source of the world— the one and imperishable.
Having thus withdrawn the elements and the principles, Maheśvara separates Pradhāna and the Supreme Puruṣa from one another.
This dissolution of both Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, which are unborn, has been described;
it is produced by the will of Maheśvara, for there is no dissolution that occurs of its own accord.
The equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) is that unmanifest (avyakta), which is celebrated as primordial nature (prakṛti);
it is the primary cause (pradhāna), the womb of the world, the principle of illusion (māyātattva), and insentient.
The twenty-fifth principle, the immutable, conscious, and absolute Self,
is sung by the sages as the witness, the Great One, the Sole Grandfather.
Thus, the eternal power of Maheśvara, which effects withdrawal, burns everything from primordial matter (pradhāna) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa); so says the Śruti: "He is Rudra."
Furthermore, Śaṅkara brings about the ultimate dissolution here for all yogins whose minds are established in knowledge.
Thus this Lord Rudra, the self-controlled one, performs the act of withdrawal;
the Śruti declares that the power which establishes and deludes is Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, who consists of that [Prakṛti], being the twenty-fifth principle, creates the entire world— both manifest and unmanifest— from Prakṛti.
The powers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are omniscient, all-pervading, and tranquil; established in their own self alone, they bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
They are the lords of all, worthy of worship by all, and possessors of eternal and infinite enjoyments;
the single, imperishable reality consists of the Puruṣa, Pradhāna, Īśvara, and Ātman.
Furthermore, thousands of other divine powers reside there;
Śakra, Āditya, and the other immortals are worshipped with various sacrifices.
For each one, thousands and hundreds of bodies are indeed spoken of due to their majesty; yet the power is but one, devoid of qualities.
Applying each respective power, the Lord Maheśvara himself creates various bodies and even devours them as a mere sport.
"He is worshipped in all sacrifices by Brāhmaṇas who proclaim the Vedas;
Rudra is the bestower of all desires"—such is the Vedic revelation.
Of all powers whatsoever, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are traditionally remembered as the principal deities who are the powers of the Supreme Self.
The primordial Lord, the eternal Supreme Self,
is celebrated as Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, whose essence consists of all powers.
Some call him Agni, while others call him Nārāyaṇa; some call him Indra, others the Viśvedevas, and still others have sung of him as Brahmā.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, Varuṇa, all the gods, and likewise the ṛṣis—
these are proclaimed to be merely the manifestations of the one Rudra alone.
Whatever specific form they resort to when worshipping the Supreme Lord,
Śiva assumes that very form and bestows the fruit [of their action].
Therefore, even by resorting to one particular division [of the path], one who propitiates Mahādeva attains that supreme state which is eternal.
But one should indeed worship the god Mahādeva, the omnipotent and eternal,
the Lord of the Mountain, whether he be conceived as possessing attributes (saguṇa) or as being without attributes (nirguṇa).
Indeed, I have already taught you the yoga that is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
however, one who desires to ascend [the path] should worship the Supreme Lord with qualities (saguṇa).
"One should meditate upon the wielder of the Pināka bow, the three-eyed one, with matted hair, clad in animal skin,
seated upon a lotus throne, and possessing a golden luster— so says the Vedic revelation."
O best of sages, this yoga with seed (sabīja) has been fully described.
Therefore, having renounced all the gods led by Brahmā,
one should worship Virūpākṣa, who abides at the beginning, middle, and end.
Endowed with the yoga of devotion, devoted to his own duty, and pure,
he assumes such a form and attains ultimate auspiciousness.
This yoga with seed (sabīja) has been fully described for the sake of ultimate cultivation;
one who practices it according to the rules shall attain the state of the Lord.
If one is unable even in this, then one should worship Hara, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā;
O best of sages, if one is incapable even there,
then one should worship Vāyu, Agni, Śakra, and the others, endowed with devotion.
And whatever other pure meditations have been previously mentioned by you here,
as well as the yoga described— both that which is seedless and that which possesses a seed.

That knowledge was previously described by me to you as being seedless (*nirbīja*). However, a wise person, devoted to that [knowledge] and with senses restrained, should meditate upon Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Virañci as having seeds (*sabīja*), as well as the gods beginning with Agni.
One should worship the Person Viṣṇu, Hari who bears four forms,
the god Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end and eternal.
Nārāyaṇa is the source of the world, the ether, the supreme state. One who constantly bears His mark, is devoted to Him, and takes refuge in Him—
this very rule is considered appropriate for the Brāhma meditation and its immediate proximity.
This supreme knowledge, which relies upon meditative cultivation, has been told;
it is that which was previously related by me to the sage Indradyumna.
This entire world, both conscious and unconscious, has the Unmanifest as its very essence;
He is the Lord, the Supreme Brahman, and therefore the world consists of Brahman.
Sūta said:
Having spoken this much, the Blessed Janārdana became silent;
the sages, together with Śakra, praised Mādhava Viṣṇu.
The sages said:
Salutations to you, Viṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise, the Supreme Self;
salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, the Universe, Vāsudeva.
Homage, homage to you, Kṛṣṇa; homage, homage to Govinda.
Homage to you, Mādhava, and homage to the Lord of Sacrifice.
Salutations to you who possess a thousand heads; salutations to you who possess a thousand eyes.
Salutations to the one with a thousand hands and to the one with a thousand feet.
Oṃ, homage to the one whose form is knowledge, whose nature is the supreme self;
homage to you, the blissful one, and homage to you who have transcended Māyā.
Homage to you whose body is hidden; homage be to you, the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Homage to the Ancient Person (puruṣa), whose essential nature is pure existence alone.
Salutations to Sāṃkhya, salutations to Yoga, and salutations be to you who are absolute;
salutations again and again to the partless one, who is to be realized through the knowledge of Dharma.
Homage be to the principle of space, and to the Great Lord of Yoga;
homage to You, the source of all higher and lower beings, who are to be known through the Vedas.
Homage to the Buddha, the pure one; homage to the disciplined one, the cause.
Homage, homage, salutation to you, the master of illusion, the piercer; homage!
Homage be to you, the Boar; homage to you, the Man-Lion.
Homage to you, the Dwarf; homage to you, Hṛṣīkeśa.
Salutation be to Kālarudra; salutation to you who possess the form of Time;
and salutation to the giver of heaven and liberation, whose self is unimpeded.
Homage to you, who are attainable through yoga, the yogin, the bestower of yoga;
to you, the Lord of the gods, the pacifier of the afflictions of the gods.
O Blessed One, through your grace, we have acquired that knowledge which destroys all saṃsāra and by knowing which one attains immortality.
Various dharmas have been heard, as well as the lineages and the Manvantaras;
the primary creation, the secondary creation, and the detailed expansion of this Brahman.
For you are the witness of the entire world, the universal Nārāyaṇa, the supreme;
O Infinite-Souled One, it behoves you alone to protect us—you are our refuge and our goal.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, I have thus related to you this entire Kūrma Purāṇa, which bestows yoga and liberation, as it was spoken by Gadādhara.
In this Purāṇa, the ancient origin of Lakṣmī is told,
along with her union with Vāsudeva for the purpose of deluding all living beings.
The creation of the Prajāpatis, the duties of the social classes, their modes of livelihood,
and the auspicious characteristics of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, exactly as they are.
The identity, the distinction, and the specific attributes of the Grandfather (Brahmā), Viṣṇu, and the wise Maheśa have been described.
The characteristics of devotees have been declared, as well as their auspicious conduct;
and the characteristics of those belonging to the various classes and stages of life have been described here exactly as they are.
O best of sages, following that, the primary creation, the sevenfold enclosure of the cosmic egg, and the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha have been described.
The exposition on the enumeration of time and the majesty of the Lord,
as well as the reclining of Brahmā upon the waters and the etymological derivation of his name.

Furthermore, the lifting up of the earth once again by means of the boar-form, the narration of the primary creation beginning with the mukhya-sarga, and likewise the other, the muni-sarga; KūrmP 2,44.75.
The creation of Rudra and the ascetic creation of the sages have been explained; and the creation of progeny by Dharma from the tamasic principle has already been described previously.
There shall be a dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the entry [of Viṣṇu] into the interior of the body,
the birth of the Lord from a lotus, and the delusion of that wise one.
The vision of Maheśa and the majesty of Viṣṇu as proclaimed by him,
as well as the bestowing of divine sight upon Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
There was an encounter with Brahmā, the supreme lord, of the God of gods;
and likewise, there was the grace of Giriśa as well as the granting of boons.
The conversation between the high-souled Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu,
as well as the granting of boons and the subsequent disappearance of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
O Brahmins, the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha was told in ancient times,
as well as the descent of the Lord from the lotus-navel of Brahmā.
Then the oneness of the Lord with Viṣṇu was declared;
thereafter came the delusion of Brahmā, and then the recovery of consciousness by Hari.
The performance of ascetic penance by the wise God of gods has been described;
thereafter, the manifestation of Maheśa from his forehead was recounted.
The creation of the Rudras has been told, as well as the prohibition by Brahmā,
the prosperity of the God of gods, and the two [episodes] concerning the granting of boons and the instructions.
The disappearance of Rudra, the performance of penance by the egg-born one,
the vision of the God of gods, and his assuming the form of Nara and Nārī.
The narration of the Goddess’s division [of her power] was told by the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
and after that, it was further told how she became the daughter of Dakṣa.
The daughterhood of the Goddess to Himavat, her very majesty,
the vision of her divine form, and the vision of her universal form (vaiśvarūpa).
The thousand names were recited by Himavat himself, his father;
likewise, there was the instruction of the Great Goddess and the granting of boons.
The creation of progeny by Bhṛgu and others, the detailed account of the lineage of kings,
Dakṣa’s attainment of the state of Pracetas, and the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
O best of sages, the dispute between Dadhīca and Dakṣa was then related,
and following that, the curse upon the sages was recounted.
The departure of Rudra, the grace of the wielder of the Pināka bow, his disappearance,
and the instruction of the Grandfather are proclaimed for the sake of protection.
The creation of progeny by Dakṣa and the high-souled Kaśyapa;
the destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu as well as the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Then the curse was pronounced upon the inhabitants of the Devadāru forest,
followed by the subjugation of Andhaka and his attainment of the unsurpassed status of a Gaṇapati.
Then follows the subduing of Prahrāda and the imprisonment of Bali;
then the subjugation of Bāṇa and the grace shown by the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
The expansion of the lineages of the ṛṣis and the genealogies of the kings have been proclaimed;
thereafter follows the birth of Viṣṇu from Vasudeva, the manifestation of Hari by his own will.
And [it describes] the vision of Upamanyu, his very practice of austerity,
and the obtaining of boons upon seeing Mahādeva, who is accompanied by Ambā and possesses three eyes.
Then follows the journey to Kailāsa and the residence there of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
thereafter, the fear of the inhabitants of Dvāravatī is narrated.
Then there is the protection by Garuḍa after defeating the mighty enemies,
as well as Nārada’s arrival and the departure of Garuḍa.
Then follows the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, and thereafter the arrival of the sages;
likewise, the daily worship of Vāsudeva and the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
Thereafter, the question of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya was declared,
concerning the purpose of worshipping the Liṅga, as well as the nature of the Liṅga and its possessor (the Liṅgin).
O best of sages, the declaration of his true nature and the manifestation of his marks were likewise proclaimed between Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Delusion regarding those two is said to be wandering both upwards and downwards;
[the remedy for this is] devotion to the God of gods and the grace of the Supreme Lord.
O best of the twice-born, the disappearance of the Liṅga, the subsequent birth of Sāmba, and the manifestation of Aniruddha have been proclaimed.
The intention for Kṛṣṇa’s departure, the arrival of the sages,
and the granting of boons by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa as he was being sent away.
The departure of Kṛṣṇa, the vision of Pārtha,
and the eternal dharmas of the ages as spoken by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Then follows the favor shown to Pārtha and his journey to Vārāṇasī,
as well as [the account] of the sage Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, whose deeds are marvelous.
The majesty of Vāraṇasī and a description of the sacred fords (tīrthas),
the pilgrimage of Vyāsa, and then the vision of the Goddess; furthermore,
the departure [of the deity] and the granting of boons have been narrated.
O Brahmins, [this section contains] the majesty of Prayāga, the glorification of sacred fields,
the abundant fruit [of visiting them], and the departure of Mārkaṇḍeya.
The true nature of the worlds and the arrangement of the luminaries are described, as well as the regions and the definitive account of the rivers.
The description of the mountains and the abodes of the celestial dwellers,
the division of the continents, and the detailed account of Śvetadvīpa.
Then the reclining of Keśava, the majesty of the Great-Souled One,
the narration of the Manvantaras, and indeed the majesty of Viṣṇu.
Then, O best of sages, follows the account of the compilation of the Vedic branches by the Vyāsas,
and the description of how that which was not originally a Veda became the Vedas.
There are also discourses on the lords of yoga (yogeśvaras) and the glorification of their disciples;
furthermore, various secret songs of the Lord have been proclaimed.
Then follow the practices of the castes and stages of life, the rules for expiation,
and Rudra’s state as a skull-bearer as well as his wandering for alms.
O twice-born ones, the narrative of the devoted wife and the determination regarding the sacred fords are told,
as well as the subduing of Maṅkaṇaka.
O Brahmins, the slaughter of Kāla has been described in brief,
as well as the entry of Śambhu and Mādhava into the Devadāru forest.
The vision of the wise God of gods belonging to the six families,
and the granting of a boon by the Lord to Nandin, have been proclaimed.
Thereafter, the occasional dissolution (naimittika-pratisarga) is described;
following that, the primordial dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya), as well as the dissolution with seed (sabīja) and yoga itself.
Having understood this, whoever recites the summary of the Purāṇa shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus and taking the goddess Śrī with him, Puruṣottama abandoned his tortoise-form and returned to his own abode.
O twice-born ones, all the gods and sages, having bowed to the Puruṣa Viṣṇu and taken hold of the nectar, returned to their own abodes.
This supreme Purāṇa was spoken in the past by Viṣṇu himself, the source of the universe, who assumed the form of a tortoise for the sake of the gods and others.
The mortal who constantly recites this with self-restraint and a concentrated mind,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
And listen now to the merit of that man of firm vows who, having written it down, gives it to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas during the month of Vaiśākha.
Completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers,
he shall enjoy vast, divine, and most beautiful pleasures in heaven.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he is born into a family of Brahmins;
by the power of his former impressions, he shall attain the knowledge of Brahman.
By reciting even a single chapter, one is liberated from all sins;
he who reflects thoroughly upon its meaning attains the supreme state.
This should be studied constantly by Brahmins on every sacred festival day (parvan),
and it should be heard, O best of the twice-born, for it destroys even the greatest sins.
On one side are all the Purāṇas together with the Itihāsas in their entirety;
on the other side is this supreme [work], which indeed excels them.
For those who desire skill in the Dharma and those who desire skill in knowledge,
there is no other supreme means than this one Purāṇa.
O you of excellent vows, just as the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa Hari, is described here as Viṣṇu, so is he not described in other [scriptures].
This Purāṇic compendium is sacred to Brahmā and is the destroyer of sins;
for herein that supreme Brahman is indeed proclaimed according to its true nature.
It is the supreme holy site among holy sites, the supreme austerity among austerities,
the supreme knowledge among knowledges, and the supreme vow among vows.
This scripture must not be studied in the presence of a *vṛṣala*;
for he who studies it out of delusion goes to many hells. (Kūrma Purāṇa 2.44.134)
In a śrāddha rite or in a rite dedicated to the gods, the Śrāvaṇīya hymn should be recited by the twice-born;
especially at the conclusion of a sacrifice, it is the purifier of all defects.
This scripture, which expands upon the meaning of the Vedas, should especially be studied by those seeking liberation; it should be heard and reflected upon as well.
Having understood this correctly, O best of Brahmins, one should cause those endowed with devotion to hear it;
thus liberated from all sins, one shall attain union with Brahman.
He who gives to a man lacking faith and likewise to one who is unrighteous,
having gone to the hells after death, descends into the womb of a dog.
Having paid homage to Hari Viṣṇu, the eternal source of the universe,
as well as to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, this scripture is to be studied.
Such is the command of Viṣṇu, the god of gods and of immeasurable splendor,
and of the great-souled Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and a brahmin seer.
Having heard this divine [teaching] from Nārāyaṇa, the venerable sage Nārada gave it first to Gautama, and from him Parāśara received it.
The venerable Parāśara also, O lords of sages, at Gaṅgādvāra,
recounted [this] to the sages, bestowing dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
In the past, Brahmā related this [teaching], which destroys all sins, to the wise Sanaka and likewise to Sanatkumāra.
From Sanaka, the blessed Devala, the greatest knower of yoga, received this supreme [teaching];
from Devala, Pañcaśikha obtained it.
In ancient times, the venerable sage Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, received from Sanatkumāra the supreme Purāṇa, which contains the collection of all meanings.
Therefore, having heard from Vyāsa this [account] which destroys the sins of you all, I have indeed spoken it;
and it must be given by you to righteous people.
Salutations to that preceptor Vyāsa, the omniscient great seer, the son of Parāśara, the peaceful one, whose self is Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to that Lord of the Gods, Viṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise, from whom the entire universe is born and into whom it is dissolved.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Upper Division of the *Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the compendium consisting of sixty thousand verses. The Upper Division is completed;
thus the *Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa* is finished.
